#9963. Training a coding model to paint watercolours with TRL and OpenEnv

On 23 August, Surya Narreddi posted a beautiful video of watercolours painted by a language model. The model writes JavaScript through p5.brush, a library that "adds natural drawing tools to p5.js". The video went viral fast, over 1.5M views at the time of writing.

The video came with a blog post explaining the training behind an earlier and narrower stage of the project, close-up flowers rather than the full compositions in the video, sadly without open artifacts yet. His site says a full technical report is coming, so ensure you follow him. The original idea is his, coming from the art and design side, where his skills are way beyond mine. My attempt is on the engineering side, reproducing the recipe in the open with every piece published.

Note: for the context behind the project, told by Surya himself, watch this video of his thesis.

In this article I try and reproduce his idea with TRL and OpenEnv. The reference pool dataset, the RL environment, the training scripts and the trained models, all open.

The whole pipeline runs on Hugging Face, end to end:

Once the two Spaces are up, the recipe is one command. Duplicate the environment and the scorer model, set two environment variables for the reward mix, and launch:

The rest of this article is the story of getting there, and every piece is in the repo.

I have followed the original blog step by step, and only changed something when strictly needed. Every idea of my own went into a list instead of into the experiment, and that list became "What I would try next" at the end, next to the full list of published artifacts. If you have already read his post, the framing and the reward design will be familiar. The new material is the open implementation, the hand-rated pool, and three reward mixes trained and compared, and it starts at The RL environment you need to build.

The paintings look loose, imperfect, handmade, at a moment when image models produce perfect (statistically average) pictures. My guess is that this contrast is a big part of why the video went viral. It reminded me of the early days of generative AI art, when the point was to explore the medium. DeepDream (2015) was a debugging tool that people turned into art, works like Edmond de Belamy (2018) came from artists probing what a GAN could do, and artists like Mario Klingemann spent those years making dreamy portraits with neural networks.

This project feels closer to those early days. In his thesis, Surya describes the path that led here. He started by prompting text-to-image models, where the prompt is the only lever you can pull, and more detail buys more control only up to a point. Training the model itself goes further. The other half of the idea is the medium. The model writes a program of about 150 lines of JavaScript that paints the image. That model output is code. You can read it, edit it and run it again, and the decision behind each brushstroke is visible. And the style comes from a restriction where the model is only allowed ten of the library's methods. More on that below.

In that same period, Anna Ridler photographed thousands of tulips, hand-labelled every one, exhibited the dataset itself as the artwork, and later trained a model on it. I found her work through the references AI agents brought back while building this project and loved it because this project does something very similar by curating a set of images by hand, and then training against them.

Most of the recent RL work on language models uses rewards you can verify. For example, math problems with a known answer, code that passes tests, or graders that are right or wrong and cheap to run. This project is closer to the older exception, RLHF, where the model learns a reward model from human preferences.

Here the reward is aesthetic preference. There is no correct answer. The real question of the project is whether you can do RL over taste.

The reward, as his blog defines it and as the RL environment I built implements it:

HPSv3 is an open 7B preference model. Give it an image and a text description, and it returns a score for how much a person would prefer that image. It was trained on a large set of human choices between pairs of images, so its score is an average of many people's taste. The pairwise judge is Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct, a general vision model called through HF Inference Providers. The pairwise judge sees the candidate painting next to four references randomly selected from the pool, guided by a written description of what to weigh (bleeds, translucent washes, soft edges), each comparison in both presentation orders, and its score is the share of comparisons the candidate wins. Its only standard is the pool, so its score is my taste, as encoded in those ratings.

Those are the weights Narreddi converged on. The pool defines taste here. That moves the work from tuning hyperparameters to building the set that decides what is beautiful.

I trained three runs with this reward. They differ only in how the weight splits between the two model judges:

I started with hps-only to validate that the pipeline could learn at all. Once the reward was going up and the metrics were healthy, there was no reason to run it longer, so I launched the two longer runs instead. The question that the longer runs ask is how much of HPSv3's power can you hand to the pairwise judge? The more weight the judge carries, the more the reward means my taste instead of everyone's, and the harder it should be to climb. Incidentally, if you push it far enough or your style is too far from the average, the model could stop entirely.

Fortunately, it did not stop and both runs with the pairwise judge on learned too. The hand-rated pool can steer the policy, at least as far as the metrics and the final paintings show. The numbers are below.

Disclaimer. If we use a frontier model, it can already generate the JavaScript code that paints watercolour from a prompt. That's the starting point. The work here is about teaching a smaller model to do it combined with a person's own artistic preferences.

The environment wraps everything that sits between the model and the reward, including the JavaScript library that the model uses for painting, the system prompt that restricts it, the headless Chromium that renders each sketch, and the gate that rejects cheats.

The library does more of the work than it seems. p5.brush, by @acamposuribe, simulates a medium rather than drawing shapes: pigment bleeds past the edges of a fill, paper has texture, strokes have mass, flow fields drag brushwork around. When the model calls brush.fillBleed(0.25) it is deciding how far the ink runs.

Note. The author of p5.brush had been trying to teach a machine to paint long before any of this. In 2022 he made a generative art series that hides a diary about teaching p5.js to draw like a child: "It is barely able to use the crayons [...] It cannot follow simple commands. I'm done for today, very infuriating." The series was meant to have three pieces, and he made two. When Surya's video went viral, he quoted it, sharing that diary and saying this work is the third piece arriving on its own.

p5.brush exposes 47 methods. The prompt allows 10: scaleBrushes, noStroke, fill, noFill, fillBleed, fillTexture, beginShape, vertex, endShape and circle. What the other thirty-seven add, lines, hatching, custom brushes, would break the watercolour look. With these ten the model can only paint filled shapes, and the library adds the bleed to every one of them.

His blog post saved me a lot of time I could have wasted iterating on the prompt. A long API reference makes the model invent methods that do not exist, and his 200 GEPA iterations converged on a strict allowlist with no documentation. I saw the same failures and wrote the allowlist by hand. My only addition to that recipe is one sentence: paint each petal two or three times, a big pass first and a smaller, more opaque one inside it. This small change made my outputs a lot more colorful.

Note. If it's the first time you hear about GEPA, it is an automatic prompt optimizer. A language model reflects in plain words on where the current prompt failed and proposes a better one, and the loop repeats.

The gate is the final piece. The sketch has to compile, use the library instead of direct p5 calls, put real pigment on the canvas, and not try to trick the scorer, for example by writing text on the canvas.

The pool consists of 178 paintings divided into two tiers based on my personal preferences, love and okay. All of them are actually generated by a model. Four open-weight models, called through Inference Providers, wrote p5.brush sketches, each one working from a real, openly licensed photo of a hibiscus from iNaturalist. A vision model gave written feedback on every sketch, over three refinement iterations. Every final render was then rated one at a time, by me, and 178 made the cut.

Here I chose four different families of models to test their different styles. These four were the open models that produced a valid sketch every time in a quick reliability check, and two other candidates were dropped for failing it. If you want to produce your own pool, you might choose others.

The tiers do real work in the reward. When the pairwise judge draws four references, half come from love and half from okay, so the policy always faces some rivals it can sometimes beat, and a win pays the same against either tier. This is one of my few deliberate changes: the original compares against its top tier only, and I kept the easier tier in the draw so a weak early policy still gets signal.

No human-made painting is in there, which is a real limitation. p5.brush is a niche library, and the human work that exists in it with accessible code is a handful of pieces, nowhere near what a training corpus would need, as his blog also notes.

The interesting idea here, as I've already discussed previously, is that the model will learn to imitate what the pool contains. If we point the environment at a different dataset, the reward would automatically change without touching a single line of code. For the dataset I generated and openly share, I also include the source sketch.

If we look closer at the judges, the two of them answer different questions. HPSv3 decides whether it is a flower, and the pairwise judge decides whether it is well painted in the style I chose.

Before anything worked, there was a long stretch of flat reward curves. If you've tried to reproduce a research paper/blog without open artifacts, you probably can relate. Every run tested what I thought was a reasonable theory about what was wrong. A run takes a lot of time, so I queued the next one while still going through the last one's results. As always, starting from something easier that works and then building on top of that was the answer. A simple control task, with no browser and no judges, was the first attempt that learned, and the reason was that my learning rate was just too low.

Another change that cost me time to find was adjusting the LoRA parameters correctly. The usual target_modules list assumes a dense model, and Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B is a mixture of experts that names most of its projections differently, so the adapter was training ten layers out of forty. I solved this by changing it to all-linear, which reaches every linear layer. The routed experts in this architecture are fused tensors that even all-linear leaves frozen, but everything else gets an adapter, and that was enough to learn.

The fix was four changes in TRL's GRPOTrainer:

These four changes unlocked the first successful run (hps-only), with the reward clearly improving.

With that configuration, all three runs learn. Both judge runs were launched for 200 steps and stopped at 110, with the reward still climbing slowly. A step takes fifteen to eighteen minutes, and the comparison between mixes was already stable, so I stopped both to save compute. Mean group reward over the first and final third of each run:

The three curves line up with how much weight my taste carries. The more the judge weighs, the lower the start and the noisier the climb. judge-led spent its first thirty steps nearly flat before it moved. It is the same move that solved the debugging. Shrink the problem until something learns, then add the hard parts back one at a time.

The pairwise judge term itself climbed in the two runs that used it. The model wins more comparisons against the pool as training advances, which is the claim hps-only could not make. No group in any run collapsed to identical rewards, the GRPO failure mode that kills the gradient. For the curious, the per-metric curves (HPSv3, paint coverage, entropy) are in the repository as CSV.

The full launch command, the hardware and the two environment variables that turn this into the other two runs are in the recipe.

In every run, the first thing the model learned was to stop producing bad paintings, the near-blank canvases and shapeless washes that score under 0.3 in total reward. In hps-only, three quarters of the rise in the group mean comes from bad paintings becoming rare. In the judge runs the collapse is even steeper: rollouts under 0.3 fall from 99 to 16 across judge-led's thirds, and from 37 to 4 in hps-led.

This is why the obvious visual, the best painting of each step, shows almost no difference in hps-only. It moves +0.034 across the run while the median moves +0.155. The learning is visible in the middle of the distribution.

What the pairwise judge changes is the top. In hps-only, paintings got more reliable without getting better. The quality of the good ones added just +0.03 to the group mean, and once HPSv3 saw petals around a centre and a stem, it stopped asking for more pigment. With the judge on, the other half of the story appears. Better here means closer to the pool, so closer to what I rated as "good" or something I liked more. That added +0.12 in judge-led and +0.16 in hps-led, the best of each step rose too, and paint coverage doubled in both runs (0.11 to 0.23, and 0.13 to 0.30) where hps-only barely moved it. With a reference left to beat, a good painting can still get better, and the model starts being rewarded for using more pigment.

One more finding. The model ignores an explicit instruction, and it is right to. The system prompt asks for fifteen to thirty filled shapes. If we look at the real mean, it is between 7 and 9, and n_shapes barely correlates with reward in any run (+0.000, −0.14, +0.07). The policy is not rewarded for obeying that sentence, so it does not obey it.

There is also a ceiling on the hps-only route. If every rollout matched its good ones, that run's mean would sit at 0.771. Whether more steps would break it is an open question.

The paintings also show something that the tables miss. Within each run, they all look similar. As training advances, the rewards inside each group get closer together, and the median paintings in the opening video look like takes of the same flower. That is GRPO doing what it is designed to do with a pool built from one subject. The pool decides what counts as variety, the same way it decides what counts as quality. If the reward only pays for matching one flower, the model learns to paint that one flower. More diverse output would need a more diverse pool, and building one is more curation work. Surya's newer compositions are an example of this. Alex Yango's animal paintings are the same recipe with different choices in the pool. This is the biggest difference between an aesthetic reward and a maths grader. Behind the number there is a very human job, deciding what belongs in the reward set. Jason Liu's essay on taste says the general version in one line. AI shifted the bottleneck from making to noticing.

Surya closes his blog with some of his favourites. Instead of picking mine, below is a wall with the 178 paintings the reward scored highest across the two judge runs, the same number the reference pool holds, in no particular order. Open it and pick your own.

To choose, you looked at many and kept a few, and that is exactly the job that built the reward of this project. Every painting of every run, with its sketch and its reward, is in the rollouts datasets, and browsable in this gallery.

Since the reward was partly based on my taste, it is fair to close with my verdict as a viewer. To my eye, judge-led is the run that ends up the most diverse and the most artistically interesting. hps-led paints convincing watercolours, but its best ones share a soft, wet-on-wet look that is almost a style of its own. hps-only converges the hardest, and most of its paintings settle on the same colours. You can judge for yourself in the gallery, which has every painting of every run, sortable by step and by reward.

This project is mostly infra. A run needs a trainer, two Spaces, an inference router and a websocket to stay healthy for hours straight, and every piece that fails quietly turns into a wrong number somewhere else. Half the work is checking that the number you read matches what actually happened.

Failures of the infrastructure were entering the reward as zeros. A render that timed out or a scorer that did not answer scored the same as a bad painting, 0.0 inside the group. Across all my runs that was about 1.5% of rollouts, and in the worst run it reached 5.2%. That trains the model on noise, so those paths now return None and the rollout is excluded from the group.

I also found a bug in OpenEnv, and sent the fix upstream. The client keeps one persistent websocket, and a socket closed by the far end stayed cached, so every later call failed even though the environment was healthy. It cost me two half-finished runs to find it. The fix is submitted upstream, and the runs launched with it have been running clean since.

The reward of a step depends on which references it drew. The pairwise judge samples four references per step, so every step faces a different set of rivals, and some draws are simply harder. GRPO itself is mostly safe, because advantages are computed inside the group and a hard draw moves the whole group together. The curve I was reading was not safe, and some of what looked like a bad step was just a hard draw. The image above is one example. Step 12 scored half a point below step 11 mostly because it drew the hardest references of the run, while the paintings themselves look close.

Rounded numbers, and only for the runs that finished.

A step is eight rollouts and takes fifteen to eighteen minutes, of which 70 to 80% is rendering. A single render takes 69 to 96 seconds against a 90 second deadline. Part of that is expected, the Space has no GPU, so Chromium renders the WEBGL canvas in software and p5.brush's bleeds and textures are heavy pixel work. Even so, I expected it to be faster, and I have not found the full cause.

A scorer can cost more than the training that uses it: HPSv3 has to be up for the whole run, so pause the Space, or set its sleep timer, when the run ends.

Everything runs on HF Jobs, with the environment as a Docker Space and metrics in trackio.

The rule of this project was to reproduce the recipe with every resource open, not to improve it, so a list of untried ideas piled up along the way. These are the ones I would actually try, in order of how much evidence there is.

Multi-step, and letting the model see what it paints. This is the first thing I would try. The original blog trains single turn, so I trained single turn, and in this setup the model paints with its eyes closed. No image ever goes in, and the only feedback it gets is one number. The evidence that a feedback loop works is the pool itself. The reference paintings came from models iterating three rounds under a vision critic, and the later rounds are better. The material that defines the reward was made with a loop the policy never gets.

Smaller models. There is evidence that 35B is more than needed. In my side experiments a 4B already wrote valid sketches that passed the gate. If a 4B can learn this, the cost of the experiment drops by an order of magnitude.

Other ideas on the list are SFT on the pool sources before starting RL, rewarding pigment explicitly, moving the judge's reference mix from easy to hard as the run advances until only love remains, widening the ten-method allowlist for more visual range (my attempts on this crashed more sketches and broke the watercolour look), and checking how consistent the pairwise judge really is by scoring the same image twice.

And the method is not specific to flowers. Alex Yango painted animals with the same mechanism, and Brendan Hogan trained canvas animations against a pool of hand-rated clips. I had also played with something similar before using Simon Willison's pelican benchmark, where code is rendered to an image and scored.

And underneath all of it sits the question this project cannot close. 178 paintings made by models define what this trained model considers beautiful. The pool is the bottleneck, and it is the part of the pipeline with no principled answer.

For anyone reproducing this, there are two deliberate divergences from Narreddi's recipe, both argued earlier in the article:

The rest, all-linear for the LoRA, infrastructure failures returning None instead of 0.0, stopping the judge runs at step 110, are decisions I had to make along the way because his blog does not specify them. His implementation is not published, so I cannot tell whether they match his choices or diverge from them.

The per-rollout numbers in this article can be recomputed from the published datasets. Nothing here depends on any Space staying switched on.

The method and original idea are Surya Narreddi's. The library is Alejandro Campos Uribe's.

#9962. Lego marketplace BrickLink in pieces after 'unusual activity' takes it offline for almost a week

Lego fans demand answers as outage approaches a week with no confirmed cause

Lego-owned marketplace BrickLink has been offline for almost a week after identifying "unusual activity on the platform," leaving fans unable to buy and sell spare bricks and minifigures.

The company initially described the outage as "necessary work" and said the site would return on November 9. That deadline has come and gone.

Visiting BrickLink's domain automatically serves the platform's maintenance page, which was last updated on November 11.

"We took BrickLink offline after identifying unusual activity on the platform," the website states. "Our immediate priority was to secure the site, protect our members and ensure the integrity of BrickLink.

"Before bringing the site back online, we need to fully understand what has happened. That means containing the issue, investigating how it happened and checking for related issues.

"This work is still ongoing and we appreciate your patience while we work to get things back online as soon as possible."

The references to security, containment, and investigation suggest something beyond routine maintenance, although BrickLink has not confirmed whether it suffered a cyberattack. The Register asked Lego for more information, but it did not immediately respond.

Some adult fans of Lego (AFOL) have criticized the lack of information since the outage began on Friday, November 6.

"Imagine how much better this would have been received if they were transparent from day one instead of pretending they have control over something they clearly don't," said one disgruntled Legohead via Reddit.

"They don't even need to say what went wrong," said another. "Just an email acknowledging the issue would be appropriate. The entire site is down, and has been for days. That warrants more than a splash page."

BrickLink was launched by Dan Jezek in June 2000 as an independent marketplace for enthusiasts to buy and sell Lego sets and individual pieces, including discontinued parts and rare minifigures.

The Lego Group acquired BrickLink and Sohobricks from investment outfit NXMH in 2019 for an undisclosed sum. NXMH had bought BrickLink in 2013 and also owned Sohobricks, a South Korean manufacturer of unofficial but Lego-compatible bricks. Lego shuttered Sohobricks in 2020.

At the time of Lego's acquisition, BrickLink had more than 10,000 storefronts on its marketplace selling Lego sets, parts, and minifigures.

The AFOL community was initially concerned about Big Brick's intention with the acquisition, fearing that it would lead to high prices closer to those on Lego's own Pick a Brick parts-ordering service.

For now, buyers and sellers would probably settle for a marketplace that's actually online. ®

#9961. Behind the Scenes of How Operation Blackout Went Down

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

A recent law enforcement operation to dismantle harmful scam centers was a big success. A threat intelligence expert walks us through what happened and why he wants more of the same.

Pushes for public-private partnerships to address escalating cyber threats have been on the industry's radar for years. Collaboration has been a focal point in cybersecurity conference panels and government initiatives. Calls for more information-sharing and analysis centers have been persistent.

As director of preemptive cyberdefense at Silent Push, Michael Sweeney had a front-row seat to this kind of partnership when his company recently took part in "Operation Blackout," a coordinated international operation to take down criminal networks operating out of West Africa.

Operation Blackout coordinated efforts by the UK's National Crime Agency, the US Department of Justice (DoJ), the FBI, and private industry partners — including Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Silent Push — to disrupt criminal networks behind pig-butchering, romance, and cryptocurrency scams. The DoJ announced that the campaign resulted in dozens of arrests, the rescue of trafficking victims, and the removal of more than 3.7 million fake social media accounts.

Related:NIST: Solo Shouldn't Mean Less Secure

As the UK's main law enforcement agency, the National Crime Agency hosted Joint Disruption Week in London in early October to bring together the DoJ and the FBI with private industry partners to share real-time intelligence. In addition to US authorities and private industry partners, the Nigerian Joint Case Team on Cybercrimes, the Nigeria Police Force-National Cybercrime Center, and Ghanaian Cyber Security Authority also participated.

The Joint Disruption Week marked the first coordinated effort specifically focused on West Africa, according to the DoJ, which noted that global commitments are essential to dismantling the far-reaching scam centers.

The goal of these operations is to tackle scam activity at the global scale it has reached today, Sweeney explains. The more people who participate, the "better off we are," he says.

"The idea is not only to stop the current scams, but also to look across all of these different events," Sweeney tells Dark Reading. "[Industry and government are] all needed together in order to get this successfully taken down."

Data taken from scams reported through the FBI's Internet Complaint Center and the UK's National Cyber Security Centre formed the initial basis for Operation Blackout. From there, law enforcement compiled information, including the domains the scammers used and the infrastructure they set up to manipulate people for money.

Then the collaboration really began. Meta provided some of the data that helped drill down to specific regions — a surprising move, since social media platforms don't generally cooperate with law enforcement, despite threat actors abusing platforms to lure in victims. Several other organizations sent signals to further paint a picture of the attacker's intent and infrastructure.

Related:Incidents Move Too Fast for Pen & Paper

Silent Push's role involved providing 35,000 domains, creating more than 70 detection rules to trigger alerts when malicious activity occurs, and fingerprinting, Sweeney says. All of those are considered the "common choke points" that help researchers and authorities map the threat actors' network patterns.

Everything was analyzed, and the data augmented each other to provide the evidence authorities needed to take down the scammers, Sweeney says.

"Once you get everyone in the room with all the data, it becomes easier to see the big picture," he says. "From that, see where the attacks are coming from, the commonalities, and who is the most important person to take down in the operation, and where you want to go to get these people."

Sweeney attributes the success of Operation Blackout and other operations he has worked on over the years to how clear the mission was; everyone was on the same page about the goals and importance of data sharing, he says. Many of the legal or jurisdiction blockers that would otherwise prevent them from sharing information and hinder actual action were removed, including data-sharing agreements with users.

Related:Why CTF Competitions May Be More Important Than Ever

A number of providers were also involved, including Starlink. While each platform offers different services, they united in a shared stance. The camaraderie and energy that accompanied it were palpable, Sweeney says.

"We come together [to] say, 'If you're abusing our services, we're going to do everything we can to stop you, and we're going to pull in law enforcement,'" he says.

One thing Sweeney would like to change is the pace; he would like to see these partnerships move faster and conduct more operations as scammers drain billions from the US economy. Threat actors who exploit vulnerable populations and employ highly deceptive social engineering tactics are only improving faster with the help of artificial intelligence.

Sweeney says the people who just report a scam or who are too ashamed to come forward at all draw him to this work. They should know they aren't alone and that people are working hard to fight back, he adds.

"Everyone really wants to stop it, so pacing may be the only frustration," Sweeney says. "Let's do more. Hit them while they're down so that more people don't have that moment where they're having to figure out how to report a scam.”

Arielle spent the last decade working as a reporter, transitioning from human interest stories to covering all things cybersecurity related in 2020. Now, as a features writer for Dark Reading, she delves into the security problems enterprises face daily, providing context and actionable steps. She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.

She previously lived in Florida where she wrote for the Tampa Bay Times before returning to Boston where her cybersecurity career took off at TechTarget SearchSecurity. When she's not writing about cybersecurity, she pursues personal projects that include a mystery novel and poetry collection.

#9960. FreeBSD Status Report Third Quarter 2026

Here is the third 2026 status report, with 51 entries.

This report is published a bit later than the last few, but we are finally here! The main reason for the delay is the recent PHP vulnerabilities issue: https://reviews.freebsd.org had to be taken down for a little while, and unfortunately some reports were still being reviewed there. But the problem is now fixed and we are back on track. As this happened in October, do not expect to read about it in this status report however. This will be material for the last 2026 status report: do not miss it!

Lorenzo Salvadore, on behalf of Status Team

Entries from the various official and semi-official teams, as found in the Administration Page.

Contact: FreeBSD Core Team

The FreeBSD Core Team is the governing body of FreeBSD.

The handover from core.13 was completed: mail aliases, the LDAP group, and the Phabricator group now contain only core.14 members.

FreeBSD Foundation: bapt@ (with most of core@ participating in monthly Foundation meetings)

We reached consensus to publish our public meeting minutes, which were previously only sent to the developers mailing list.

bapt@ created a survey for FreeBSD developers on the use of AI and LLMs. He presented the results to core@, and a summary was shared with developers. 140 developers responded.

Policy: 88% want the Project to adopt a policy, either a formal, written policy (49%) or light guidance and best practices (39%). 6% said that AI should be explicitly discouraged, and 3% that the existing contribution rules are sufficient.

AI-assisted code: 35% said it must be disclosed, 25% that it must be reviewed more strictly than human code, 22% that it should be treated like any other contribution, and 16% that it should be rejected outright.

Safeguards: mandatory human review (78%) and mandatory disclosure (69%) were requested most often, followed by provenance or licensing documentation (47%) and mandatory testing (39%).

Disclosure: 84% want AI use disclosed, either always (48%) or when its involvement is significant (36%). 79% want AI-assisted commits marked in the commit log, and 56% prefer a tag that names the tool.

Concerns: the main concerns about quality are correctness and subtle bugs (39%), licensing and provenance (26%), and maintainability (21%). 75% are somewhat or very concerned about copyright and licensing.

Principles: accountability, meaning that a human remains responsible (91%), and transparency (78%) were selected most often, and preserving code quality was the top-ranked goal for a policy.

Other uses: 65% would allow AI-generated documentation with human review. 54% would allow AI tools on Project infrastructure, most of them with restrictions, and 29% would not.

The FreeBSD Foundation asked for a core representative on the committee for the upcoming user survey. jrm@ volunteered.

On 2026-07-20, a 150 MB binary file was mistakenly committed to the ports tree. The commit broke mirroring to GitHub, which rejects files larger than 100 MB, and added a file of questionable licensing to the repository history. On 2026-07-21, core@ decided to freeze the ports repository to limit the number of commits that would need to be rewritten, and worked out a plan with clusteradm@, portmgr@, and the Git administrators. kevans@ published a signed statement on 2026-07-22 to explain the freeze and to make clear that the ports tree had not been compromised. The offending commits were removed by rewriting the history of the main branch, and package builds from the old hashes were stopped. New server-side hooks now guard against a recurrence.

The FreeBSD Foundation asked core@ to recognize it as an open source steward. We settled on a statement of support, which was published on the announce and developers mailing lists.

We reviewed the draft announcement for 14.5-RELEASE and the proposed schedule for 15.2-RELEASE.

We dealt with conflicts between developers and external contributors. Decisions were communicated to the parties involved.

jrm@ committed a clarification of the commit bit policy.

We handled correspondence on a number of topics, including the current and future AI policy work and the impact of increased AI/bot-driven scraping on FreeBSD infrastructure.

We are defining the scope of a funded secretary role, which may serve the whole project rather than only core@. Examples from other non-profits and FreeBSD working groups are being used as a reference. There is rough consensus to move the role towards a project management assistant. A proposal was shared with the FreeBSD Foundation and feedback is pending.

imp@ created an AI working group made up of people with diverse opinions on the topic. The working group will use the developer survey results as input for a policy on the use of AI/LLMs. The kickoff meeting of the group will be held on October 7. Final reports are expected in Q4.

We are continuing the previous Core Teamâs work on staggered terms. We consider ourselves a transitional Core Team and plan to invoke the bylaws' staggering provision, with the change taking effect in 2027. Before the 2027 election, we will designate which members step down after one year and which serve a full two-year term; the vacated seats will be filled in that election.

Efforts are underway to modernize and centralize the FreeBSD Projectâs policy documentation, which is currently inconsistent, poorly visible, and reliant on unwritten "tribal knowledge." imp@ is working to consolidate existing guidelines, resolve policy contradictions between project groups, and formally record long-standing traditions. Additionally, this initiative will identify gaps where new, formal policies are needed to ensure smooth, efficient operations. We hope to have this wrapped up by the end of Q1 2027.

We are documenting the responsibilities of each liaison role and will publish the document once it is complete.

We are evaluating tooling to track our tasks, documents, and correspondence. We began using a CryptPad instance set up by bapt@ and clusteradm@.

We discussed writing down the Project norms for what content is reasonable for Project spaces, such as the wiki and repository metadata. Over the years, we have developed a tradition of avoiding politics, religion, and other contentious issues unrelated to the Project, and need to write it down and bring it in line with open source norms.

We are discussing the structure of portmgr@ and how to revamp the team.

adrian@ and some clusteradm@ members are preparing a budget, prioritizing work, improving documentation and processes, and planning to recruit new team members in 2027.

srcmgr@ has a new policy for returning developers, which asks for some recent work or plans before access is restored, and portmgr@ has something similar. We are discussing whether it makes sense for these policies to be aligned across teams.

Monthly meetings are scheduled through December 2026.

We are planning a short introduction and update followed by a question and answer session.

Contact: FreeBSD Release Engineering Team

The FreeBSD Release Engineering Team is responsible for setting and publishing release schedules for official project releases of FreeBSD, announcing code freezes and maintaining the respective branches, among other things.

The Team managed 14.5-RELEASE, leading to the official RELEASE build and announcement in September. Planning has started for the upcoming 15.2-RELEASE, which is due to arrive in December.

The Release Engineering Team continued providing weekly development snapshot builds for the main, stable/15, and stable/14 branches.

Links: Cluster Administration Team members URL: https://www.freebsd.org/administration/#t-clusteradm

Contact: Cluster Administration Team Contact: Philip Paeps

FreeBSD Cluster Administration Team members are responsible for managing the machines the Project relies on to synchronize its distributed work and communications.

In this quarter, the team has worked on the following:

Regular support for FreeBSD.org user accounts.

Regular disk and parts support (and replacement) for all physical hosts and mirrors.

Frequent interventions to thwart denial of service by bots.

Improvements to cgit on our global mirror network.

Work continues to refresh the software running on FreeBSD.org cluster machines. We have started putting production workloads on stable/15. As part of this work some workloads are being moved around to different machines. This work is ongoing at the end of the quarter.

The clusteradm team refreshes the production package builders (circa 35 physical machines) on a roughly six- to eight-week cadence. These machines run FreeBSD current snapshots.

Other machines are upgraded on an as-needed basis, keeping up with security fixes depending on how exposed they are.

At the time of this writing there are 143 physical machines in the cluster. We have 45 machines on current, 33 on stable/15 and 59 on stable/14.

Most of the remaining stable/13 installations will be upgraded to stable/15 or decommissioned.

Current locations are Australia, Brazil, Japan (two full mirror sites), Malaysia, South Africa, Sweden, Taiwan and United States of AmericaâââCalifornia, Chicago, New Jersey, and Washington.

Our mirror site in Taiwan is experiencing an extended outage. A new mirror site in Taiwan is being deployed at the beginning of 2026Q4.

One of our mirror sites in Japan will get a complete hardware refresh in 2026Q4.

The hardware and network connection have been generously provided by:

Cloud and SDN Laboratory at BroadBand Tower, Inc

Department of Computer Science, National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University

New official mirrors are always welcome. We have noted the benefits of hosting single mirrors at Internet Exchange Points globally, as evidenced by our existing mirrors in Australia, Brazil, and South Africa. If you are affiliated with or know of any organizations willing to sponsor a single mirror server, please contact us. We are particularly interested in locations in Europe.

See generic mirrored layout for full mirror site specs and tiny-mirror for a single mirror site.

In July a committer inadvertently pushed a large binary file to the ports repository, necessitating a freeze and subsequent rewrite of the history. The clusteradm team rewrote the history of the ports tree and ensured that the new history was visible on all our internal and external mirrors in the shortest possible time. Improvements were made to our Git infrastructure and automation to prevent this happening again.

The FreeBSD Projectâs infrastructure continues to be under constant attack from scrapers collecting training data for large language models ("AI"). The companies training these models have largely moved scraping operations from their ownâââeasy to identifyâââinfrastructure to botnets ("residential proxies"), making them difficult to block at the network edges without significant collateral damage. The Cluster Administration Team spent a considerable amount of time again this quarter mitigating these distributed denial of service attacks.

https://cgit.FreeBSD.org is a particularly popular target for trainers of probabilistic malware. We experience a constant torrent of scrapers running on infected computers and appliances all around the world. To spread the load of these attacks, the clusteradm team increased the number of cgit nodes on our mirrors. This quarter we deployed additional https://cgit.FreeBSD.org mirrors in California and in Paris.

Item #1 is the big priority, the Web Crawlers problem.

tl:dr; we know about it; we have spent a great deal of time analyzing it; since we know its cause, the symptoms are not particularly interesting; and this has been raised and acknowledged as a serious issue to/by core@. There is not much more that Bugmeisters themselves can do here.

Gluttons for punishment may wish to read: https://wiki.freebsd.org/MarkLinimon/Crawlers

Item #2 is generating a policy about LLM-derived contributions.

This depends on portmgr feedback which Mark Linimon requested quite some time ago.

The overview is that the contents of patches in the Bugzilla database is in much better shape than it was two years ago, and Mark continues to try to triage them weekly; but also that Mark keeps getting dragged away from working on this by other issues.

We still have not set up weekly conference calls or some other method of coordination. Without that, these issues tend to just remain stuck. We could definitely use help here.

In this quarter we slightly increased the Problem Report count. The throughput, however, is much higher, especially for ports. This may be due to the auto-notifier customizations we previously implemented.

For the src tree, in the last 90 days we have received 329 new Problem Reports and closed 269. For ports, the count was 2208 and 2138 respectively.

We do not currently maintain statistics about how many of these actually generate commits, although we do believe the number to be non-trivial.

Mark Linimon has taken on the long-term project of making sure that the submitted patches all apply. However, he does not claim to be a QA person and to be able to evaluate their aptness by himself. He is out of his depth here.

The general takeaway is that, with user education, we are getting better-quality Problem Reports this year. In particular, the ones with patches are being tested for applicability within a week or two of their arrival, and corrected if needed.

We have created many new Bugzilla accounts by user request. The number of new-account requests has increased this quarter. In Q3 2026 we added 164, which is not quite 2 per day.

Some annoying script permission problems on production were fixed. This re-enabled the weekly reports.

Base system version 14.3 was disabled for new bugs, and version 14.5-STABLE was created.

Contact: Pierre Pronchery

This is my second quarter in the FreeBSD Foundation as part of Alpha-Omegaâs Security Engineers In Residence (SEIRs) initiative. Thanks to the input received from the Security Team, I have integrated a staging instance of Forgejo with a self-hosted LLM, demonstrating the potential of new capabilities for the Security Team, without breaching any confidentiality requirements. This system is capable of dealing with incoming security vulnerability reports, by:

Drafting an initial response for the submitter

Issuing an immediate, automated analysis of the issue submitted

Preparing a template for an eventual Security Advisory (SA) or Errata Notice (EN)

Checking the SA or EN drafts for conformity

Automatically signing the final SA, EN, and corresponding assets

This is implemented like a typical, modern CI/CD system with Forgejoâs runner tool as a GitHub-compatible workflow. The aim is to leverage LLM capabilities for our processes, in accordance with the current workflow, without compromising on confidentiality nor on the necessity for quality review by us mortal members of the security team.

Significant polishing is still required, but the corresponding instance in production should be useful even without the LLM part. The automation of the more repetitive tasks of the workflow is expected to help us deal with the steady amount of incoming reports, and to extend capabilities from our individual minds into the team as a whole.

In parallel, I have not spared my efforts towards compliance with the European Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) for the FreeBSD Project. After importing pkgconf in FreeBSDâs base system during the last quarter, I went through a number of iterations for the framework generating Software Bill of Material (SBOM) artefacts during the build. Prepared together with Tuukka Pasanen, the framework is available for review in D56474 and I now believe it to be a serious candidate for integration. I would like to thank everyone who has been providing feedback already! This has helped tremendously to find a balance that feels more right than at any time earlierâââat least to me. A separate request for review for the meta-data is now available as well, D60352, which currently generates a total of 218 artefacts for an amd64 build. The balance consists of about one artefact per base package generated, as well as one artefact per library actually used during the build. This way, the complete chain of dependencies can be tracked, while keeping the granularity close to individual third-party projects or internal components.

I would also like to extend my thanks to Alice Sowerby and to Peter Hansteen for an awesome workshop about CRA compliance during EuroBSDCon 2026 in Brussels, this past September 2026. If you have missed it, you may be in luck, as we are gearing up to deliver it again at a future event. Do not hesitate to reach out to us if you are interested, together with your rough location and flexibility for travel, so we can have a more accurate impression of the times and places we should aim for.

Sponsor: Alpha-Omega, The FreeBSD Foundation

Links: Cyber Resilience Act Readiness URL: https://github.com/FreeBSDFoundation/all-projects/tree/main/Cyber%20Resilience%20Act%20Readiness

The Foundation is running a project through 2026 to actively prepare the FreeBSD Foundation, Project, and community for the EU Cyber Resilience Act. There are six main areas of focus: Security and Vulnerability Handling, SBOM Toolchain, Public Documentation, Community Legislative Engagement, Public Project Repository, and Communications.

Over Q3, the project has continued to move from planning into implementation, with particular focus on readiness for the CRAâs vulnerability and incident reporting requirements that came into force for manufacturers on September 11, 2026.

The Foundation has created a cyber security policy and CRA reporting protocol to support the Foundation in meeting its obligations as an open source software steward. Both have been developed with input from the FreeBSD Core and Security Teams and document how the Foundation will work with the Project and respond if CRA reporting obligations are triggered for the Foundation as a steward. Note that the European Commission has clarified that reporting obligations for stewards begin on December 11, 2027. These documents will remain internal resources for the time being.

Technical work on the Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) toolchain has continued through development, testing, and review. The proposed approach for generating SBOMs for the FreeBSD base system is being refined in response to feedback and still requires further review and supporting changes before integration. Work is also progressing across the wider SBOM ecosystem, both through the Foundation and in the community, including planned support for ports, SPDX-compatible license information, and CycloneDX and SPDX SBOM support in pkgconf.

Public CRA guidance is now available on the FreeBSD Foundation website, providing an overview of the legislation alongside dedicated guidance for FreeBSD business users and community members. This gives FreeBSD users clearer information about how the CRA may affect them, where their responsibilities may sit, and how to work with FreeBSD in meeting their CRA obligations.

The Foundation has continued to engage with the FreeBSD and wider open source communities, especially the Eclipse Foundationâs Open Regulatory Compliance (ORC) working group. At EuroBSDCon 2026, we collaborated with Peter Hansteen to run a day-long CRA and SBOM tutorial. We also presented an update on this project at the FreeBSD Developer Summit.

Project updates and meeting notes continue to be published through the public project repository. As we move into Q4, the focus will be on progressing the SBOM implementation and upstream work, improving the discoverability of our public CRA guidance, and working with the FreeBSD Project to identify key manufacturer needs that relate to their CRA obligation to adopt a secure software lifecycle by December 11, 2027.

The FreeBSD Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) effort has been continued during Q3 2026. At last, getting SBOM into FreeBSD source is manifesting itself and hopefully will be finalized in Q4. Thanks to Pierre Pronchery, there is a Phabricator review ongoing: D60352 for FreeBSD source. Also, ports have one for reviewing: D60441 made by Mathieu Arnold.

As an option for SBOM output, there are currently available SPDX 2.2 and Lite 3.0.1. CycloneDX SBOM tool is in work in progress and still needs some love to be as qualified as the output for SPDX. In the future, all SBOM outputs will be under one tool, which will be named sbomtool, and as both solutions rely on pkgconf, they will have CycloneDX when it lands in FreeBSD source.

Additionally, several new SPDX License Identifiers have been accepted. All three are in FreeBSD source: * BSD-2-Clause-pos-unchanged * BSD-Source-Code-no-disclaimer * BSD-Source-alt-GPL

There are several updates from BSD-2-Clause to BSD-Source-beginning-file in review:

sys/arm/arm/busdma_machdep.c: Correct SPDX-License-Identifier

sys/powerpc/powerpc/busdma_machdep.c: Correct SPDX-License-Identifier

sys/powerpc/powerpc/busdma_bounce.c: Correct SPDX-License-Identifier

sys/x86/x86/busdma_machdep.c: Correct SPDX-License-Identifier

sys/x86/x86/busdma_bounce.c: Correct SPDX-License-Identifier

sys/kern/subr_busdma_bounce.c: Correct SPDX-License-Identifier

Additionally, many third-party repositories have received SPDX License Identifiers, such as libxo (thanks to Juniper for that), and others. Some projects do not want headers, and some are still in active development.

Review Phabricator changes. SPDX License Identifier corrections are at a very low level to review.

When pkgconf CycloneDX is available, help review and test it.

Links: fts(3) manual page URL: https://man.freebsd.org/cgi/man.cgi?fts(3)

Contact: Jitendra Bhati Contact: Alan Somers

The fts(3) directory traversal library, used by find(1), rm(1), ls(1), chflags(1) and other utilities, historically relied on path-based syscalls that fail in capsicum(4) capability mode.

This quarter fts gained a new fts_openat() entry point that accepts a pre-opened directory descriptor, a per-entry fts_dirfd field, and a conversion of its internals to fd-relative operations, with ABI compatibility preserved through ELF symbol versioning. A traversal can now run entirely inside a Capsicum sandbox.

As a first consumer, chflags was capsicumized to perform its work through chflagsat() on descriptors opened before entering capability mode, confining it to the hierarchies named on its command line.

This work was completed as a Google Summer of Code 2026 project.

Contact: Hans Rosenfeld

Ongoing work on this project aims to integrate the existing proof-of-concept work into FreeBSD, and to add the following usability features:

a user-friendly configuration method to override individual bits, parts or even whole CPUID functions as needed, while keeping the rest of the host CPUID information or a pre-defined CPUID configuration

a user-friendly configuration method for the hypervisor signature reported by bhyve

a set of predefined CPUID configurations based on common x86 architecture levels, perhaps also including a set of CPUID data for a few real CPU models, and a user-friendly configuration method to choose one for a VM

There was a last minute change to the configuration syntax. Instead of using two different options cpuid.enable and cpuid.disable to enable or disable features by name, there is now a single cpuid.features option. This option accepts feature name, either prefixed with - to disable them, or prefixed with + or no prefix to enable a feature.

In addition to the abstract x86 architecture models, a number of CPU models have been implemented as pre-defined configuration file snippets. This currently ends with the Icelake generation for Intel and the Bulldozer generation for AMD.

Many more cpuid configuration options have been introduced to ease writing of CPU model configurations, such as cpuid.brand for the CPU Brand String or cpuid.vendor to override the vendor identification.

The constraints checks have been extended to allow defining bitmasks for values that can only be numerically lowered.

A new configuration option cpuid.check has been introduced to override the default action regarding the constraints checks. It takes the values fail (the default), warn, none, and fix.

Default cache configurations have been added to the x86 architecture models and all pre-defined CPU models.

A new cpuid.hypervisor option allows easy overriding of the hypervisor identification in CPUID function 0x40000000. The real hypervisor identification and feature flags can still be queried by guests from CPUID function 0x40000100.

Update manpages bhyve(8), bhyve_config(5), and bhyvectl(8).

Get the whole wad reviewed and committed into FreeBSD.

Contact: JosÃ© Alonso CÃ¡rdenas MÃ¡rquez

Bhyvemgr is a bhyve management GUI written in Freepascal/Lazarus on FreeBSD. It needs a bunch of tools, mostly installed on base system, and some installed from ports/packages. The main goal is to be a desktop application with focus on desktop users to easily and quickly setup and run virtual machines on FreeBSD hosts.

Starting with version v2.0.0, bhyvemgr was migrated to client/server architecture. As a result, a server component was developed. This new component is called bhyvemgrd.

Bhvemgrd supports two ways to run privileged tasks: mac_do/mdo (FreeBSD >= 140000) and mac_do/setcred/exec_paths (only for FreeBSD >= 1501501). The process itself run under an unprivileged bhyvemgrd user.

During last two quarters, there were many bugfixes and improvements to Bhyvemgr.

These are some highlights that were added:

Add support to use VNC unix sock (vnc.sock) when FreeBSD >= 1500509

Add support for storage snapshot (only if zfs is enable)

Move to client/server architecture (unixsocket, json, etc). The bhyvemgr keeps like a client and a new bhyvemgrd app is used like a server.

Remove privileged functions/procedures. Now they are part of bhyvemgrd.

Remove sudo/doas support. It is not necessary anymore because privileged tasks will trigger from bhyvemgrd service.

Replace remote-viewer support (virt-viewer) with vncviewer (tigervnc-viewer). The vncviewer needs less dependencies and it can be ligther than virt option.

Bhyvemgr and Bhyvemgrd supports aarch64 from 15.x to 16-CURRENT and amd64 from FreeBSD 14.x to 16-CURRENT. Bhyvemgr can be compiled or installed from sysutils/bhyvemgr with gtk2, qt5, or qt6 interface support. Bhyvemgrd can be compiled or installed from sysutils/bhyvemgrd.

People interested in helping or supporting the projects are welcome.

Current bhyvemgr version: 2.1.0 Current bhyvemgrd version: 1.2.0

Contact: Alfonso S. Siciliano

The goal of this project is to provide a simple feature in bsdinstall(8), the FreeBSD system installer, to install and configure a graphical environment. The installer should ask users whether they want to install a desktop environment and, if so, automatically install and configure everything needed with minimal or no user intervention. After reboot, users should be presented with a graphical login screen.

In the first 2026 status report, a possible solution was described: a shell script of approximately 400 lines of code to install and automatically configure the components required for a graphical desktop environment, including GPU drivers, Xorg, KDE Plasma, and SDDM. After a call for testing, which received a significant amount of feedback from users, review D56167 was submitted to add the new desktop script to bsdinstall.

After the review was submitted, several discussions took place about the proposed implementation. As a result of the review, it was requested to split the script into smaller components and move part of its functionality into separate ports. The review, D56167, is now obsolete. Several possible approaches were then analyzed and tested.

The chosen solution is to create new ports with flavors.

The base port provides the tools to build menus and/or return to the script a list of packages to install. The menu utilities are implemented as shell scripts because the design of a Lua API for the text user interfaces is still in progress.

Each flavor provides a pkg-post-install-lua(5) script to configure the package installed on the new system. pkg-post-install-lua was chosen instead of the pkg-post-install(5) shell script because it will make it easier to reuse the code if it becomes necessary to use pkg-trigger(5) in the future.

The following four new ports with flavors, with a total of 26 packages, have been created and submitted to Bugzilla:

Base port utilities: bsdinstall-desktop-checks, bsdinstall-desktop-users with menu support.

Base port utility: bsdinstall-gpu with menu support.

Flavors: -amd, -drm, -intel, -nv304, -nv340, -nv390, -nv470, -nv580, -nv595, -nv610, -nvaddons, -nvoptimus, -radeon, -scfb, -vbox, -vesa, -vmware.

Base port utility: bsdinstall-dm with menu support.

A new draft of the desktop script has also been completed in the project repository. It is significantly different from the original script and is now approximately 100 lines of code. A new review to add the desktop script to bsdinstall will be submitted after the new ports have been added to the Ports Collection.

This is still an experimental feature. In the future, depending on user interest and feedback, the desktop script can be further improved to support additional desktop environments and graphical tools.

Contact: Hayzam Sherif

Sylve is a modern, unified system management platform for FreeBSD. It provides an integrated web interface for managing virtual machines (via Bhyve), Jails, the networking around them, and ZFS storage.

The backend is implemented in Go, while the frontend is built with Svelte. The project emphasizes a minimal system footprint. By default, it does not require any packages outside of the base system.

Optional runtime dependencies, required only when their respective features are used, include:

Samba 4.x (for example net/samba424) for SMB file sharing

The port pulls in these dependencies for convenience to the user, but by itself, Sylve needs no dependencies to run.

We published two tagged releases this quarter: v0.3.0 on August 24, which shipped the networking, migration, replication, and backup work reported last quarter, and v0.3.1 on September 7, the latter improving cluster recovery, backups, migration, and guest storage management.

Migration between cluster nodes now transfers the bulk of the ZFS data while the workload is still online, followed by a final incremental transfer and a guarded cutover.

Backups now commit related datasets and VM disks as coordinated generations, with stronger restore and recovery workflows.

Deeper ZFS and ARC telemetry and scheduled S.M.A.R.T. tests were added.

VM storage workflows were redesigned in v0.3.1, with explicit semantics for ejecting and deleting attachments.

A protected local CLI and interactive console were added for common VM, Jail, networking, and lifecycle operations.

Certificate and Dynamic DNS management are built in, including free Sylve.app hostnames with managed TLS, plus Cloudflare and Namecheap support.

The user documentation received a major overhaul, with task-oriented guides for all major features.

Sylve now requires libvirt 12.5.0 or newer for VM management; FreeBSD 15.0 or newer remains required.

The FreeBSD Foundation has expanded its support for Sylve with a new grant for parts of the next phase of the platform.

Native OCI container management through Podman.

An App Gallery with templates for deploying applications in Jails and containers.

NFS sharing and automatic ZFS dataset tuning.

A mobile app for managing clusters, operating-system updates from the interface, and ZFS scrub schedules.

End-to-end testing and clearer migration documentation.

Sponsors: The FreeBSD Foundation, Alchemilla Ventures (Development), IPTechnics LLC (Infrastructure & Testing)
