#9928. Adapting CPython for yk

Earlier this year I wrote a post on yk, which can automatically add JIT compilers to C interpreters. Since then weâve applied yk to more interpreters, fixed various bugs, and improved performance notably. Towards the end of October I showed some data where on our benchmark suite1 yklua is 2Ã faster than the PUC Lua interpreter it takes as a base.

I was quite pleased with myself until someone brought me down to earth by asking âhow do you know if this works for large interpreters?â Itâs a fair question: PUC Lua is at least an order of magnitude smaller2 than CPython or CRuby and whoâs to say if it would work with much bigger interpreters? We had looked at CPython a year or so ago, but at that point yk was missing several obvious things that CPython would need, so we quickly moved on. A lot has changed since then, and a quick LLM experiment got far enough to suggest it would be worth looking again.

Happily, having taken a deeper look, CPython not only works when adapted for yk as ykcpython3, but there are meaningful performance gains to be had â not only relative to normal CPython, but also relative to Pythonâs experimental JIT4. Roughly speaking, this is the result of 3-4 daysâ work on ykcpython directly; there was a separate week and a half of generic yk bug fixing necessary to get to the point that I could look at ykcpython itself.

Here are the âfinalâ numbers from my brief odyssey on ykcpython and the AWFY benchmark suite:

In this table cpython is ânormalâ CPython 3.15.1; cpython_jit is CPython 3.15.1 with the experimental JIT turned on; and ykcpython is commit 31b4d387. Times are in seconds (lower is better) with means and 99% confidence intervals bootstrapped from 30 process executions, running on a 64 core AMD EPYC 7773X Debian machine in performance mode (download the repeatable experiment and the raw data). On each row the fastest entry(s) are shown in bold.

A simple summary of the table is: ykcpython is faster than cpython on every benchmark except DeltaBlue (where itâs about 2.5% slower); and faster than cpython_jit on 8 out of 13 benchmarks.

The point of this post is not to pretend that ykcpython is in any way ready for people to use â it definitely is not! Nor is it to pretend that one can expect performance on a wider set of programs to be as good as the numbers above â it definitely wonât! My view is that benchmark suite performance is a hoop to jump through rather than an end in itself: a system which benchmarks well might perform poorly in the real world; but a system which benchmarks poorly nearly always performs poorly in the real world.

Rather, I wanted to use this post as a way of showing what itâs like to adapt an interpreter for yk5: the stages I went through; and to give a sense of how the just under 450LoC I added were enough to achieve a meaningful effect. Luckily I had a sense that this might be a useful journey, so I was able to write enough stuff down to be able to flesh out this full post.

If you havenât read the earlier yk post, hereâs a very brief refresher. Given a lightly modified C interpreter6 as input, yk produces a VM with a meta-tracing JIT compiler as output7. yk doesnât aim to produce the fastest possible JIT compiling language implementation: rather, it aims to make the language implementation you know and love somewhat faster while retaining 100% compatibility. Put another way a âykifiedâ interpreter is a fork of the existing C version of the interpreter, with (hopefully!) a handful of adjustments.

As with any meta-tracing JIT compiler, yk identifies hot loops in the guest language (e.g. Lua or Python), and traces the interpreter (i.e. records what the C code is executing while it is interpreting the guest language). It then optimises those traces and converts them to machine code.

yk requires interpreters to tell it where potential loops in the guest language are via the YkLocation struct. Optionally â though if you want to get good performance, definitely necessary! â interpreter authors can add optimisation hints that embed knowledge about the language or its common idioms of use such as âat this point this seemingly dynamic value almost never changesâ. In general, working out where to put YkLocations is relatively easy, but working out where to put hints requires a much greater understanding of the interpreter, and careful measurement to understand which do and donât help.

The challenge I face when adapting an interpreter for yk is that I rarely know the interpreter well, if at all. Rather than trying to do everything at once, I have learnt to start off as simple as possible: I try and do the minimum changes that lead to some traces being recorded and compiled to machine code. This can be trickier than it seems: Iâve got to understand the build system8, and work out where to put some semi-sensible YkLocations. Iâve also learnt to make sure that the languageâs test suite works from this very first step: keeping it working thereafter is not only much easier, but it lessens the number of times one attempts optimisations that are unsound.

For a simple interpreter, you might get a basic JIT compiler from an interpreter with fewer than 10LoC (Lines-of-Code) changed. For somewhat bigger interpreters, a few more changes tend to be necessary. For example, yk doesnât like âthreadedâ interpreters that use goto between opcodes, because it doesnât give it enough opportunities to intercede and see whatâs going on. Fortunately, such changes are not generally too big.

Since it had been a long time since I looked at CPythonâs internals9, I started with the part I was vaguely familiar with. As I later discovered, this is now called the âtier 1â interpreter. Quickly hacking in support for yk highlighted several missing things in yk (from basic atomic loads to not-implemented-bit-widths in sub, minor incompatibilities (e.g. reading an environment variable after a CPython test had wiped it), and flat out bugs (from stackmap fixes to not doing silly things after fork). Fixing all those took me around a week and a half; Iâm not going to talk about them in detail in this post, because theyâre generic fixes that arenât ykcpython specific.

My adaption of the tier 1 interpreter is deliberately minimalistic. Most of the changes in the 200LoC diff are small one-offs that arenât hugely interesting: we need CPython to use its (builtin but non-default) switch-based interpreter; and yk uses a shadow stack, so CPythonâs C stack resizing needs to take that into account too. The most interesting thing I did was to add YkLocations at backwards jump opcodes, which I expected to be enough for some half-sensible traces to be created.

I wasnât expecting this first version of ykcpython to be faster than CPython â if nothing else, it contained almost no optimisation hints â but it was much slower than I expected. It was definitely creating traces, and they were executing correctly â the test suite passed, albeit taking more memory than Iâd like10 â but something clearly wasnât right.

Fortunately, it didnât take very long to work out what. 4 years ago, CPython added support for quickening under the heading of âspecialisationâ. Quickening is a simple, clever technique for improving interpreter performance that rewrites âgenericâ opcodes (e.g. âadd objectsâ) to âspecialisedâ, faster, opcodes (e.g. âadd two intsâ) when possible, deoptimising back to the generic opcodes if necessary. I tend to think of quickening as giving a decent portion of the benefit of a JIT compiler without all the bother of generating machine code11. The problem for yk is that sometimes a programâs opcodes can transition between specialised and unspecialised opcodes a large number of times, and the simple way Iâd added yk support meant that each transition implicitly threw away the associated trace and created a new one. In most cases, traces werenât used long enough to overcome the cost of creating them.

There are techniques which can overcome this problem, and I did briefly experiment with them, but I then recalled a conversation I had with some CPython developers last year. A quick look inside CPython confirmed my recollection: CPython contains a âtier 2â interpreter as well. This isnât a completely new interpreter; rather it is an alternative implementation of core parts of the main interpreter loop, mostly intended for CPythonâs experimental JIT compiler.

A very quick experiment later suggested that the tier 2 interpreter was â at least at a basic level â a better fit for yk12. I thus ripped out the tier 1 support and added support for yk in the tier 2 interpreter. Happily, tier 2 support is even easier than tier 1 support, consisting of a mere 80 LoC. To give you a quick idea of what yk support looks like, hereâs the part that attaches YkLocations13 to the (start of) loops:

For the rest of this post, Iâm going to be using yk and the tier 2 interpreter as the starting point for ykcpython.

When optimising any language implementation, itâs important to know where its performance sits in the wider performance landscape. To understand how ykcpython was doing, I used two other baselines: âstockâ CPython; and CPython with the experimental JIT. I configured cpython as follows:

Note that Iâm deliberately using the same version of LLVM for both cpython and cpython_jit because the latter requires LLVM-21. ykllvm â the fork of LLVM used in yk â is based off a version of LLVM about 6 months later than LLVM-21. That might slightly distort comparisons, but itâs a small enough difference that the effects hopefully are fairly minor. Bearing that in mind, ykcpython is configured as follows:

I used our fork14 of the AWFY benchmark suite, simply because I know how to run it without thinking.

The next challenge is to define a metric, or metrics, to report performance. Every metric has the potential to mislead and many are difficult to understand. In my opinion, the least worst single metric is wall-clock time: how long does my program take to run from start to finish? This doesnât capture everything we want to know, but it captures a lot, and itâs easy to understand.

Most importantly this metric implicitly includes start-up and warm-up time. In other words Iâm deliberately choosing a timing metric which tends to favour normal interpreters and âpenaliseâ JIT compilers. To somewhat offset that, we run each AWFY benchmark for 10 in-process iterations (i.e. run the whole benchmark in a for 0..10 loop) so that we also get some sense of how optimisation benefits longer-running programs.

The big performance table at the start of this post uses a custom benchmark runner on an idle machine. All the timings from now on in the post are from me running time once as a normal user without being too careful if the machine is completely idle or not: when starting to optimise an interpreter, itâs not practical to wait an hour to benchmark every change on many benchmarks, when the effects are generally quite large15.

There are various ways one can go about optimising an interpreter for meta-tracing, all of which have pros and cons: the sequence of optimisations Iâm showing here is just one way of going about things16.

Letâs start with the mandelbrot benchmark on cpython:

In other words, I ran the benchmark with 10 in-process iterations and a parameter of 500. The AWFY harness prints out how long each iteration took. As is common â but definitely not universal! â for an interpreter, cpython had fairly consistent times from one iteration to the next.

For this benchmark, cpython_jit takes 6.746s (0.58Ã CPython) and ykcpython takes a whopping 13.70s (1.17Ã CPython)17:

There are a couple of useful things to notice here. First, we can see warm-up occurring: ykcpythonâs first iteration is slower than subsequent iterations. Thatâs OK in my book: yk isnât really intended for programs running in a fraction of a second. Second, the 102% cpu and user time that is higher than wall-clock time are due to yk running trace compilation in threads. That allows the interpreter to continue executing, reducing perceived pauses.

The first thing I do in this situation is look at the âhigh-level IRâ (HIR) of the traces that yk has produced to see if things look sensible:

The logfile contains 11 traces, of which 1 is a âloopâ trace. In general, loop traces are where yk is most effective, and the non-loop traces are the price we have to pay to get the promised land of loop traces. In this case, a simple profile showed that most execution time is spent in the solitary loop trace, which is a promising start for yk.

At this point, doing much more with the HIR than this high-level analysis is difficult, because the output is 20,772 lines of this sort of thing:

Even if youâre used to this syntax and way of thinking, it can be incredibly hard to see the forest for the trees: thereâs just too much stuff. And that isnât just a problem for humans (or AIs) reading this: more HIR means more machine code which implies slower execution.

My first port of call when optimising an interpreter is to tackle interpreter dispatch. When an interpreter is executing a program, it continually asks âwhat is the opcode of the current instruction? Is it an add or a sub or â¦?â and then it dispatches to the code that performs the appropriate action. Itâs probable that a large chunk of that 20KLoC of HIR is the interpreter loading an opcode from memory and checking what kind it is. ykâs trace optimiser has various classic compiler tricks up its sleeve, but in this case they donât really help, because in most cases between the same instruction being loaded twice from memory, some other code will be called that yk has to assume might have mutated that memory. This isnât unnecessary conservatism: Python programs really can mutate their functionâs instructions!

I was particularly lucky because the tier2 interpreter uses âexecutorsâ which are traces of (optimised) instructions. Those instructions are immutable in the context of a given executor: should a Python functionâs instructions change, any associated executors will be invalidated. That means that we can attach a simple monotonically increasing integer code ID to a _PyExecutorObject and know that for a given code ID, an opcode at index I will always be the same.

This allows us to use the single most effective optimisation hint in yk: idempotent functions. In essence, an idempotent function says âfor the same inputs this function will always produce the same outputâ18. âAlwaysâ here really means âalwaysâ! Idempotent is a very strong guarantee that yk cannot help you uphold: if you fail to do so, your system will go wrong in weird ways.

Although yk provides a helper yk_idempotent_load function, we need something more specialised. Fortunately itâs not hard to write what we need:

Unsurprisingly, the yk_idempotent attribute tells yk that idempotent_load_opcode is an idempotent function. That means that if, in a particular trace, the function is called with parameters that are constant values then yk can remove the idempotent function call and replace it with its output. The __asm__ line is there to encourage LLVM not to inline the function19 (if the function is inlined, yk no longer knows there is anything idempotent there).

Using this requires changing just a few lines in the core interpreter loop. The most important lines are simply this:

Promotion (e.g. yk_promote)20 says âthis variable is expected to be semi-constant: record its concrete value and specialise the trace to it, but insert a guard in case that value later changesâ. Imagine I have yk_promote(x) and when a trace is later recorded, x happens to be 3. The trace will record guard true (x == 3): if on later runs x is not 3, the guard will fail and the trace will deoptimise; if the guard succeeds we know henceforth that x is definitely 3.

In other words, in the context of the traces weâre recording, yk will see calls to idempotent_load_opcode with constant arguments, allowing it to replace the function call with a constant result. The point of this isnât just to remove the cost of a load: rather, exposing constant data to ykâs trace optimiser allows it to do a much better job of optimising traces. The effect in this case is quite something:

In other words, that simple change has not only made ykcpython 2.7Ã faster, but it is now 0.43Ã cpython and 0.74Ã cpython_jit! In other words, a simple PR that changes 30LoC has made this benchmark over twice as fast as CPython and 25% faster than CPythonâs JIT. Another way of judging the effectiveness of this optimisation is that it has reduced the 20,772 lines of HIR output to 7,648 lines21.

However, before we get carried away, this isnât enough to make all benchmarks magically quicker. I have learnt from experience to rotate between benchmarks to avoid over-training22. In this case I decided to look at the deltablue benchmark, which I know from yklua can be a tough target. The situation in ykcpython turned out to be worse than I expected: cpython takes 7.67s, cpython_jit takes 6.20s, and ykcpython (with our idempotent change) takes 37.51s. Ouch!

My next port of call is to run YKD_LOG=2 which prints warnings if a trace canât be compiled. Sure enough:

For now Iâm going to skip âtrace too longâ. In essence yk has a fixed limit for âthis trace looks to be so long that itâs probably not usefulâ. The limit was too low, so I increased it unilaterally before doing the work for this post. Exactly what the right value is I donât know. Indeed, I think that this crude heuristic probably needs replacing with something more sophisticated: doing that is a problem for another day.

Letâs move onto the âunimplementedâ warning: I havenât got around to implementing complex atomic instructions yet, so as soon as one of those is encountered, yk has no choice but to give up on that trace entirely. If it happens to be a hot part of a benchmark, that can absolutely kill performance. In this case, happily, the atomicrmw warnings just so happened to come from functions which we really donât want to inline into the trace anyway.

One of tracingâs virtues is that it aggressively inlines functions, but that can inline checks which fail too often on subsequent executions. For example, one function we inline by default is _PyObject_GC_Link which checks to see if enough objects have been allocated for garbage collection to be worth scheduling. If weâre unlucky, we may trace an iteration of a loop which happens to schedule garbage collection: in nearly every subsequent execution, the resulting guard will fail, and weâll take a somewhat slower path. The solution here is to mark such functions as yk_outline:

Functions marked yk_outline become calls in a trace. There are probably a number of functions which should be marked as yk_outline, but I marked the two that happened to cause the aborted warnings and that also obviously we donât want to include in a trace anyway. Doing so improved execution time to 36.63s (about 2.5% faster), so theyâre clearly not the major cause of the slowdown in this case.

Just when I was starting to fret, profiling execution showed that, to my surprise, deltablue was only spending about half its running time in JIT-compiled code, where one would expect it to be spending 90%+. It turns out that the main reason for this is that not all executors have a _JUMP_TO_TOP opcode and werenât being traced.

My quick fix was to add a YkLocation at the first opcode in an executor. The one line fix does just that: it means that yk starts tracing as soon as it enters an executor. Doing so improves deltablueâs execution time to 8.64s (4.23Ã faster than before). Thatâs still 1.13Ã CPython, but itâs a lot better than before!

At the time I made this change I didnât fully think about how adding a YkLocation at the start of an executor might interact with the YkLocation already added to _JUMP_TO_TOP. As luck would have it, I accidentally stumbled on a reasonable combination: _JUMP_TO_TOP tends to jump to the instruction at index 1. Still, I suspect that there might be a better way to add YkLocations to executors, but one canât solve every problem all at once: itâs time to move onto the next thing!

Our earlier use of idempotent loads made such a huge impact on interpreter dispatch that itâs easy to overlook that it was a simple, shallow, change: it only optimised loading an instructionâs opcode kind. Instructions contain a number of other fields that are equally amenable to idempotent loading.

There are various ways one can go about optimising these additional fields. I could, for example, have replaced the definitions of some static functions in header files. To keep things simple, I defined a macro which can generate the two-parameter functions we need, and then nobbled some other macros to call it at appropriate points. With the resulting change deltablueâs performance improves to 8.09s â weâre now within 10% of cpythonâs performance.

As we saw earlier, not all functions are good candidates for inlining into a trace. yk has a very simple heuristic â stolen shamelessly from RPython/PyPy â which is to mark functions containing loops as âoutlinedâ. In other words, if C calls a function f() and f contains for (...) { ... } then yk will not inline calls to f.

The fundamental reason not to inline functions-with-loops is that tracing unrolls loops, and that tends not to be a good idea. First, some loops execute vast numbers of iterations, which would cause counter-productively-long traces. Second, loopsâ iterations are often controlled by dynamic, ever-changing values: unrolling would specialise the trace to just one of those values, giving suboptimal performance on every other value.

There are however a small number of functions in an interpreter which we actively want to unroll. Typically those functionsâ loops satisfy two properties: they only run a small number of iterations; and the number of iterations depends on an aspect of the userâs program that changes rarely. For example, a function called unpack_args(int num_args) which contains for (int i=0; i

yk thus provides a yk_unroll attribute, which informs yk that a function that might otherwise be outlined should in fact be inlined and its loops unrolled. Rather than slog through every function in CPython looking for candidates, I did a simple grep/sort in hir to see which (implicitly non-inlined) C functions appear most often in traces23:

bcmp is the standard libc function: all of the other functions are in CPython itself. Not all of those functions will have loops in them, but the chances are that most do. What I do in such a situation is go down (or, depending how you look at it, up) the list and look at the code in each function. I did that for a couple of benchmarks to ensure I got some coverage of common functions.

The two most commonly called CPython functions immediately looked like good candidates. _PyFrame_Initialize is the most obvious of the two, containing almost exactly the pattern I most like to match on:

_PyFrame_ClearLocals is slightly trickier: it contains a while loop involving pointer arithmetic, but it didnât take me long to convince myself that it was a good candidate.

Earlier we made _PyObject_GC_Link not inlineable, so we donât want to reverse that! Similarly, do_lookup looks values up in a dictionary, so we want to keep that outlined: it depends on an often-changing dynamic value.

PyLong_FromSsize_t and PyLong_FromLong were harder to judge. These functionsâ inner loops depend on dynamic values, but my best guess is that they tend to be fairly stable in practice. I will be keeping an eye on these functions in the future, because I only have medium confidence that I made the right initial call.

As these examples suggest, I am generally fairly cautious about adding yk_unroll: inappropriate placings can easily help one benchmark and make many others worse. I thus tend to only mark one or two functions as yk_unroll, benchmark, and then move on. In this case, I did 5 small PRs, with the end effect that json went from 11.52s to 10.85s.

In general most function calls in C are direct: f() calls a function called f. However a minority of functions are indirect: f is a generic pointer whose value can be any compatible function. This is commonly used in interpreters to allow run-time dispatch to type specific code.

By default, yk cannot inline through indirect function calls, because without knowing exactly what pointer is being called, it canât reliably reconstruct the path that execution took24. Fortunately, we already have the tool we need to solve this problem: yk_promote! If yk sees an indirect function call with a constant pointer it knows exactly what function is being called and can inline as normal. The common pattern I use is:

yk_is_interpreting() is true during ânormalâ interpretation; false during tracing; and (because itâs a constant false) removed during tracing. In other words, yk_promote is only called during the tracing phase. yk_is_interpreting() is fairly fast (much faster than yk_promote()) so this idiom is a small but useful performance win.

However, there is often a second problem. yk only puts the tracing machinery into a function if it can statically prove that it is reachable from a traceable path. Commonly, functions called from indirect calls cannot be statically proven to be traceable and thus they still leave an outlined call in the trace. We can solve that with the yk_indirect_inline function which tells yk âthis function can be reached from an indirect call and should be considered for tracingâ25.

Profiling a couple of benchmarks quickly showed several potential candidates26. My experience is that not all indirect call sites are good targets for promotion: for example, of the interpreters Iâve looked at so far, inlining malloc and free indirect calls has rarely been profitable. However, I quickly alighted upon a couple of promising candidates.

Letâs start with the less promising, but easier to explain, one: benchmarks like deltablue and json call len on lists and strings. Simplifying slightly, sq_length is a pointer to a function inside a CPython type, so this becomes an indirect call in traces. In the case of len([...]) the function thatâs ultimately called is list_length:

where PyList_GET_SIZE boils down (slightly elided) to a simple load a->ob_size. Thatâs the sort of code that yk loves to see inlined in a trace!

The resulting PR has to do a slightly annoying dance to make yk accept the yk_promote call. In essence, if yk_promote were to be statically inlined into a function which ykllvm determines doesnât need to be traced, odd things happen, and so ykllvm throws a static error. In this case, the function that âshouldâ contain the yk_promote can get inlined in multiple paths, one of which falls foul of this check. A hacky fix is to pull the promote out into a function which isnât statically inlined27. I then did a second PR to inline range construction and iteration.

You may notice that in both of these PRs I have marked a much larger number of functions yk_indirect_inline than I have benchmark evidence for. The reason for this is a variant of something I mentioned above: my experience of indirect call sites is that either nearly all targets benefit from indirect inlining or none do. This clearly isnât an iron law of the universe, but what it means is that I tend to look at all the possible targets, and mark them as yk_indirect_inline if they look sensible. So far, I have rarely regretted doing so.

Collectively these two PRs drive jsonâs performance down to 10.41s, though the effect on deltablue was too small to say anything either way. As I get further into optimising an interpreter for yk this is common: not all benchmarks benefit from all optimisations.

At this point, youâve probably got a good sense of how I approach ykifying an interpreter. I raised a few more PRs before realising that I wasnât going to add much useful conceptually to this post: it was time to finish this stage of work off and write it up.

Before I started this little journey, I wasnât entirely sure if yk would work at all â let alone âwellâ! â on an interpreter the size and complexity of CPython. The early stages didnât entirely dispel my worries: there were lots of missing pieces, and quite a few bugs, that needed fixing in yk for ykcpython to work at all. The fact that ykcpython does work, and works fairly well, is proof that at least one big, complex, interpreter can be ykified with relative ease â and that it can be surprisingly competitive on performance.

Of course, I am lucky in many ways. yk already had decent foundations, thanks to several peopleâs hard work. The tier 2 interpreter in CPython made my life a lot easier than it might otherwise have been. Small benchmarks, like the ones Iâve used in this post, tend to flatter (meta-)tracing as a JIT compiling technique. And when it comes to ykifying interpreters, well, Iâve been round the block a few times.

But I donât want to completely underplay things. 3-4 days isnât that long to spend on an interpreter like CPython. It will take a lot longer than that â even with the wonder of LLMs to speed up the journey â to do a thorough job and squeeze all the juice that ykcpython can expose to yk. Similarly, I have only looked at a handful of benchmarks: itâs unlikely that ykcpython will magically speed up a wide range of programs yet, as there will be many other parts of CPython that need to be considered for optimisation. A lot of this will not be rocket science, but it is work, and not all of it can yet be automated.

I also havenât made any performance optimisations (yet!) to yk for ykcpython specifically (though I have fixed a couple of bottlenecks that I had previously been able to ignore). In particular, one thing I am entirely confident in is that ykcpython will generate HIR patterns that yk doesnât yet optimise effectively: fixing those will improve ykcpythonâs performance for free, possibly quite a bit. Even without that, ykcpython has highlighted additional bottlenecks in yk that had never previously been an issue: each time one of those is fixed, ykcpython will magically get faster.

In a sense, this is one of the nice things that yk offers: improvements to yk nearly always benefit every ykified interpreter. Itâs why I could bring ykcpython up to speed in a short period of time: I wasnât writing a JIT compiler from scratch, I was reusing a generic toolkit. For example, the various missing pieces and bugs that ykcpython highlighted in yk will almost certainly make ykifying the next interpreter that bit easier â and hopefully future improvements to yk will benefit ykcpython even further!

Acknowledgments: Edd Barrett and Lukas Diekmann did much of the original work on yk. Shopify and the Royal Academy of Engineering generously funded the underlying research. Chris Seaton was the person who made the work on yk possible.

#9927. Germany Busts 'Crime-as-a-Service' Investment Fraud Outfit

Authorities seized more than 100 servers and arrested seven as part of a crackdown on a fraud network spanning more than 50 countries.

You see an online advertisement promising quick returns from trading cryptocurrency, foreign currencies, and stocks. You give the "investment firm" your information, and an operator calls you and convinces you to transfer a small amount of money into a platform. You make early profits quickly, so you deposit increasingly large sums of money. But when you attempt to withdraw your earnings, the operator stalls for a while until finally cutting off contact.

This pattern is familiar to victims of investment fraud, a multinational criminal industry that relies on social engineering to convince would-be investors that they're about to make substantial gains before pulling the rug out from under them.

Europol today shared news of the disruption of one such operation, an investment fraud scheme with potential victims across more than 50 countries and a company allegedly supplying fraudulent trading platforms and leads to criminal groups. According to a press release, Europol and Eurojust supported an international operation involving authorities in Albania, Cyprus, Finland, Germany, Israel, Kosovo, and North Macedonia.

Related:Getting Past the Post-Quantum Cryptography Discovery Phase

The German Itzehoe Public Prosecutor's Office led the operation, targeting a company suspected of supplying phony trading websites and multiple call centers to criminal groups; investigators estimate losses to exceed 4 million euros.

International authorities searched 17 locations, including a call center in Kosovo, leading to the seizure of 100 servers and the arrests of seven suspects.

The law enforcement action reflects a multiyear investigation that began in 2022, according to Europol, when a German couple reported they could not withdraw money invested through an online trading platform. This led to two previous "action days" by authorities, one in 2022 (involving two arrests and the seizure of evidence) and another in 2025 (involving more arrests and seizures of money and evidence).

"Analysis of the material recovered exposed the suspected infrastructure provider and its links to call centre operators, paving the way for the latest operation," the press release read.

A Eurojust press release provided further detail regarding the extent of the operation. The analysis of evidence seized during the second action day exposed a company based in Cyprus and Israel allegedly offering "crime-as-a-service," supplying criminal groups with fraudulent websites that funnel targets into the central investment scam.

The data of potential victims visiting these websites and expressing interest would be sold as leads to call centers, which contacted the victims to persuade them to invest their money, leading to repeated demands for additional investments. Authorities identified suspected call center-operating clients of this company in Albania, Kosovo, and North Macedonia.

Related:Cyber Experts Weigh In: How to Fight Artex & AntiFox

The fraud operation guaranteed significant returns for trades in cryptocurrencies, foreign currencies, or stocks, according to Europol. But authorities found that the seemingly legitimate platforms were run by "brokers" that used phony profits and social engineering tactics to convince victims to keep investing. Additionally, investigators also found the operators used affiliate marketing services and deceptive advertisements to lure in potential victims.

Austin Anderson, director of threat intel at cybercrime disruption firm Netcraft, tells Dark Reading that operations like these that target upstream providers can help disrupt investment fraud operations at scale.

"Fraudsters have increasingly specialized in one piece of an attack's supply chain, as seen in this scheme where websites collected personal data that was sold to call centers to ultimately coerce funds from victims," he says. "While this can breed sophistication in each actor's niche, it also introduces fragility when a large dependency like the call center is disrupted. Ultimately, without arrests that remove fraudsters from the market, these operations only temporarily disrupt operations while actors rebuild their infrastructure."

Related:Japan Pushes Emergency Funding for Cybersecurity as AI-Assisted Breaches Rise

After cutting his teeth writing for independent gaming publications as a teenager, he graduated from Emerson College in 2016 with a Bachelor of Science in journalism. He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

#9926. How UK AISI and EvalEval Are Making Benchmark Results Reproducible

The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.

AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema. This next phase of the collaboration puts that shared infrastructure into practice.

As AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly important sources of evidence about model and system performance. Yet results are reported across many formats, platforms, and outlets, often without enough information to reproduce them. Running the evaluations again may itself be prohibitively expensive.

EvalEval's mission is to improve this ecosystem through a shared reporting schema, Every Eval Ever, and an open platform, Evaluation Cards, that brings evaluation results and the information needed to interpret them into a common structure.

This builds naturally on AISI's work to make evaluation more efficient through OptStop, more statistically rigorous through HiBayES, and more standardised in areas including transcript analysis and capability elicitation. Together, AISI and EvalEval are working to diagnose gaps in evaluation reporting and build shared infrastructure to close them.

Transcript-level transparency matters not only for reproducibility, but also for analysis and diagnosis. In this new phase of the collaboration, AISI is making publicly reported evaluation methods and findings available through Evaluation Cards where appropriate. The release includes verified results, context, and configuration information for the five benchmarks in the paper's main experiment:

These results cover six frontier models: Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4. The release also includes results from two related cyber evaluations—Cyber CTFs and The Last Ones—which use a different, partially overlapping set of models. The data accompany AISI's paper, How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation, which studies how benchmark performance depends on inference-time compute and evaluation protocol.

Performance on Humanity's Last Exam changes with evaluation protocol and inference compute. Each curve shows the cumulative share of attempted tasks solved within a given token count, using the earliest observed success per task. When models received correctness feedback from an oracle after each attempt, they continued to solve additional tasks as token use increased.

When results are openly released with setup information, researchers and practitioners can examine individual studies more closely and compare findings across the wider ecosystem. Where other reports lack these details, releases like AISI's provide verified reference points for interpreting evaluations in context—for example, by helping researchers understand how setup choices may influence reported performance. As more evaluators adopt EEE, open comparisons like these can support broader and more reliable meta-research.

AISI's Terminal-Bench 2.0 results alongside other reported evaluations for the same models, under different evaluation setups.

We are excited about this adoption and look forward to further standardising and sharing evaluations with AISI and other AI evaluation organisations.

The EvalEval Coalition is a research community developing scientifically grounded research and robust deployment infrastructure for the evaluation ecosystem. Its goal is to improve evaluation science, address the lack of consensus around documenting evaluation applicability and utility, and broaden coverage of the impacts that matter for scientific research and policy analysis.

The coalition's flagship projects include Every Eval Ever, a shared schema and repository for evaluation results, and Evaluation Cards, which combines benchmark metadata, evaluation-run data, and model metadata into interpretable records. Together, they make it easier to understand when apparently similar scores were produced under meaningfully different conditions.

The UK AI Security Institute is a research organisation within the UK government's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. Its mission is to equip governments with a scientific understanding of the risks posed by advanced AI. AISI conducts research and builds infrastructure to understand advanced AI capabilities and impacts, develop and test mitigations, and inform policy.

The line that matters for practitioners is quiet: apparently similar scores can be produced under meaningfully different conditions.

Once you've watched a benchmark move just by changing inference-time compute or the elicitation protocol, "Model A beat Model B on X" without a card is marketing, not comparison. Evaluation Cards that ship verified results with configuration — especially transcript-level context where it's appropriate — are how eval becomes a contract instead of a leaderboard screenshot.

One ask I'd put to teams adopting EEE: which fields get skipped first under deadline pressure (seed, tool access, attempt budget, oracle feedback), and do you treat a missing field as "do not cite the delta" rather than "assume defaults"?

Reproducible reporting won't remove disagreement. It will make the disagreement about the right variables.

#9925. Fresh European Fridge Attacks Put Cold-Chain Security in Focus

Beyond food storage, the same combination of Internet connectivity, remote access, and inadequate security practices can put temperature-controlled infrastructure across other critical sectors at risk.

A second wave of attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe this week has heightened concerns about the broader "cold chain's" vulnerability to similar attacks, given that supermarkets aren't the only businesses that rely on cold storage.

As in mid-October, an unknown threat actor appears to have gained access to refrigeration controllers at multiple European supermarkets and switched the systems to defrost mode, raising temperatures to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) and causing food spoilage.

Reporting by the BBC, Reuters, CNBC, and other outlets suggests the latest attacks were smaller in scope compared with the first wave in October that affected more than 700 retail and grocery stores, primarily in France. A smaller number of stores in Belgium, Germany, the Netherlands, Portugal, Poland and Spain were also caught up in the October attacks.

Related:How to Assess OT Incident Response Preparedness

BBC reported the new attacks as impacting "dozens of supermarkets" in seven European countries including Belgium, Luxembourg, Estonia, Ireland, Sweden and Finland. Spokespersons from several supermarket chains that include France's Carrefour, Belgium's Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt Group, and Sweden's Coop chains confirmed varying but relatively limited impacts from the new attacks.

In a Nov. 2 statement, Carrefour said a cyberattack targeting its refrigeration systems had impacted 15 out of 700 stores in Belgium. In an undated statement, US-based Copeland, which manufactures technologies for regulating commercial refrigeration systems, alluded to a cybersecurity incident affecting refrigeration systems in France, which it said related to a discontinued generation of supervisory controllers.

No individual or group has claimed responsibility for either the first or the second wave of attacks, and the motivation behind it remains a mystery. European authorities are currently investigating the attacks.

Researchers, including those at France's CERT, have linked the hacks so far to Internet-connected refrigeration controllers made by Denmark-based Danfoss, Italy-based Dixell, and Copeland. Organizations using these controllers often connect them to the Internet to enable remote maintenance and support, but in doing so also potentially expose them to unauthorized access and remote attack by threat actors.

Risks include unpatched vulnerabilities in these technologies that attackers can exploit, like three in Danfoss' AK-SM 800A controllers that researchers at Claroty disclosed this August and another two they reported the same month in Copeland controllers. Weak configurations and poor security hygiene are other major problems.

Related:Why Europe's Freezer Hacks Spread So Far, So Fast

"Misconfigurations and systemic hygiene failures represent the vast majority of the threat surface," says John Gallagher, vice president at operational technology (OT) and Internet of Things (IoT) security vendor Viakoo. "While unpatched vulnerabilities exist in older firmware, they are rendered dangerous only because basic architectural hygiene was skipped, especially [when] making them Internet-facing."

Common mistakes that include widespread use of default passwords, vendor-shared service codes, or static credentials across hundreds of locations make brute-forcing trivial, Gallagher adds.

The weaknesses are not confined to supermarket refrigeration systems. The same combination of Internet connectivity, remote access, and inadequate security practices can put temperature-controlled infrastructure across other critical sectors at risk, according to security experts.

Sean Tufts, field chief technology officer (CTO) at Claroty, points out that "pharmaceutical storage and distribution, food distribution centers, and industrial facilities all rely on connected operational technology to maintain precise environmental conditions."

Related:Les supermarchés de l'UE paient d'un firmware de réfrigérateur non mis à jour

The level of exposure will vary depending on how these systems are deployed, connected, and secured. But many organizations that rely on remotely accessible refrigeration or temperature-control equipment face similar challenges around asset visibility, third-party access, and securing legacy systems, Tufts says. "The same types of weaknesses can exist across different industries, even if the equipment and operational requirements differ."

The potential consequences of a compromise, Tufts says, can vary by sector.

"A disruption to pharmaceutical storage could compromise temperature-sensitive medicines, while an incident affecting food distribution could lead to spoilage and supply chain disruptions," he notes. "Industrial environments may face additional operational consequences depending on the materials and processes involved."

The supermarket attacks are a reminder that refrigeration and temperature-control systems are part of essential operations and not just back-of-house equipment, Tufts adds. Organizations should identify these assets and know how they connect to the Internet and third parties.

"Where remote access is necessary, use a VPN, strong authentication, or a centralized secure-access tool with session tracking." Changing default passwords, keeping firmware current, and segmenting are also recommended security practices, he says.

Gallagher says that while it's unclear how the attacks on the commercial refrigeration systems played out, the most straightforward theory is the threat actor likely compiled a target list by scanning the public Internet for specific controller fingerprints, such as those tied to Danfoss, Dixell, and Copeland. They then likely deployed an automated script across that target list to exploit known web vulnerabilities or push default credentials, triggering the defrost mode simultaneously.

Gallagher says the same attacks that worked on commercial refrigeration systems can potentially work across almost any form of OT and IoT systems. That's because these systems often are managed outside of IT, lack automated controls to keep firmware and passwords updated, and have porous network borders. "The growth over the last three years in operational ransomware and in cyberattacks causing physical damage shows that these attacks are on the rise and not specific to any one kind of system."

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#9924. Welcome RL Environments to the hub

Reinforcement Learning environments give new capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents. Therefore, Hugging Face Hub now has a special place for RL Environments.

An environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome. The resulting rewards can measure an agent's performance during evaluation or provide a learning signal during training. For an introduction to this interaction loop, see our blogpost on environments. Within the environment, the agent will perform a set of tasks that are represented as datasets. Therefore, environments can be split into broadly two parts: tasksets and runtimes. In this release, we are focusing on the tasksets.

An RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that shows up in the new RL Environments filter. The Use this dataset button gives you the command to run it in that framework. There is no new repo type, no registry, and no sign-up. There are already environments in Harbor, Verifiers, and NVIDIA NeMo Gym.

Every RL paper or framework uses its own way to find environments. Custom hubs, runtime registries, independent task datasets, or a GitHub list of tasks with a custom loader. This means that many of the published environments are siloed: if you publish an environment for one framework, users of the other three can’t load it. If you want to train on an environment from another framework or a new paper, you’ll need to port it by hand.

We think this is the wrong shape. An environment is tasks, tests, containers, and a reward rule, which are data with a runtime on top. The Hub already stores data, versions it, gates it, previews it, and serves it to millions of people. It does not need a second system to hold environments. It needs a way to say "this data is an environment, and here is how you run it."

The frameworks keep doing what they are good at. The Hub does what it is good at, which is hosting, discovery, and versioning. Nobody has to own the catalogue. In fact, catalogues can run on other platforms too, powered by the hub.

The dataset repository hosts your environment files. The framework runs them locally or on a supported cloud backend. Hugging Face Jobs can run cloud workloads, and Hugging Face Sandboxes, built on Jobs, provide interactive command execution. The tags describe compatibility and generate loading commands; adding a tag does not start a job or sandbox.

The RL Environments filter. Go to huggingface.co/datasets?other=rl-environment. Every dataset with the rl-environment tag appears there, whatever framework it works with.

Framework tags. Four environment frameworks are registered as dataset libraries:

Each framework tag puts the framework's icon on the dataset page and adds a generated snippet to Use this dataset.

A dataset can carry more than one framework tag. That is the point. Tags describe compatibility, and compatibility is not exclusive. Each listed framework must support the files in the repository; adding a tag does not convert them.

Choose the example for your framework and run it in a separate Python environment with the prerequisites listed below.

Harbor can load task directories from a Hub repository. The oracle agent runs the task's reference solution, then the verifier scores the result. It does not call a model.

The viewer shows the task's reward, verifier output, and logs. This checks the task and its reference solution before you try a model agent.

The Harbor integration of verifiers v1 can run the same task directories in different runtimes, such as Docker. It also supports different harnesses, including a minimal bash harness.

Here repo is the full Hugging Face Git URL, while dataset is the name and version in that repo's registry.json. This loader uses Harbor's registry conventions, so a bare Hub repo ID cannot replace both values.

OpenEnv's Harbor integration can run the same task directories with an agent such as OpenCode and return the verifier's reward alongside the agent's trace.

The command downloads the dataset's tasks/ directories, runs one task in Docker, and writes the result. The default connection uses a temporary Gradio tunnel so the sandboxed agent can reach OpenEnv's model proxy. Read the verifier result and the number of model calls:

A reward of None means no verifier reward was produced; inspect error before interpreting the run as a model failure. This path expects Harbor task directories.

NeMo Gym supports evaluation and RL training: its environments collect trajectories and compute rewards, while a training framework updates model weights. For example, the Structured Outputs dataset pairs prompts with JSON schemas. Its verifier rewards schema adherence; it does not check whether the generated content is factually correct.

The best part is that this gives one repo and one discussion tab where people report broken tasks from all major frameworks. So when an author fixes a bad test, every framework gets the fix on the next pull.

Open your dataset card and add this to the YAML header:

That is the whole integration. Keep rl-environment, then list every framework that can load your files. If your environment works with a framework we have not registered yet, open a PR to the list of supported libraries.

We opened PRs to tag some of the environments people already train on. If you maintain one of these, merge the PR and your environment shows up in the filter.

The first version generates one default snippet per framework. Per-config snippets are next, so a repo with several task sets can show the right command for each. After that we will look at structural detection for frameworks with strict layouts. It would also be really cool build custom task UIs, we’ve been experimenting with this here:

The bigger goal is for framework tagging to be automatic everywhere. OpenEnv already does it on upload. If you maintain Harbor, Verifiers, Nemo Gym, or any other environment framework, add the tags in your push path. It is a few lines, and every environment your users publish becomes visible to everyone else.

If you train agents, go browse the filter. If you build environments, publish and tag them, whether they cover coding, tool use, games, robotics, or another task. Include the files, a working run command, and the rule that produces the reward so others can use them. If your framework is missing, contribute it to the list of supported libraries.

#9923. libreagi - save OS models

Open models should outlive the places that host them. LibreAGI is a private BitTorrent tracker where members keep copies of the models most likely to disappear.

Credit grows with size and time, and a model with one copy earns four times the base rate. The rare ones need the most help.

Any format, from safetensors and GGUF to ONNX, under Apache-2.0, MIT or the Qwen Community License. Each file is checked against its source commit, and staff review every model.

A signed public catalog lists every model, hash and source, so anyone can rebuild the swarms if this site goes away.

The public channel is open to anyone, with no account needed. Come and ask questions before you apply.

InfoQ Homepage News Author Q+A: finprim is a Case for One Financial Validation Library in TypeScript

Nov 12, 2026 6 min read

finprim, which is an MIT-licensed TypeScript library that puts IBAN, BIC, card, sort code, VAT, routing number and loan calculations behind one API, has published its fifth release, 0.1.4. The repository has 81 stars.

InfoQ asked author Oluwatosin Adelaja what pushed him to build it, and where he wants it to stop.

Adelaja: Honestly, it came from doing the same work too many times. At Sprint Technology Solutions we had several products, and each one ended up with its own copy of the same financial validation, sort code checks in one place, IBAN formatting in another, card validation somewhere else, all written slightly differently by whoever got there first.

The moment it really landed for me was on a payout flow. We had account and sort code validation on the web side, and then the mobile app needed the same thing. Rather than share it, the validation got rewritten for mobile, and the two copies drifted. One of them was a little stricter than the other, so a bank detail that the web form accepted would get rejected on mobile, and we had people re-entering details that were actually fine. It took longer than it should have to track down, because nobody thinks to check whether two "identical" validators are actually identical. The fix was easy once we found it, but the real problem was that there were two of them at all.

I hit the same shape of thing again later building a daily pay feature for NHS workers, where the same rules needed to hold on web and on mobile. That is when I stopped treating it as a one-off chore and started thinking it should just be one library, written once and tested once, that any product could pull in and trust.

InfoQ: What was missing that justified a unified library rather than assembling existing single-purpose packages?

Adelaja: You can absolutely wire together a pile of single-purpose packages, and plenty of teams do. The problem is what you are left maintaining. Each package has its own API shape, its own types, its own idea of what a valid result looks like, and often its own dependencies. So you end up writing a layer of glue code just to make them agree with each other, and that glue becomes its own thing to test and keep working.

finprim's bet is that financial validation is coherent enough to live behind one consistent API. The same shape of input, the same shape of result, and the same typing approach across IBAN, sort code, card, VAT, all of it. And zero runtime dependencies, so there is no tree of other people's packages to audit or keep patched. For something sitting in the path of a payment, I wanted fewer moving parts, not more.

InfoQ: What concrete class of bugs do branded types prevent, and why not rely on plain runtime validation?

Adelaja: The bug class is the one where a string that was never validated gets used as if it had been. To the compiler, a validated IBAN and a random string are both just a string, so nothing stops you passing the wrong one into a function that assumes the value is good. It compiles fine, and then it fails at runtime, which in this domain means it fails in the middle of a live transaction.

Branded types close that gap. A validated IBAN comes back as its own distinct type, not a plain string, so if you try to use an unchecked value where a validated one is required, the compiler rejects it before the code ever runs. The runtime validation still happens, that does not go away. The branding just guarantees it actually happened and that nobody quietly skipped it on some code path. It moves a whole class of "we forgot to validate this one route" mistakes from production back to compile time.

InfoQ: For something handling payment data, how do you think about trust, what can you guarantee, and where do you draw the line?

Adelaja: The honest answer starts with being clear about what finprim is and is not. It validates and formats financial data. It does not store anything, it does not send anything over the network, and it does not process payments. No database, no telemetry, no outbound calls.

So the guarantees I can actually make are narrow and specific. It checks values against published standards, IBAN structure, checksum rules, card network ranges, and tells you whether they are well formed, deterministically, without logging the sensitive values it is handling. That last part is deliberate. You do not want account numbers or card numbers turning up in logs, so the library does not put them there.

Where I draw the line matters just as much. finprim does not tell you a payment is safe to make, it is not a compliance tool, and it is not a replacement for the checks your payment provider runs. It confirms the data is shaped correctly before it goes anywhere. Treating a validation library as more than that would be the real mistake.

InfoQ: How do you source and maintain the correctness of 80+ IBAN formats, VAT quirks and card ranges, and how is it tested?

Adelaja: The rules come from the published standards rather than from me guessing. IBAN is checked against the ISO 13616 country formats, card numbers use Luhn plus the published network ranges, VAT uses the documented per-country formats, and so on. Where there is an authoritative spec, that is the source of truth.

On testing, each validator runs against known-good and known-bad values taken from those reference sources, so the tests check behaviour against the standard, not just against themselves. Overall coverage is around 91% of lines and 88% of statements. The core validation modules are the most heavily covered, the IBAN, card, VAT, routing, BIC and sort code logic sits around 94% of lines with full function coverage, and the thinner coverage is in the optional React bindings rather than the validation itself. I would rather be straight about that split than quote one headline number, because the part that actually handles financial data is the part that is tested hardest.

Keeping it correct over time is mostly manual, I update the formats as the standards change, and this is one place the outside contributors have genuinely helped, because people using it in different countries spot edge cases I would never hit on my own.

InfoQ: SEPA and ACH generation is a big jump from validation into transaction generation. Where do you want finprim to end up?

Adelaja: That is a fair thing to push on, because generation is a genuinely different job from validation, and I do not want to pretend otherwise. Validating an IBAN is self-contained. Producing a SEPA credit transfer file or an ACH batch means taking on formatting rules, sequencing and a lot more responsibility for getting something exactly right that is going to be submitted to a bank.

Where I want finprim to sit is as a validation and formatting toolkit first. I am deliberately cautious about the generation side. If it does move into producing standard file formats, I would want that to be safe, well-tested generation of documented formats, not finprim turning into a transaction engine or a payments platform. I would rather it did one layer really well than spread itself thin doing a half version of what a payment provider already gives you.

Narrower tools exist, such as ibankit for IBAN and BIC alone, and on DEV a commenter called the Dinero.js approach solid while warning that teams get burned when a library's precision assumptions diverge from the processor's.

Adelaja is a senior full stack engineer. All five releases have stayed within 0.1.x, so upgrading has meant patch releases rather than code changes, and there is no dedicated migration guide, so the README and release notes are the reference.

#9921. Phishing-Resistant Isn't Enough; Yubico Takes Aim at Identity-Verification Gap

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

The new YubiID service bridges identity verification with credential enrollment and recovery across existing identity platforms, closing an important authentication gap. Plus: post-quantum YubiKey beta.

Yubico wants to help employers verify a person's identity before enrolling login credentials — and again when the employee needs to regain access after losing a key or mobile device.

On Tuesday, the maker of YubiKey authentication devices unveiled YubiID, a subscription service entering limited early access that links identity verification with credential enrollment and account recovery. Announced at Yubico's inaugural YubiNation user conference in San Francisco this week, the service integrates with major identity providers, including Microsoft Entra, Okta, and Ping, and supports enrolling credentials on YubiKeys and mobile phones. This extends Yubico's reach to organizations that have decided against deploying hardware keys.

The launch addresses a growing recognition that protecting a login to be phishing-resistant is no longer enough. It does not establish that the right person received the credential or that someone requesting a replacement is the legitimate owner. Yubico field CTO Derek Hanson described that shift at the FIDO Alliance's Authenticate conference last month, saying the help desk "has moved from an operational control to an actual security control in most enterprises."

Related:Cyera's Oasis Security Buy Is All About AI Agent Control

Yubico is working with a group of unnamed "large organizations" as design partners and hopes to make YubiID generally available in the first half of 2027, CEO Jerrod Chong tells Dark Reading. The company has not revealed pricing.

According to Chong, the problem YubiID addresses used to be an afterthought: confirming that a key reaches the right person and that someone reporting it as lost is that person. The new service provides a baseline identity-verification capability, but customers can also use their own verification process or rely on other providers. Planned integrations with Clear, Nametag, and HYPR will allow organizations to combine providers whose coverage differs by region.

For most enterprises, this is a familiar scenario: Employees prove their identities to HR in one part of the office, then collect their login credentials from IT in another part. Connecting these steps reduces opportunities for impersonation because identity verification is required for both initial enrollment and enrollment of replacement credentials.

"Recovery is such a weak spot for credential management," Andrew Shikiar, executive director and CEO of the FIDO Alliance, tells Dark Reading.

Digital identity credentials provide enterprises with a way to reestablish a user's identity during recovery without relying on knowledge-based secrets, he says. Solving the recovery challenge involves more than just technology; it also requires policy, regulatory alignment, user behavior change, and business process design.

Related:USA Fencing Lunges Into the Hidden Identity Challenge in Amateur Sports

For organizations already investing in Okta, Ping, or Microsoft Entra, YubiID coordinates verification and enrollment; it does not replace those identity platforms. Yubico has built connectors to enroll credentials from those providers and also supports homegrown identity systems.

"We're not being an IDP," Chong says. "I think that there are more opportunities for collaboration than competition."

The practical benefit is tighter coordination. An organization can connect its chosen verification process to enrollment in the identity systems employees already use, rather than managing those steps as disconnected workflows. That becomes especially relevant for enterprises running multiple identity providers, where the employee's immediate need is simply to receive working credentials, regardless of which platform manages the account.

For a company onboarding 10,000 temporary workers ahead of the holiday season, YubiID can support both administrator-assisted, in-person enrollment and remote enrollment and verification. The benefit of giving the company multiple ways to connect identity checks to access setup, Chong says, is as much operational as security-related — fewer disconnected steps between verifying a worker and getting that person authenticated — though he did not provide figures on potential time savings or reductions in help-desk work. Interest is strongest among organizations with large, distributed, or seasonal workforces, including transportation, retail, healthcare, consulting, and global services companies.

Related:Flaws in Passkey Implementation Show Old Attacks Still Work

Yubico is entering a market where identity providers and verification specialists already offer overlapping onboarding and recovery capabilities. Microsoft Entra's verified account recovery became generally available in May, using identity verification to help users regain access and register authentication methods without relying on a conventional manual help-desk process. Nametag and HYPR — both planned YubiID integration partners — also sell workforce verification and recovery capabilities. Beyond Identity already connects Nametag's identity checks to passkey enrollment and recovery, while 1Kosmos combines identity verification with passwordless authentication.

YubiID's differentiator is connecting verification and enrollment across platforms, rather than tying the workflow to a single identity provider, Chong maintains. Yubico also brings its hardware business into those relationships: It makes the devices where many customers' authentication credentials reside. Chong connects that experience with the challenge of distributing keys, verifying recipients, and enrolling replacements across a global workforce.

Hardware is not required. Support for credentials on mobile devices could appeal to customers who find hardware key distribution too difficult. Those customers haven't necessarily rejected the keys' security benefits; rather, the logistics are "sometimes quite challenging," Chong says.

Federal agencies could also use employees' existing PIV credentials to establish their identities when enrolling FIDO credentials on YubiKeys or mobile authenticators, Chong says, while noting that those workflows are future potential capabilities and not fully available at launch.

Separately, Yubico announced a public beta program for a post-quantum-ready YubiKey. The beta YubiKey will support NIST-standardized post-quantum algorithms, though it did not specify which ones. Yubico has tested early implementations with Chrome and Firefox, with early keys sent to federal labs and hyperscalers. The company expects to submit the key for FIPS validation within about a year, depending on beta testing and customer feedback, although completion is not guaranteed.

Despite being "crypto-agile," Chong confirms that the beta devices cannot receive firmware upgrades, meaning organizations would later need to replace those keys if different algorithms are required.

"Doing firmware upgrades safely across the Web is not trivial," he says.

A June executive order directs agencies to transition high-value assets and high-impact systems to post-quantum cryptography for key establishment by the end of 2030 and digital signatures by the end of 2031. Organizations evaluating the beta keys will need to test both the new cryptography and the process for replacing and enrolling devices.

Yubico ultimately envisions providing verifiable proof that a person authorized a specific AI agent action, but Chong confirms that agent-authorization capabilities are not part of this launch. While the combination of Yubico's back-end services, applications, and hardware keys forms the foundation for additional use cases, for now the YubiID service focuses on verifying people, enrolling credentials, and handling recovery.

"In a simple way to look at it, we're offering an end-to-end solution rather than just a YubiKey solution," Chong says.
