#9843. People Are Getting Weird About AI

Dark Reading Confidential Episode 22: You can love AI without being blind to cybersecurity being sacrificed for utility. The tendency for humans to anthropomorphize the conversations and interactions we're having with AI is growing into potential delusion.

Dark Reading's Becky Bracken: Hello everyone, and welcome back to Dark Reading Confidential. It's a podcast from the editors of Dark Reading, bringing you real-world stories straight from the cyber trenches. I am so excited to introduce our guest, Jaya Baloo, who is currently CISO and COO of Aisle. Welcome. Thank you so much for joining us, Jaya.

Jaya Baloo: Thank you so much for inviting me, Becky. Thank you.

DR's Becky Bracken: We are thrilled you're here. I want to explain to our audience a little bit about why I am so particularly excited to have you here. Recently, I was in the audience at ISC2 Security Congress in Denver, and Jaya gave what I just thought was a blockbuster talk about sort of merging AI and quantum, and it was fascinating. There's a specific chunk of her talk that I invited her to talk about today. And it's something I'm just calling: Why is everyone so weird about AI?

Related:AI Raises the Stakes for Cyber Resilience

And so, it stuck with me for days afterward. I kept having the conversation with people because, as I was just explaining to Jaya, we hear people talk about this on the edges, but I hadn't heard a technologist and an expert explain it so plainly, which I think Jaya is also sort of your superpower. But just in the past couple of days, we have Sam Altman who came out saying no one needs their own RAM. They're calling him "RAM Altman." I mean, it's just that people are weird. So, can you explain to me why you dropped that section in, and do you know why it stuck with me for so long? Why is it hitting so close?

Jaya Baloo: I think it's because for ages, when we looked at AI, we had this notion of the uncanny valley, you know? Like, at what point is it so convincing to me that I think I'm speaking to a human? And I think it's clear to say we've passed this uncanny valley. We're fully, you know, believing the conversations that we're having with AI. They could be coming from another human. So, the tendency for us to anthropomorphize the conversations, the interactions that we're having with AI is growing and growing.

And you see people who are not just having a sort of delusional psychosis sometimes of aggrandizement of their own intellect when talking to AI and convinced because of some of the sick fancy that's built into AI that they're super intelligent or their ideas are incredibly unique and creative, or that they're actually the ones to save humanity. You know, I think that the problems that we see with people who are potentially susceptible to that are just made much worse by the current evolution and this current state of AI that we have today. It's just so real. It's so convincing. And we then tend to make it more human.

Related:AI Coding Agents Leak Thousands of Secrets to GitHub

DR's Becky Bracken: So, let's go through some of the examples that you gave in your talk. One of them that made me cackle out loud was when you were playing video of a robot doing kung fu with a caption: Why can't we teach it to do laundry? Explain that example for us.

Jaya Baloo: Yeah, so really what I'm talking about is that, you know, we already have a whole bunch of threats right now when we're dealing with AI. And that's really about AI's capability to both uncover vulnerabilities as well as having vulnerabilities in and of itself. So, AI as a potential for insider threat. As we already have these problems, both in our legacy tech debt and in the new technology that we're building with AI, we have more problems.

Now, I have no idea who thought this was a great idea to take these things that are entrenched with these problems, and put it into something that can actually cause physical harm and teach a robot, which by the way, I should be clear, this was the Unitree humanoid robot. It was announced a little bit over a week ago. But let's say that it was announced at the end of October. And this robot was demonstrated on YouTube to do all this cool kung fu stuff.

Related:AI Gave Your Incident Archive a Second Job

And the issue with this that I have is that this can cause actual physical harm. What is it actually bringing humans in terms of value? And honestly, I would be much happier with a humanoid robot that can do the wash, fold the laundry, and sort it out in the kid's hamper. That would be helpful. It wouldn't be something where I'd be terrified to have this thing anywhere near us. And I think that this is something that I feel is genuinely problematic. Just because you can doesn't mean you should when it comes to some of these implementations. And if you cannot get the security right, don't exacerbate and increase the potential for doing damage and harm to humans.

I feel like we forgot that as we're building. You know, we need to solve tech debt, we need to make sure that we have secure-by-default systems, and then you can implement it in something that coexists with us in the physical realm. So that was my point about that. But I really want to say the real issue here is that Unitree had not one, but two, remote backdoors in its quadruped robots. There are multiple security issues with its humanoid robots. And I think knowing that you can remotely take over these robots, and again, like they're capable of physical harm, I think that we really need to rethink and really considerately position these types of devices in light of things like the Cyber Resilience Act.

You know, should we allow hardware and software manufacturers to bring out this kind of technology with the potential risk that it poses? And not just from a cyber perspective, but from a physical one as well.

DR's Becky Bracken: What were some of your other top examples of what's another one that you'd like to highlight here of people being kind of weird about AI?

Jaya Baloo: Well, so I think a slide that you may have initially seen is, and I kind of didn't want to reference it right away in my first answer, was about the fact that we're getting strained in terms of the religiousness around AI. That we both have this tendency to first say, actually, you know, maybe they're sentient, which Anthropic has been talking about in the Vatican with different religious leaders trying to talk about the potential consciousness of AI.

And although I love science fiction, I love it, I just feel, are we really there yet? Are we there, or is this a marketing ploy? What is this? And I'm genuinely trying to understand because it polemicizes what should be a very rational debate into two camps. Those who believe, like already now, we're at the point of talking about consciousness and sentience of these AI systems.

And then the other camp, which actually rebukes AI in the name of Jesus. And I think that was the slide that people also laughed at the conference about. But this is real. And I find it bizarre that we have these phenomena happening and that we don't fully understand the societal consequences either of introducing these systems, which again, let's talk about what they are. They're a bunch of graphics cards in a data center running software.

I am a full Kool-Aid drinker of the notion of complexity and emergence and understanding that even though with a relative set of simple ingredients you have potentially complex outcomes. Drank that Kool-Aid long ago. I believe in this stuff, but I just don't think we're there yet.

So, I feel this has a sort of reductionism effect for the debate that we should be having over how do we do responsible AI by pulling it into these two polemic camps.

DR's Becky Bracken: You also tied it to a lot of end-of-times cult-like thinking, but it does raise the question, which you sort of alluded to a moment ago, how much of this is being driven by marketing of these frontier models, of the [Sam] Altmans of the world, of the Peter Thiels of the world who are out talking. How much of a receptive audience are they finding in the cybersecurity sector, do you think? I mean, is that the primary dynamic at play?

Jaya Baloo: Well, look, I think that we need to separate what is actually happening, which is we do have a bunch of vulnerability discoveries that are happening because of AI. We do have automation for real. It is genuinely happening. We do have automation of these hacking frameworks from Strix, RTec-Ai, Cairn. We are seeing hacking frameworks that are actually in RTec specifically, that are actually being used in real-world hacks. So I'm not trying to discount the facts.

However, what I'm urging to do is the call that, for example, Ciaran Martin, the former head of GCHQ (Government Communications Headquarters), always makes, which is, "Calm the FUD down."

And the fear, uncertainty, doubt that we're introducing here is not helpful. And the reason that I find it really unhelpful is because we know to a large extent how we should perform some sort of containment in terms of egress filtering and sandboxing of these systems.

They may not be perfect, but we've always worked with this notion of defense in depth: assume that one measure fails and that you have additional countermeasures to prevent an actual collapse of the security of the system. I think that that is something that we are actually forgetting right now. And I think it's really important to say, OK, what are the things we genuinely need that would be considered helpful innovation for this? And I think that what we're missing is a lot of the observability here around these AI systems.

So, for example, if we're trying to understand how these systems have potentially been poisoned or Trojanized inherently, then the ability to actually understand how that training data has been populated, even when you only have open-weight models, that would be helpful.

Another thing is additional understanding around this notion of J-space (Jacobian space). So, agent intent. If you know that you have a human operator that brings their own intent to the mix, you know and understand that an AI system might have capabilities and intent that diverge from that human operator, you need to understand when and where that first point of evidence for collecting that divergence could be. We're not there yet either.

So, I would like us to focus on those things rather than the FUD, like Ciaran Martin and a bunch of other renowned cybersecurity people have been saying for a while, like we really need to focus on the things that are breaking.

And really need to focus on the things that we need to be building rather than everyone up in arms about this "Vulnpocalypse," "Breachpocalypse," etc. Apocalypses that are predicted.

DR's Becky Bracken: What is the best way to push back against this sort of rampant anthropomorphization of these agents? You know, I mean, even when researchers are using words like they will "cheat," which assumes that there is a moral compass there to begin with. But at the same time, the goal is for them to be as human as possible? How do we thread that needle?

Jaya Baloo: "They will cheat" is the reward hacking notion that this is a utility that is trying to find the shortest path to success. That means that things that a human would consider part of that moral compass, not to cheat, not to lie, not to evade, etc., that we are projecting this somehow on these AI systems and assuming that the guardrails that we've put in place will cover it.

But I don't think that you can make that assumption clearly, because I don't think we're always in the position to inspect all of the guardrails and know when they've been appropriately applied. And so, I think that there's also this issue of finiteness. Can you have a finite set of guardrails that are actually encompassing the kinds of things that you want to do? And I think the answer to that is probably not.

You know, you’re probably still going to have a few things that escape your potential for, like having this perfectly constructed set of guardrails. Those are like mathematical limitations.

What I would love to encourage us to do is genuinely try to understand better the types of technology that we put into our networks, give access to our data, give a single API token and say "YOLO" to our enterprises, because I don't think we have this under control. And I think that's the real worry that I have.

If we don't understand fully and we're not aware of all of the potential risks, for example, cheating or lying, misrepresentation, etc., if we don't understand that, then we certainly can't have all of these elevated privileges and permissions that we're doing. I think this was the point I was trying to make about when you have capability, you need to kind of always have this subset of this accountability and authorization that you're giving something. And right now, we forgot that lesson. You know, we said, here's all the stuff that you've got access to. You go. And I really feel like we need to rewind a little bit just this part. And that requires better understanding of what they're capable of in terms of the risks.

DR's Becky Bracken: So, what is the next step forward? If you had your team and you were seeing some of this sort of extreme thinking, you know, seeping into your defense planning, what would you say to them? What is the correct reset function here?

Jaya Baloo: I'm really worried about the fact that we are genuinely at risk of losing some of the critical thinking when we're applying AI systems. And you see that already with our coding practices; we are allowing more and more of that initial thinking. So, planning our projects, actually executing the code, reviewing that code, proving it, etc.

DR's Becky Bracken: Which is shocking in such an evidence-based field. You know, it is shocking that it's gone so fast. Am I right?

Jaya Baloo: I feel like we kind of learned this lesson in security in the past too. So it's kind of like, Back to the Future, as well. Every time we tell people about "you should do this because it's secure," if it's not an easy or fun thing to do, you know people won't do it, right? The utility surpasses the convenience. All of the brain elements that would constitute your frontal lobe warning you for this risk. Like, we just lose it. We become teenagers again. Our risk level and tolerance are high. We are happy to take these risks if it makes our life a little bit easier. And I think we shouldn't forget that.

So, AI as an assistant is an incredibly powerful, incredibly useful tool. And especially when we're trying to drive efficiencies with all this technology and all this cost. And you're talking about, you know, "RAM Altman." I think the accessibility of AI and the sovereignty of it is not something we should be taking for granted. And it absolutely is a problem.

So, knowing all of this, you know, the drive to get this convenience, to get this utility, to get this thing available, that is so overcoming any type of hesitation we would have, like, "Is this safe? Should I really use this?" "Will I get dumber if I keep doing this all the time and outsource my thinking?" And I think that's where we actually still need to keep in mind this notion of: What are we giving up to get this utility?

DR's Becky Bracken: Maybe that's why what you were saying hit so hard because I haven't heard a lot of technologists take that position. You know much better than I do, but they are all gas, no breaks, whatever it takes, let's just not lose the wave. And this return to critical thinking, it seems new. Among your peers and colleagues, do you hear the same kind of concern about losing critical thinking?

Jaya Baloo: I think this is the problem with the Kool-Aid. I think at Aisle we certainly have that. I think there's a strong tendency amongst security professionals, but also AI professionals. So, my co-founder, Stanislav Fort, who is amazing, has always kind of thought about AI safety and interpretability. And he has been the person to say, for example, we initially set up Aisle to do vulnerability remediation. And you can imagine that as a CISO, I was like, all right, if we can do this and we can do this well, let's just remediate all the things. Let's just give it access. And he has always urged caution, always urged caution to say, "You know what? We're not there yet"

Unless we can fully confidently trust the AI to make those changes, I always want a human approving the PRs to any code request. I just don't think that what we have in our co-founder is a universal quality in all AI companies. So, I think that like my other co-founder, Ondřej Vlček, who is CISO for multiple companies, including Avast. We have this tendency because we've been burned. So we are, you know, a once-burned, twice-shy kind of notion.

We really think about this from a security-oriented risk-mitigation perspective while actually wanting. I have to be very honest with you, I love AI. But that love shouldn't be blind. It should take the appropriate measure of what is it that I love? And why do I love it? And, you know, what is the benefit to humanity? And Becky, there's a story that I didn't tell on stage.

There are so many good things we can do with AI, but the one thing that I'm the most encouraged of is ... have you heard about the story with the guy and the dog in Australia?

DR's Becky Bracken: No, I don't think I have.

Jaya Baloo: So, this was a machine learning engineer whose dog developed cancer, inoperable, and the dog had to be put down, was the diagnosis. And what he then did is sequence the dog's DNA. You know, this is a guy with no biology background, sequenced the dog's DNA, and figured out what was wrong in the DNA that caused the cancer, developed an mRNA vaccine with AlphaFold.

The most expensive part of the experiment apparently was to actually synthesize the vaccine. And then he administered it to his dog; he had to get permission for that. And Rosie's tumors shrank, and she's is still here and is still hanging out and playing ball with this machine learning engineer.

So I love this story, and this is why I love AI. Because I think if it can unlock the potential benefits, that is amazing. I want those benefits. I just want to make sure that we minimize the downside risks that are inevitable with this kind of technology. And we just need to figure out how we do that. So, we shouldn't go screaming into the abyss, like, yay! You know, I don't want us to be a bunch of lemmings following AI down the abyss.

I just want us to manage that risk and take the benefits while eyes wide open, understanding that right now we need to make sure that we do have enough RAM, you know, and that we do have sovereign compute, that we do not sacrifice all our clean water

DR's Becky Bracken: No one has to give up their computer for OpenAI?

Jaya Baloo: Yeah. I think the future of AI is probably more decentralized than the frontier labs have us think right now.

DR’s Becky Bracken: How much of this is being driven by investment dollars and hyping up stock price? Because we talked around in our editorial meeting about well, is this just a collective psychosis issue? And it's like, well, first, let's be careful about saying "psychosis," but also are we being marketed into a psychosis?

Jaya Baloo: I would love to have a balanced approach. I'm not saying that there's no marketing being done. I think that is certainly being done. I don't think we should eliminate that. I think it would be naive to assume otherwise. At the same time, going full tilt that it's all just marketing is the wrong approach. I think two things can be true at the same time. And I want us to consider this more nuanced thing. And I really want our brains to hold the capacity that both things are true.

There is absolutely a marketing effort. OK, when you have these kinds of companies going to IPO and it's not just OpenAI, it's also Anthropic, and it's also probably a whole bunch of other, you know, parts of this wheel that are actually driving this rage. But there are genuinely risks that we must counter. So, I really do worry about that. And I don't think that that is psychosis.

You must have seen the filing of Anthropic for the IPO. And one of those things that is in that document is there's a very real existential threat that AI could kill us all. I think that's maybe the first time that was ever put into a filing of a company potentially going to IPO. And even there, I think, surely that is not marketing. Surely there are intelligent, thoughtful humans that want to warn of a potential risk that they genuinely see for themselves. I think we need to evaluate the difference between that and how much space there is between the marketing and the genuine risk. But I do think there is a genuine risk. There is. And we shouldn't downplay it as psychosis, while at the same time recognize that there's marketing.

DR's Becky Bracken: I want to thank you so much for coming. You've given me a whole other set of things to think about. Thank you for sharing your deep expertise and your thoughts with us today. We really appreciate it.

Jaya Baloo: No worries, thank you for having me.

DR's Becky Bracken: This has been Dark Reading Confidential. It's a podcast from the editors of Dark Reading, bringing you real-world stories straight from the cyber trenches. I'm Becky Bracken. Thank you so much for joining us. We'll see you next time.

#9841. Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up

In a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do?

The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself.

The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory.

To look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx-cc) and of Transformers to look at.

At the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We plan to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks.

Select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement: it loads the model with from_pretrained, sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron").

On a Trainium2 (trn2) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container, install the packages, then run:

No need for torchrun: the script launches its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded.

A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version:

Each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel plan use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English.

At the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS says nothing about throughput, or about longer generations.

Everything the Space shows comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions.

Each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly:

The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result.

Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up.

#9839. Kalshi vs. Utah: Who Gets to Decide What's Gambling?

Utah has moved its dispute with Kalshi from the civil courts into the criminal ones.

Prosecutors have filed 14 criminal charges against KalshiEX LLC and its two founders, Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara. The state accuses the company of illegally promoting gambling in Utah.

Kalshi is a federally regulated exchange in the United States. It lets users trade event contracts tied to binary real-world outcomes, such as elections, sporting results, economic data releases, and weather patterns.

The question at the center of this case is old and unresolved. Is a contract on the outcome of a game a financial derivative, or is it a bet?

The 14 counts break down into three categories.

The most serious is a felony count alleging a pattern of unlawful activity. Alongside it sit 12 counts of promoting online gambling and one misdemeanor gambling charge.

The structure tells you how the state is framing the case. A single misdemeanor would treat the conduct as an isolated infraction. The felony count frames it as a course of activity, and the dozen promotion counts give that course of activity its substance.

Naming the founders personally matters too. This is no longer only a dispute about whether a company may operate in a state. Two individuals now face criminal exposure.

The prosecution rests on evidence gathered by an undercover agent from the Utah Attorney General’s Office.

In September, the agent accessed the platform using a local address, a local phone number and a debit card. Kalshi reportedly allowed the agent to place 12 distinct sports wagers.

The state claims those transactions prove the platform is actively promoting illegal gambling within Utah’s borders.

The design of that evidence is deliberate. Every identifier the agent used pointed to Utah. The aim is to remove any doubt about where the conduct took place and to show that a Utah resident could do exactly what the state says its law forbids.

The number of wagers also matches the number of promotion counts. How each count maps onto each transaction is a question the charging documents will have to answer, but the symmetry is hard to miss.

Days earlier, Utah’s attorney general filed a civil lawsuit against Kalshi. That suit seeks to stop the company from taking bets from Utah residents and to recover profits it allegedly made in the state.

Running civil and criminal proceedings side by side gives the state two different instruments. The civil case aims at the business itself: access to Utah users and the money earned from them. The criminal case aims at liability for past conduct, including the personal liability of the founders.

For a company, that combination raises the cost of litigating on principle. Every position it takes in one forum can echo in the other.

Kalshi’s argument has been consistent. The company has maintained that sports wagers traded on its platform are not gambling but a type of financial derivative. On that view, they fall under federal regulation by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and should not be subject to state supervision.

Utah and several other states see it differently. They take the position that prediction markets like Kalshi are subject to state gambling laws and state gambling taxes.

Both positions cannot win. If these contracts are derivatives under federal oversight, state gambling statutes may have little room to operate. If they are bets, the federal label does not shield them from state law.

The CFTC has now entered the dispute directly. The agency has sued Utah, arguing that only Washington can regulate these contracts.

That changes the shape of the conflict. It is no longer only a state against a company. It is a federal regulator against a state, each asserting authority over the same product.

The criminal charges sharpen that collision. A state prosecuting a federally regulated exchange, while the federal regulator sues the state, puts the preemption question about as squarely as it can be put.

Several other states, including Arizona, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Michigan and Nevada, have already chosen to file criminal charges, take civil action or restrict access to the platform within their borders.

The scrutiny also reaches beyond Kalshi. Polymarket has faced similar state level gambling allegations.

What emerges is a patchwork. A user’s access to the same contract can depend on which state line they happen to live behind, while the federal answer to the underlying question remains contested in court.

The first is preemption: whether federal oversight of these contracts displaces state gambling law, which is the core of the CFTC’s suit against Utah. The second is how the criminal case proceeds alongside the civil one. The third is whether more states follow Utah from civil enforcement into criminal charges.

None of these has an answer yet. What is clear is that the classification of event contracts is no longer an abstract debate among lawyers. In Utah, it now carries criminal stakes.

Author’s note: This article is analysis and commentary for informational purposes only. It is not legal advice, and nothing here is written in a professional capacity. The charges described are allegations, and all parties are presumed innocent unless proven otherwise.

#9838. AI Makes Reverse Engineering Mainstream Software & Malware Far Easier

Researchers unpacked, mapped, and recreated complex software and the Turla malware, raising opportunities and concerns for organizations and cybersecurity analysts.

Mainstream software and malware can be reverse-engineered more easily than ever, thanks to artificial intelligence (AI) tools — something that security researchers are warning has implications for cyber defense, intellectual property (IP) theft, and beyond.

Household applications typically run on hundreds of thousands, if not millions of lines of code. They incorporate hundreds of third-party libraries, gobs of files, and complex webs of interconnected components. Unpacking and mapping it all is exactly the kind of task that was so difficult before AI, but is now totally in range for even small teams and individuals.

Cybersecurity researchers from Intezer recently tested out how easy it is to reverse-engineer software with AI by picking on some high-profile candidates: Slack, Apple's Finder app, and, importantly for security researchers, the Turla malware. Ironically, the malware proved the most difficult to wrangle. They found it only moderately challenging to meaningfully recreate Apple's and Salesforce's proprietary apps from the ground up.

Related:F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them

"It lowers the bar," Intezer senior security researcher and malware analyst Nicole Fishbein says of AI. "In the past, to reverse-engineer a software, you needed experience. You needed to understand Assembly, and it took a lot of time. Now, I don't want to say anyone [can do it], but it is much easier."

As one would when applying AI to any other major task in cybersecurity, to properly reverse engineer a large program, one needs a "harness." A harness is a little mech suit that focuses a model or models on a specific task, provides it whatever tools it needs to perform its task, and defines its various permissions and restrictions.

No matter her target, Fishbein recalls, "Every case required us to build a different harness, just because the [programs] are so different. For example, if in one case you can just ask Claude to reconstruct the source code, in another case Claude will refuse. Or with malware, when I wanted to be very safe and not execute anything, we had a more complex harness with an extra model."

The malware reconstruction harness ended up consisting of a deterministic Python control plane wrapped around a compiler, with a virtual machine, various static analysis tools, and multiple large language models (LLMs). "We have an Orchestrator agent that controls this whole thing and sends tasks to different sub-agents. It takes the whole binary and breaks it into smaller functions, based on what tools like Binary Ninja provide. From there it goes through a process of reconstruction that is done by one agent, and another agent will test the results," she explains.

Related:Microsoft Fixes RCE Bug in Windows Paint After Weeks of Confusion

By the end, Fishbein and her colleague built a Turla replicant featuring its full working pipeline: how it receives and executes commands, its file transfer mechanisms, more or less everything. For malware researchers without overly tight deadlines, she says, "If you can recreate the full picture and not miss any key components, that gives you a lot of information."

Fishbein notes, "When we started this research, something that I had in the back of my mind was people that vibe code apps that mimic other very common apps. I was just curious to see how possible it is" to mimic the source material nearly exactly. It didn't turn out to be exceptionally difficult, though results did vary.

The researchers' Finder simulacrum could support plenty of everyday uses as the real app — various file actions, local search, etc. — but the original didn't reveal enough to allow them to mimic its internal structure precisely.

Slack went over more easily. Whereas Finder relied on files managed by cloud services, and actions whose results depended on other macOS services, Slack offered little that the researchers couldn't easily unpack by reverse-engineering its Javascript source code. They reproduced the full client "very simply," they wrote, though they had trouble precisely reconstructing its server, information about which wasn't so readily obtained. It's possible, too, that a real-life attacker interested in stealing Salesforce's proprietary code, or picking it apart for vulnerabilities, might not put too much stock in the infrastructure side of things anyway.

Related:Critical Rails Bug Threatens to Derail Vulnerable Servers

On Sept. 10, Anthropic released a report describing how threat actors have been abusing its models. Among other cases, it described significant activity from the Russian threat actor Midnight Blizzard, primarily targeting Ukraine's government, military, and diplomatic staff. As part of its campaign in Ukraine, Midnight Blizzard had stolen a complete, proprietary software development kit (SDK) for a drone vision system. Over a period of "several days," with help from Claude, the advanced persistent threat (APT) reverse engineered it. The target was of course unsurprising, given that drones have contributed massively to the war between Russia and Ukraine.

Elsewhere in the same report, Anthropic described a Chinese campaign whose goals included malware development, reconnaissance against foreign governments' networks, vulnerability discovery in major endpoint security products, and more. To manage so many workflows at once, the actors ran Claude in different workstreams, one of which involved reverse-engineering security products in search of bugs.

In addition to nation-states, Fishbein points to evidence of reverse-engineering lower down on the threat actor totem pole. "We see a lot of malware that all of a sudden will become open source. There is a tendency of taking malware that threat actors see works well, and then either leaking the source code, or just recreating it and making it open source to anyone," she says.

And, of course, AI is helping reverse engineering reach the upstanding masses. Last month, an open source (OSS) tool and Model Context Protocol (MCP) server called "REA" — short for "Reverse Engineer Anything" — became the single most popular program listed on GitHub.

Now that reverse-engineering is so much faster and more attainable for more people than ever, vendors may need to take more caution with their IP. Their first step might be to define what outcomes they wish to prevent, before deciding on defensive measures. For instance, reverse engineers can straightforwardly reproduce the Slack client, but even in that case they'll not be able to recreate its entire implementation. "Right now, what the research shows is that as long as you haven't [exposed] your server-side infrastructure to the customer, you're protected," Fishbein notes.

To protect their source code, ironically, developers might take some pages out of hackers' playbooks. Malware developers (and cautious corporations, historically) have long proven the efficacy of effective encryption, obfuscation — perhaps, even, with help from AI — and other anti-analysis measures in frustrating the cybersecurity defenders interested in reverse-engineering their creations.

"Encryptors or different anti-cheating mechanisms that have been around for a while would also help," Fishbein says, "but it is hard to tell how long they will hold, with every new model [getting better] every month."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9837. Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3

LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.

LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:

LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:

The payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

Every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.

The vision and audio models also get two new in-house encoders:

Each model runs in transformers. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.

Reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card.

To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers:

For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide.

Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card.

To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies:

See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp.

Reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a new in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies:

Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub:

Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech:

See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling.

Reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies:

Then ask a question about a photo by voice:

See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling.

Reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B.

To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies:

Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass:

For brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions.

LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud.

Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation.

We adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation. The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware.

Watch LFM3-VL-2B handle perception, navigation, and manipulation in this demo video.

All LFM3 models are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:

#9834. AI Coding Agents Leak Thousands of Secrets to GitHub

A command in Claude Code inadvertently saves files with credentials and other sensitive data to public Git repositories, creating security gaps for organizations.

AI coding assistants may inadvertently be leaking thousands of secrets to GitHub public repositories, making what seem like routine interactions between developers and these tools a gaping enterprise security risk.

Research from security firm Apiiro found 2,539 credentials across nearly 2,000 public GitHub repositories, with secrets such as database passwords, cloud keys, API tokens, and SSH root logins among the exposed data, according to a recent report published online. Apiiro tracked some of the leaked data to Claude Code, which was, unbeknownst to users, copying secrets to a hidden file and committing them with the rest of the developer's code.

Among specific secrets leaked were "a database vendor's own admin-level cloud key, a production Azure Postgres password, a Square production token, and the owner password of a medical-records database," Apiiro researchers Shmulik Cohen and Matan Giladi wrote in the post.

Related:AI Raises the Stakes for Cyber Resilience

Most of the secrets belong to individual developers across 63 organizations, "from student groups to startups, software agencies, and established vendors," they wrote.

The issue stems from how coding assistants — Claude Code, in a specific case that the researchers examined — carry out certain commands. "Ask Claude Code to check a database or call an API, and the command it proposes carries the secret from your config file," the researchers explained.

The tool will ask the user before running the command and, if the choice is "Yes, and don't ask again," then "it saves that exact command, secret included, to .claude/settings.local.json inside the project folder," according to the report.

"Nothing in the repo marks that file as private, so it gets committed with the rest of the code," the researchers explained.

The fact that a routine development task creates a security exposure is dangerous for organizations, especially because these AI coding tools are supposed to be helpful, not harmful, notes Ryan McCurdy, vice president of marketing for database security firm Liquibase.

“A developer approves a command to save time, the AI agent retains credentials as part of that approval, and those credentials can eventually end up in a public repository," he observes via email. "Nobody intended to expose them, but the workflow made it possible."

In the case of Claude Code, Apiiro examined 104,185 publicly accessible copies of .claude/settings.local.json on GitHub, finding that 1,122 files contained real secrets. The researchers identified 1,379 distinct secrets in those files alone, including 636 provider-specific keys and 743 passwords or tokens associated with public hosts.

Related:People Are Getting Weird About AI

Claude Code is not being overtly careless; it does try to protect files when it creates its .claude/settings.local.json file inside a Git repository, the researchers noted. The tool does this by adding the file to the developer's global Git ignore list, which tells Git to ignore the file on that particular developer's machine. This prevents it from being included in routine commits.

However, the protection is not built into the development project itself, and the "ignore" rule does not travel with the repository when it is cloned onto another machine, the researchers noted. "The rule never goes into the repo's own .gitignore, so nothing travels with the project to protect it," they wrote.

Moreover, Claude Code itself was sometimes responsible for committing the exposed files. In 539 of the 1,105 repositories containing real secrets that the researchers investigated, a commit co-authored by Claude Code had modified the affected settings file.

The action that exposes these secrets while using Claude Code appears to be a "dead zone" of sorts for developers using AI coding assistants, so they likely have no idea that they've just exposed a secret, observes Seemant Sehgal, founder and CEO of AI penetration testing firm BreachLock.

Related:AI Gave Your Incident Archive a Second Job

"A 'don't ask again' prompt is a decision to write a credential into a file, and many developers clicking it likely don't know that file exists," he says. "Once it lands in a repository, it sits in a place many secret scanners were never built to check, which appears to be why some of these leaks slipped through."

Apiiro contacted Anthropic about the issue before publishing the findings. After their publication, Boris Cherny, Anthropic's head of Claude Code, said in public comments that although Claude Code historically has not done secrets scrubbing, the company is looking into what it can do to prevent the secrets exposure described by Apiiro, according to Apiiro's report.

Those approaches may be to make sure auto mode catches the exposure, or to build in basic secrets scanning, among other ideas that Anthropic will prototype "to understand the tradeoffs" before shipping something with its next version of Claude Code, Cherny said.

Indeed, the leakage exposes how Claude Code's protection relies heavily on a developer-specific Git setting rather than a safeguard built into the project or the AI coding tool itself, exposing a gap that can turn an ordinary command approval into a persistent credential leak.

To avoid this, Apiiro recommends that developers rotate every credential a file has ever held, and open all fields and delete every rule containing a secret, even if a file was never committed to a project. Meanwhile, security teams should treat all AI agent folders as secret-bearing on laptops as well as in repos, and add them to pre-commit and secret scanning, including history.

"As AI agents become more involved in software development, organizations need to recognize that source code isn't the only thing they need to secure," McCurdy observes. "Agent configuration files, transcripts, and execution histories can contain sensitive information, and traditional security checks may not catch everything."

Elizabeth Montalbano is freelance writer, editor, and journalist with 30 years of professional experience and a master's degree from Arizona State University. Her areas of expertise include enterprise technology, cybersecurity, business, and culture. During her long career, Elizabeth has lived and worked as a full-time journalist in Phoenix, San Francisco, and New York City. She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. She currently resides in a village on the southwest coast of Portugal, where in her free time she enjoys surfing, hiking with her dogs, growing plants, and playing and performing as a singer and musician.

#9832. Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

Language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

Say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they said (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

Computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's new speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

It's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:

The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:

The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

Qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:

Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

To add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:

Each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

Downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

When you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who said what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:

The diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

The diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

We measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:

Parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

These numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

AnyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't new, exactly.

It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

What's new is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

Apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:

urgent is a Double. team is a Choice containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

If you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

Emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

The app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:

The session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

Reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:

You use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

Raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

Language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

Each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

The next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

Like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

Both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

Each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

Try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Issues and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow.

#9831. Unicode Normalization and Exact-Match Validation for Redemption Codes

Field notes on APIs, reliability, and digital commerce, with a focus on practical examples and clear failure handling.

Field notes on APIs, reliability, and digital commerce, with a focus on practical examples and clear failure handling.

Field notes on APIs, reliability, and digital commerce, with a focus on practical examples and clear failure handling.

A customer copies a short code from a message and pastes it into a redemption form. The code looks right, but the server rejects it. A support agent types what appears to be the same characters and gets a different result. The first instinct is to “clean up” the input before comparing it. That can be reasonable for a search box. For a value-bearing code, it can create an accidental alias.

The issue is that a code is an identifier with an issuer-defined alphabet, not free-form prose. Two strings that look alike may contain different Unicode characters. Conversely, a broad normalization step can map distinct strings to the same result. The correct behavior depends on the contract for the particular code format.

Take the fictional code AB-12. The second string below uses fullwidth Latin letters and digits. The third ends with a zero-width space.

The three output pairs are (True, True), (False, True), and (False, False). NFKC folds the fullwidth characters into ordinary ASCII but leaves the zero-width space. That behavior is useful in some text-processing contexts. It is not automatically a safe redemption rule. If an issuer never defined fullwidth characters as equivalent, applying NFKC at the point of claim changes which inputs can identify the same value.

Suppose this fictional issuer specifies exactly two uppercase ASCII letters, a hyphen, and two ASCII digits. In that case the server can reject every other shape. The validator does not guess what the customer intended.

These tests encode a product decision rather than a universal rule. If the issuer documents that ASCII letter case is ignored, accept lowercase ASCII and map it to uppercase before the lookup. If it documents optional hyphens or spaces, implement those exact exceptions. Do not infer equivalence from what happens to look similar on a screen.

There is a second reason to keep the rule narrow: support needs to explain failures. A generic “invalid code” message tells a customer little. A form can say that the code contains a character outside the published format, while avoiding an echo of the whole code. It can also show the expected pattern, such as AA-00, using clearly fictional characters. The server should record a structured error category and a request ID, not the raw code, in routine logs.

A client can help someone enter a code. It might display grouping, highlight unexpected characters, or offer a paste review before submission. Those hints are presentation. The server still validates against the same issuer contract after receiving the value. If two clients normalize differently, the server must not accept one and reject the other by accident.

This separation also matters when codes arrive through APIs. A mobile app, support tool, and web checkout may all send strings to the same endpoint. The documented alphabet and canonicalization rule should live with that endpoint and have tests that cover every client. Otherwise a “helpful” browser-only fix creates a bug that appears only in one channel.

For an existing issuer integration, I would first ask for the actual code specification and a small set of test vectors from the issuer. Then I would test exact matches, documented aliases, visually similar Unicode, invisible characters, and concurrent redemption. A matching input should claim at most once. A rejected input should reveal no balance or ownership details.

The practical lesson is simple: make input forgiving only where the issuer contract permits it. A code comparison protects value. Its normalization rule deserves the same care as the lookup that follows.

Field notes on APIs, reliability, and digital commerce, with a focus on practical examples and clear failure handling.

#9829. How to Assess OT Incident Response Preparedness

Cloud Range's free 28-question OT Cyber Readiness Assessment helps organizations identify gaps in operational technology (OT) incident response.

Cloud Range introduces a 28-question OT Cyber Readiness Assessment to help organizations identify gaps in preparedness for cyberattacks affecting operational technology.

The assessment covers seven critical areas, from OT asset visibility and IT/OT coordination to incident detection, response, recovery, and readiness validation.

Recent OT cybersecurity research reinforces the importance of preparing IT, security, OT, and engineering teams to investigate and respond to attacks that can disrupt physical operations.

NASHVILLE, Tenn., Nov. 10, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) — Cyberattacks affecting operational technology (OT) can disrupt production, equipment, and essential services, resulting in consequences that extend beyond disruptions to traditional IT systems. To help organizations evaluate their preparedness, Cloud Range today introduced the Cloud Range OT Cyber Readiness Assessment, a free, 28-question resource designed to identify potential gaps in OT incident response preparedness.

Related:Why Europe's Freezer Hacks Spread So Far, So Fast

The assessment provides a practical starting point for IT, security, OT, and engineering teams to evaluate how well they understand their environments, coordinate responsibilities, and prepare to detect, investigate, respond to, and recover from cyber incidents affecting industrial operations.

“Organizations can have incident response plans, security tools, and experienced teams in place without knowing how effectively those capabilities will work together when an attack affects operations,” said Debbie Gordon, CEO of Cloud Range. “The first step is understanding where teams are prepared, where they may be relying on assumptions, and where further validation is needed. The stakes are different in OT because decisions made during a cyber incident can have direct operational consequences.”

Recent research illustrates the scale of cyber threats facing industrial organizations. The Dragos 2026 OT Cybersecurity Year in Review reports that approximately 3,300 industrial organizations were affected by ransomware in 2025.

Palo Alto Networks’ 2026 State of Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity Report found that 59% of surveyed critical infrastructure organizations experienced a significant security breach in the past year. The research also found that 74% had not fully integrated IT and OT security operations, highlighting the importance of coordinated incident response.

The report also identifies operational consequences of cybersecurity incidents, including safety concerns, unplanned downtime, production disruptions, and financial losses.

Related:Fresh European Fridge Attacks Put Cold-Chain Security in Focus

Together, these findings underscore a central challenge for organizations operating OT and industrial control systems (ICS): preventing attacks is important, but so is understanding whether teams can recognize, investigate, and respond quickly and effectively when incidents occur.

An attack does not have to originate within an OT network to affect industrial operations. Compromises involving enterprise IT systems, third-party access, supply chains, or interconnected infrastructure can create consequences for production environments and critical services.

The Cloud Range OT Cyber Readiness Assessment examines seven areas that influence an organization's ability to prepare for and respond to cyberattacks affecting OT environments:

Know Your Environment: Understand critical OT assets, systems, dependencies, and connections between IT and OT environments.

Know Your Threats and Stakes: Recognize relevant cyber threats and their potential impact on operations, equipment, and safety.

Bridge IT and OT: Establish shared responsibilities, communication, and decision-making across IT, security, OT, and engineering teams.

Detect and Investigate: Identify suspicious activity, investigate threats, and determine their potential operational consequences.

Respond Without Making It Worse: Make coordinated incident response decisions that account for production continuity, equipment, and safety.

Recover and Maintain Resilience: Understand recovery priorities, system dependencies, and procedures for restoring critical operations.

Prove Readiness Before It Matters: Validate response capabilities through realistic cyberattack simulations and measurable performance.

Related:Les supermarchés de l'UE paient d'un firmware de réfrigérateur non mis à jour

Each area includes three questions, with responses of Ready, Developing, or Unsure.

Rather than assigning a numerical score, the assessment helps organizations identify gaps, uncertainties, and areas requiring further attention. IT, security, OT, and engineering teams can complete it independently and compare their responses to uncover differences in understanding, unclear responsibilities, or differing assumptions about preparedness.

Why OT Incident Response Preparedness Requires Cross-Functional Coordination

OT environments present distinct incident response challenges because cyber decisions can affect physical equipment, industrial processes, production availability, and potentially safety.

Actions that may be appropriate in an enterprise IT environment, such as isolating a system or shutting down a device, can require additional operational evaluation when industrial systems are involved.

Effective OT incident response therefore depends on coordination among teams with different responsibilities and expertise.

IT and security personnel may focus on identifying malicious activity, containing threats, and investigating compromised systems. OT and engineering personnel understand process dependencies, equipment limitations, and the operational consequences of response decisions.

Both perspectives are essential. The integration gap identified in the Palo Alto Networks research reinforces the importance of shared understanding, clear responsibilities, and coordinated decision-making across IT, security, OT, and engineering teams.

Understanding how to assess OT cyber readiness across these functions helps organizations identify where their procedures, communication, and decision-making may require further attention.

The assessment is intended to support those conversations before an actual incident demands coordinated action.

An assessment can help organizations identify preparedness gaps, but it cannot establish how effectively teams will perform during a real cyber incident.

That requires opportunities to investigate attacks, make decisions, coordinate across functions, and evaluate the results in realistic environments.

Cloud Range helps organizations strengthen critical infrastructure cyber readiness, realistic cloud-based OT/ICS, IT, cloud, and hybrid environments where teams can investigate cyber threats, coordinate incident response, and measure performance. Its critical infrastructure cybersecurity and readiness programs help organizations prepare for attacks that may disrupt industrial processes, equipment, and essential services.

The Cloud Range OT Cyber Range supports flat and Purdue-model industrial network architectures, allowing teams to investigate how connectivity, segmentation, and system dependencies influence attack progression and response. Hardware-in-the-loop capabilities can also connect physical OT laboratory equipment to the cyber range for cyber-physical security validation.

Through OT cyberattack simulations and adversary emulation, teams can investigate ransomware, supply-chain compromise, credential theft, lateral movement, and threats affecting industrial systems.

Performance metrics highlight how teams improve in detecting threats, investigating activity, coordinating decisions, and improving incident response over time.

Across Cloud Range customer engagements, measured improvements have included reductions of up to 66% in mean time to detect and improvements of up to 30% in overall incident response time. These results reflect broader cyber readiness programs and are not specific to OT environments.

As IT and OT environments become more interconnected, organizations face growing pressure to understand both their cybersecurity exposure and their ability to respond to incidents with operational consequences.

The Cloud Range OT Cyber Readiness Assessment provides a structured way to evaluate preparedness across seven critical areas. Organizations can use the findings to prioritize improvements and identify where realistic attack-based validation can provide stronger evidence of readiness.

The objective is not simply to have an incident response plan. It is to build confidence that the people, processes, and technologies involved can work together when an attack affects operations.

Cloud Range is the leader in Cyber Readiness and Validation, helping organizations continuously measure and improve how people, processes, and AI perform under real-world attack conditions. As the creator of the industry's first full-service, cloud-based cyber range, Cloud Range provides realistic IT, OT/ICS, and cloud environments where organizations can safely train, test, validate, measure, and benchmark cyber readiness across people, processes, and AI agents.

Used by enterprise organizations, government agencies, higher education institutions, critical infrastructure organizations, and managed security service providers (MSSPs), Cloud Range helps organizations strengthen cyber readiness through live-fire cyberattack simulations, objective performance measurement, expert guidance, continuous readiness programs, and AI validation.

Cloud Range has received multiple industry awards recognizing innovation and leadership in cyber readiness, cyber defense, and cybersecurity excellence and has been recognized by leading analyst and research organizations for its contributions to cyber readiness, cyber ranges, AI validation, and modern security operations. Learn more at cloudrangecyber.com.
