#9824. Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

Today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

Participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to plan for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

But making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

The pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many new science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Figure 1. New public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

When organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an important part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

Publicly available genomic data has proved important in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support new research that others can build upon.

This is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

Making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an important first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

To explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026

The inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

Participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

Beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge

The CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be announced through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or company building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

We also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

#9823. F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them

New AI Harms Taxonomy traces how harm moves through AI systems, from misleading chatbot answers to compromised autonomous agents, and identifies where defenses can intervene.

LOS ANGELES (November 10, 2026) — AI now shapes how we search, communicate, decide and run our digital lives. But when it goes wrong, how does it actually hurt people? F-Secure’s new AI Harms Taxonomy maps 26 distinct harms to consumers, tracing the path each one takes to reach a person. The result is a clear view of where protections can step in, and who is in the best position to help.

Developed by Dr. Megan Squire, Principal Threat Intelligence Researcher at F-Secure, the taxonomy tackles a blind spot in how AI risk is discussed. Most frameworks list what could potentially go wrong, but stop short of connecting those harms to the systems and companies that could prevent them. F-Secure’s research goes further by mapping every layer between an AI-enabled threat and its impact on a consumer, then pinpointing where defenses need to go.

“As AI systems become more capable, the consequences of their mistakes can extend well beyond a bad answer,” said Dr. Squire. “The people building them have a responsibility to understand how they can fail and who gets hurt when they do, and to put safeguards in place before that harm happens.”

Related:AI Makes Reverse Engineering Mainstream Software & Malware Far Easier

The taxonomy reflects how the risks themselves are changing. It used to be a criminal going after a person directly, but now AI sits in the middle, which adds new players and new ways for things to go wrong. An assistant acting on someone’s behalf can be manipulated into doing damage, and a chatbot can mislead with complete confidence. Underneath, the trouble often starts in how an AI handles instructions and memory, or in the other services it’s connected to.

The research currently maps 26 harms across five relationship types and 19 intermediary layers, with 24 defenses designed to address risks at different points. Examples range from AI-generated voice and video impersonation to agents making harmful financial decisions, exposing personal information or acting on outdated context. It also examines attacks in which malicious instructions are hidden in content an AI system processes, potentially influencing what an agent does or what a chatbot tells a user.

One of the framework’s central findings is that responsibility for preventing AI harm is spread across several parties. Some risks can be handled by security software on a person’s own device. Others have to be dealt with further upstream, by the companies that build AI products and the systems behind them, including how an AI remembers things and which other services it connects to. Sorting out which is which makes it clear where a defense belongs and who has to build it. It also undercuts the idea that people can stay safe on their own just by spotting suspicious content or double-checking what an AI tells them.

Related:Microsoft Fixes RCE Bug in Windows Paint After Weeks of Confusion

This question of who’s responsible gets more urgent as AI moves from producing information to acting on it. A chatbot that gets an answer wrong can mislead someone, but at least that person is part of the exchange. An agent with access to a person’s accounts and the services linked to them can cause real consequences without that kind of back-and-forth. Protections need to be built around what these systems actually do, which starts with understanding how the two differ.

This research is part of a wider effort at F-Secure to build trust into the AI era. F-Secure Trust, announced alongside a strategic alliance with Quantum AI Lab QuTwo, is the company’s work on protecting people in a world where AI agents increasingly act for them. TrustGuard is designed to help protect people during AI interactions, while TrustPath aims to secure their digital journeys from discovery to delivery. The AI Harms Taxonomy gives that work a research foundation by spelling out the risks the protections need to address, and it makes clear that meaningful safeguards also depend on the companies building and running AI systems.

Related:Critical Rails Bug Threatens to Derail Vulnerable Servers

Today’s digital threats go far beyond just scams. F-Secure’s Illuminate Research team studies people and technology as they actually interact, exploring the messy realities of trust, deception, and online resilience in the AI era.

The AI Harms Taxonomy is available on the Illuminate Research Hub.

F-Secure is a human-first, AI-powered consumer cyber security experience company with 38 years of expertise in tackling digital threats. We help digital service providers turn trust into a high-value growth engine — protecting their customers while enabling them to live their best digital lives in a world of relentless, AI-driven scams. With billions of digital interactions secured each year, tens of millions of consumers protected globally, and over $10bn in partner value created, we deliver proven impact at scale.

#9822. Granite Switch 4.1.1 — Update models like you update software

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint.

Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.

#9821. Artex: The AI Pen-Test Tool Hackers Turned Into a Weapon

Forks of the open source Artex framework, along with 45 similar pen-testing tools, remain capable of executing credential attacks and cloud breaches at machine speed across multiple industries.

AI penetration-testing tool Artex has proven to be a boon for threat actors large and small, taking familiar attacker playbooks and deploying them at machine speeds — ushering in a potentially new era for defenders looking to get ahead of AI-enabled threats.

In July, independent developer Autumn-27 published Artex to GitHub, an open source, multiagent AI penetration testing framework written in Go. It is, by intention, a legitimate tool. However, as is so often the case with pen-test tools (such as, famously, Cobalt Strike), threat actors found a way to take advantage of it for malicious use. By late summer and early fall, a range of threat actors were using it as part of their toolkit.

Artex is capable of brute-forcing passwords, dumping databases, enumerating and abusing APIs, and more. This positions it for credential compromise and lateral movement in its own right, but the agentic element means Artex can operate at inhuman speeds. Microsoft saw an AI agent move from scanning GitHub for secrets to exfiltrating data from an Azure Key Vault in five minutes, for example.

Related:Inside an AI Attack Against a US Retailer

Steve Winterfeld, advisory CISO for Akamai, tells Dark Reading that while legitimate tool misuse is a known quantity, AI reduces the effort and expertise required to execute complex attacks. "What is particularly noteworthy about the Artex campaigns is the acceleration in speed, coordination, and autonomy," he says. "Activities that previously required deliberate integration can now be chained together and executed with limited hacking skills."

At the end of October, Artex's creator deleted the original GitHub repository due to rampant abuse, but many forks of the tool remain, so the threat remains. But even if all the forks went offline and Artex was no longer a going concern, the underlying threat of frameworks like it is far from over.

GitGuardian yesterday, for instance, detailed 45 different agentic attack frameworks (Artex "siblings" as the researchers called them) that are all capable of conducting attacks autonomously with the help of an AI model. Depending on the tool, these pen-testing frameworks are capable of end-to-end attacks against a network, Web application targeting, and/or autonomous coding. Some even include built-in command-and-control functionality. That's not to say these tools are inherently bad — pen-testing tools have many legitimate use cases — but it does illustrate the wide range of options for today's attacker.

The best-known incident to date involved China's Storm-0940, which adapted Artex source code into its own offensive infrastructure. Last month, around Oct. 10, the actor used the Artex framework to launch a massive password-spraying and credential-stuffing campaign against more than 300 specific user accounts at eight critical organizations, making more than 151,000 authentication requests in the process. On average, this represented 2,900 attempts per minute without triggering automated lockout or alert.

Related:CISA Announces Enhanced Reporting Form for Cyber Incidents

When this largely failed, Storm-0940 pivoted to target ConnectWise's internal infrastructure. Attackers exfiltrated trusted OAuth application credentials belonging to ConnectWise's Cloud Backup application, allowing them to compromise more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft 365 and Azure environments within three hours of initial targeting.

Abuse extends far beyond a single threat actor or objective. Microsoft last week published a blog post discussing how a financially motivated Cambodia-based threat cluster tracked as Storm-3358 started using Artex in its attacks against financial organizations primarily (but not exclusively) in Southeast Asia. Microsoft said it observed Storm-3358 using Artex in combination with conventional automated tools to scan systems connected to the public Internet, exploit vulnerabilities, and install open source remote access Trojans (RATs).

Related:Operação de influência russa tem como alvo generalizado a América Latina

Microsoft added that other threat actors have used Artex agents "to scan and exploit vulnerabilities in Web applications, use Web shells for persistence on compromised Web servers, compromise credentials from public sources and compromised systems, and use compromised cloud identities for persistence and data exfiltration."

CrowdStrike on Oct. 29 connected Artex-powered espionage activity to a threat actor it tracks as Vapor Panda, India's CERT (CERT-In) tracked a financially motivated threat actor hitting financial institutions, and as of Nov. 4, Censys observed more than 1,400 internet-exposed Artex console deployments. That said, because Internet exposure is not required for use, Censys estimated actual global use to be higher.

Recent Artex activity stands out because much of the story involves things security practitioners have seen time and time again. Pen-test tool abuse, nation-state tooling moving downstream to financially motivated attackers, password spraying, supply chain attacks, AI — it's a threat intelligence greatest hits album. But Guillaume Valadon, head of cybersecurity research at GitGuardian, tells Dark Reading what stands out to him most is the fast pace of attacks and the agent's initiative to accomplish the user's goals.

"At GitGuardian, we wanted to see how Artex handles secrets, so we ran it in a sealed lab," he says. "Artex ships no secret scanner, yet in every run where it acted, it found eight of the nine secrets. This included an AWS key recovered from git history. The model improvises on its hunt to reach the Artex user's goals."

Matt Snyder, Aviatrix head of security operations and threat research, says he was most surprised at how, despite the sophisticated nature of Artex's framework, the operational maturity of many threat actors deploying it appears to be low (given how many hosts remain Internet-exposed).

"AI is lowering the skill floor for offensive operations without improving operational discipline. The framework may be sophisticated, but the operational security surrounding many deployments is not," Snyder says. "This creates a dangerous combination in which more people can launch capable attacks, while poor security leaves their infrastructure, tooling, and potentially victim information exposed to anyone on the Internet."

Increasing sophistication for lower-grade attackers means, as always, defenders should be ready. Microsoft's Storm-3358 blog includes extensive indicators of compromise and recommends considering tools like defensive honeypots, which trick attackers into thinking they netted a valuable target.

Check Point advised in a blog post last week that organizations should expect greater automated pressure against exposed infrastructure. "Internet-facing systems should be continuously tested and hardened, with particular attention paid to weak authentication, exposed APIs, credential leakage, remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities and cloud storage permissions," the blog post read.

Censys principal security researcher Silas Cutler offered encouraging words. Because the underlying tradecraft is conventional, the fundamentals still hold, he said, "Enforce MFA, monitor your attack surface, and practice good credential hygiene."

#9820. November Patch Tuesday: An Overflowing Cornucopia of CVEs

Microsoft serves up an actively exploited Outlook zero-day, and a wave of critical Exchange, SharePoint, Windows Search, and LDAP bugs that exhausted defenders need to prioritize fast.

November offers up a veritable Patch Tuesday feast of vulnerabilities that are more likely to be exploited. In its second four-digit Patch Tuesday release in a row, Microsoft today addressed 1,093 security vulnerabilities, with 63 rated critical, and one zero-day in the mix (CVE-2026-124194, CVSS 6.5) that Microsoft confirmed is under active exploit.

"Most security teams haven't quite recovered from the last month of bumper-to-bumper critical vulnerabilities, emergency patches, and '2shell'-branded everything, and we're yet again at another Patch Tuesday," says Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence at Watchtowr.

"Teams are really starting to feel the strain of working out what actually matters when there is fire after fire every day demanding immediate attention," he adds. "Our advice hasn't changed … start with what you actually have exposed to the Internet, then what's already being exploited in the wild, and only then everything else. Before going into panic mode, check whether you even use the vulnerable component, or meet the prerequisites for exploitation."

Related:OnlyFans Copyright Takedowns Expose Compromised Websites

To that end, security teams should prioritize CVE-2026-124194, and not just because attackers are already targeting it. It's a spoofing vulnerability in Outlook that may not allow code execution, hence its moderate severity rating, but could allow the disclosure of an account’s NTLMv2 hash — and in turn, the target's login.

"To exploit it, an attacker sends a target a malicious Office file and convinces them to open it," explained Satnam Narang, senior staff research engineer at Tenable, in his monthly Patch Tuesday commentary. "If the attack succeeds, the attacker captures the victim's NT LAN Manager v2 (NTLMv2) hash, a value derived from their Windows password. The attacker may be able to relay it to other systems to sign in as the user, or crack it to recover the password."

Security teams should also prioritize a pair of critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities, in Exchange and SharePoint, respectively, that each open targets to any attacker with a low-privilege login.

The first, in Exchange Server (CVE-2026-118207, CVSS 8.8), "belongs in this week's emergency window for every Exchange Server Subscription Edition server you run," Automox researchers warned in their monthly Patch Tuesday bulletin, and "all an attacker needs to start is a low-level login."

It's an improper input validation that could allow an authenticated attacker with low-level access to send the server a specially crafted request and run code with no user interaction.

Related:The Evolving Cybersecurity Lexicon: Vulnerability Discovery to Resilience

"Code on an Exchange server reaches every mailbox it hosts," warned Automox researchers. "And Exchange usually holds broad rights in Active Directory, so the mailboxes are just the start."

Meanwhile, an important-rated flaw (CVE-2026-120002, CVSS 9.9) in SharePoint Server is an elevation of privilege vulnerability that needs quick addressing, according to Automox.

"The flaw is incorrect authorization," the researchers noted. "That 9.9 comes from a changed scope: a successful attack reaches past the vulnerable SharePoint component itself. An attacker who already holds a low-privileged account sends requests over the network and elevates their privileges, with no user interaction required."

Another critical RCE to watch out for, according to Automox, is CVE-2026-110043 (CVSS 8.8/10), a one-click heap-based buffer overflow in Outlook that uses the Preview Pane as an attack vector. A target must select a weaponized email so it displays in the Preview Pane for it to trigger the attacker's code, which runs with that user's permissions.

"Patch internet-facing Exchange and SharePoint servers, and book the Exchange restart now," the Automox researchers advised. "Push the Office update this week, then check the installed build, because a fully patched Windows dashboard says nothing about Office. Rank by score and assessment, not label."

Related:Ivanti ICS Zero-Day Attacks Highlight Vendor Patching Hurdles

Dustin Childs, head of threat awareness at the Zero Day Initiative (ZDI), also identified a Windows Search RCE (CVE-2026-116928, CVSS 9.8) as needing immediate attention.

"We start with Windows Search, which is reached through Exchange Server," he said in his November Patch Tuesday blog post, where he also listed 30 potentially wormable CVEs to patch quickly. "This bug allows an unauthenticated attacker to send an email with a specially crafted attachment that triggers the bug when the server automatically indexes it. The recipient never opens anything. It is a zero-click code execution bug on a high-value target. It’s also a CVSS 9.8 and clearly more severe than any of the nine patches Exchange receives this month."

And finally, Childs pointed to CVE-2026-119958, an RCE bug in Windows Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP).

"This patch addresses a bug that allows an unauthenticated attacker to exploit an out-of-bounds (OOB) write (CWE-787) by sending crafted LDAP calls over the network, with no user interaction," he warned. "Since it runs code in the LDAP service context, it could be quite destructive, especially on Domain Controllers. Test and deploy this one quickly."

Childs also recommended testing and deploying patches for the wormable bugs quickly, especially for network-facing services like DNS, DHCP, LDAP, and Exchange.

While the cornucopia of CVEs this month, especially on the heels of the record October Patch Tuesday, may feel overwhelming, security teams should stick to best practices and not get overwhelmed, advises Tyler Reguly, associate director of security R&D at Fortra.

"I don't know about everyone else, but I'm tired," he says via email, adding that he believes that, eventually, AI will finish turning up old bugs and teams can once again look forward to smaller Patch Tuesday releases. "I can only imagine that if I’m tired, admins and operations teams everywhere are also tired. I believe that we will make it through to the other side, if we prioritize updates and focus on what really matters. The noise is coming at us from all sides, and we need to cut through it and figure out what really matters to the business."

#9819. Transformers Model Integration Contracts

On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:

It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

Our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:

It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:

The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

#9818. Making Agent Harnesses Readable Lets Teams Edit Agent Behavior Without Breaking It

Tencent is a Chinese multinational recognized as one of the world's largest internet, gaming, and social media companies

Tencent is a Chinese multinational recognized as one of the world's largest internet, gaming, and social media companies

Tencent is a Chinese multinational recognized as one of the world's largest internet, gaming, and social media companies

Authors: Ruhan Wang, Yucheng Shi, Zongxia Li, Zhongzhi Li, Yue Yu, Junyao Yang, Kishan Panaganti, Haitao Mi, Dongruo Zhou, Leoweiliang (Tencent Hunyuan)

1]Tencent HY LLM Frontier 2]Indiana University 3]University of Maryland, College Park 4]University of Georgia 5]National University of Singapore \contribution⋆Work done at an internship at Tencent Seattle †Lead Project Collaborator. \headercontentProject link: https://ruhan-wang.github.io/Harness-Handbook/

The capability of a modern AI agent depends not only on its foundation model but also on its harness, which constructs prompts, manages state, invokes tools, and coordinates execution. As models, APIs, execution environments, and application requirements change, the harness must be continually modified to add capabilities or adapt existing behaviors. Before a human developer or coding agent can make such a change, they must identify all code locations that implement the target behavior. This is difficult because production harnesses are often large, tightly coupled, and behaviorally distributed across files, functions, execution stages, and state transitions, whereas modification requests describe what the system should do and repositories are organized by files, functions, and modules. Existing approaches to code search, repository indexing, and long-context processing make code easier to inspect, but they still leave developers and coding agents to recover this mapping themselves. Behavior localization is therefore a central bottleneck in harness evolution. We introduce the Harness Handbook, a behavior-centric representation synthesized automatically from a harness codebase through static program analysis and LLM-assisted behavioral structuring, which organizes implementation knowledge around system behaviors and links each behavior to the corresponding source code. We also introduce Behavior-Guided Progressive Disclosure (BGPD), which guides coding agents from high-level behavior descriptions to relevant implementation details and verifies candidate locations against the current source. We evaluate Harness Handbook on diverse modification requests from two open-source agent harnesses. Handbook-Assisted planning improves behavior localization and edit-plan quality while using fewer planner tokens. The largest gains appear for changes involving scattered implementation sites, rarely executed code paths, and cross-module interactions. These findings indicate that evolving complex agentic systems depends not only on generating edits, but also on determining where those edits should be made.

Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have accelerated the development of agentic systems [1, 2, 3]. These systems extend model capabilities by interacting with tools, APIs, and complex execution environments [4, 5, 6, 7]. Such interactions are not governed by the foundation model alone. They are coordinated by the harness, which constructs prompts, manages state, invokes tools, and controls execution across system components. The harness therefore determines how model capabilities are translated into system behavior. As models, APIs, execution environments, and application requirements evolve, the harness must be adapted accordingly. Harness evolution has consequently become a recurring engineering challenge in modern agent development [8, 9, 10].

In practice, harness evolution requires changes that add capabilities, adapt existing behaviors, or refine execution workflows [11, 12]. Traditionally, human developers make these changes by reading the repository, tracing the relevant behavior, and editing its implementation. Coding agents are increasingly expected to perform the same work from natural-language requests [7, 13, 10, 14]. However, a modification request describes what behavior should change, but it does not identify where that behavior is implemented. Whether the modification is performed by a human developer or a coding agent, the first step is therefore to locate all relevant implementation sites.

Finding every relevant implementation site is difficult in production-scale harnesses [15]. A large harness may span hundreds of functions across many files, with execution logic distributed across stages and connected through shared state. As a result, a single behavior may depend on several nonadjacent implementation sites.

We refer to identifying all implementation sites associated with a behavioral request as behavior localization. In a large and structurally complex harness repository, this task is costly for both human developers and coding agents. Human developers must invest substantial time and effort in building a mental model of the system and tracing behavior across files and execution stages. Coding agents face an additional constraint from limited input context, which prevents them from examining all relevant code at once. They must therefore explore the repository iteratively and may still overlook scattered or rarely executed paths [16, 17].

Existing approaches to repository understanding make codebases easier to explore. Repository maps, code search, code summarization, repository memory, and long-context editing help coding agents find, inspect, and retain relevant code [16, 18, 19, 17, 20]. However, these approaches organize information around files, functions, and modules, whereas a harness modification request describes a desired behavior. They may identify individual pieces of relevant code, but they do not show how those pieces work together to produce the behavior or whether every affected location has been found. The coding agent must still connect these pieces and infer how the requested behavior maps to the underlying implementation. This missing connection is the gap we address.

We address this gap with Harness Handbook, an operational behavior representation that connects system behavior to source code. Instead of organizing implementation knowledge by files and functions, the Handbook organizes it by what the harness does and links each behavior to the code that implements it. Developers and coding agents can therefore identify the relevant behavior first and then navigate directly to the corresponding code. We construct Harness Handbook instances automatically using static program analysis and LLM-assisted behavioral structuring. To evaluate whether the Handbook improves harness modification, we use realistic requests from two open-source agent harnesses and compare Baseline and Handbook-Assisted planning on the same tasks. Handbook-Assisted planning improves behavior localization and edit-plan quality while using fewer planner tokens. These results show that making the connection between behavior and implementation explicit can make harness evolution more accurate and efficient. Our contributions are as follows:

Our work is closely related to three research directions: agent harnesses, harness evolution, and repository representations for coding agents. We briefly review each direction and discuss how Harness Handbook differs from existing approaches by introducing an explicit operational behavior representation for behavior localization.

Recent work has increasingly recognized the agent harness as a first-class software abstraction that extends foundation models into deployable agentic systems. Rather than treating prompting, tool use, memory, and execution logic as implementation details, Code as Agent Harness formalizes the harness as an executable and stateful software layer supporting reasoning, acting, feedback, and coordination [15]. Complementary surveys and engineering efforts further characterize the harness as the runtime infrastructure responsible for prompt construction, state management, tool invocation, control flow, and interactions with external environments [21, 22]. This abstraction has been widely adopted by modern agent frameworks and production systems. Frameworks such as AutoGen and OpenHands expose modular runtime components for agent orchestration, tool execution, environment interaction, and multi-agent collaboration [23, 13]. Industrial systems such as Claude Code and Codex similarly emphasize harness design as a key factor in building reliable long-running coding agents [24, 25]. While these works establish the importance of agent harnesses, they primarily focus on harness construction and system design rather than understanding and evolving existing production-scale harnesses.

As coding agents become increasingly capable, software engineering efforts are gradually shifting from manually implementing functionality to automatically evolving the underlying harness [7, 13]. Recent work has begun to investigate harness engineering, adaptive harness optimization, and automated harness repair [10, 14, 8, 26, 27, 28]. These approaches improve the capability and reliability of agent systems by constructing, adapting, or repairing harness implementations. Our work addresses a complementary problem. Rather than directly modifying harness implementations, we study the prerequisite challenge of harness evolution: behavior localization. Harness Handbook enables developers and coding agents to identify where behavioral changes should be made before reasoning about how to modify the underlying implementation.

Recent work has proposed various representations to improve repository understanding for coding agents, including structural repository representations, repository indexing, repository memory, and natural-language artifacts [29, 18, 19, 30]. These representations improve repository navigation, code retrieval, and editing by organizing implementation knowledge into more accessible forms. However, existing representations remain fundamentally implementation-centric, organizing information around source code, repository structure, or execution infrastructure. They do not explicitly capture how system behaviors emerge across distributed execution stages, functional modules, and shared states. In contrast, Harness Handbook introduces an operational behavior representation that explicitly bridges behavioral requirements and their underlying implementation, enabling behavior localization before repository exploration.

Harness Handbook has three parts for understanding and modifying an agent harness. The representation organizes source around runtime behavior (Section 3.1). The construction pipeline builds this representation from a repository (Section 3.2). The modification workflow uses the handbook to guide code changes and automatically resynchronizes it after every non-empty repository diff (Section 3.3).

Source repositories show where code is stored, but they do not directly show how a runtime behavior unfolds. One behavior may cross several files, execution stages, and shared states. Harness Handbook reorganizes this information around behavior while preserving links to the source. As Figure 1 shows, it contains an L1–L3 document tree \mathcal{D} and a complementary state-register view \mathcal{Z}.

Figure 1: Overview of the Harness Handbook representation. Its three-level hierarchy progresses from a system-level overview to stage-level component overviews and source-backed unit details. The navigation pane provides component and state indexes for direct access and cross-stage tracing.

A reader normally starts at L1 (system overview), which summarizes the architecture, execution model, major stages, and global data flow. The reader then moves to L2 (component overview) for the responsibilities, inputs, outputs, dependencies, and local state of a selected stage. Finally, L3 (unit deep dive) links that stage to source-grounded implementation entries. The complementary view \mathcal{Z} records state relationships that cross stage boundaries.

Two rules keep the representation useful. Progressive disclosure means that readers move from L1 to L3 only when a task requires more detail. Behavior–implementation alignment means that every active L3 locator must still resolve to the current repository. If a locator cannot be revalidated, its entry is frozen and excluded from localization until it is refreshed. The repository therefore remains the authority for implementation details.

Construction builds a handbook from a repository \mathcal{R}. The leaf mode g∈{function,file}, which remains fixed for the lifetime of the handbook, determines the granularity of L3 entries: in function-as-leaf mode each L3 entry covers a whole function or one or more contiguous regions, whereas in file-as-leaf mode each L3 entry represents a file.

The two modes differ in how the stage skeleton is obtained. function-as-leaf starts from a seed skeleton \mathcal{S}_{0} containing the stage and state-register definitions; we use it when a trustworthy seed skeleton that faithfully reflects the harness’s execution stages is available and function-level L3 entries fit the available budget. file-as-leaf instead infers the stage skeleton rather than starting from a seed; we use it when no such seed is available or when function-level organization would exceed the available budget. Both modes produce the representation described in Section 3.1, and Algorithm 2 defines the two branches.

Once g is chosen, construction proceeds in three phases, illustrated for the function-as-leaf branch in Figure 2.

Figure 2: Construction pipeline for Harness Handbook. Static analysis extracts source-linked facts, behavioral organization maps source units to execution stages, and hierarchical synthesis builds the L1–L3 handbook.

After construction, the handbook serves as a behavior-oriented guide for modifying the repository. Given a request q, the workflow uses the handbook \mathcal{H} together with its corresponding repository \mathcal{R}. The leaf mode g remains unchanged throughout the process.

The workflow consists of four steps. First, Behavior-Guided Progressive Disclosure (BGPD) localizes the requested behavior through coarse-to-fine handbook navigation. It progressively reveals relevant information, follows it to candidate source locations, and verifies those locations against the current repository. This process produces a set of source-grounded evidence for planning. Second, the planner converts the evidence into an edit plan \mathcal{P} and action declarations Γ. Third, a separate executor applies \mathcal{P} to the repository. Finally, any non-empty diff triggers handbook resynchronization. Algorithm 1 summarizes the complete workflow.

Algorithm 1 Handbook-Guided Modification with Automatic Resynchronization

Rather than treating all source locations equally, BGPD uses the handbook to identify candidate sites from coarse to fine. It then verifies these sites against the current repository.

Localization begins at the level of execution stages. BGPD first uses L1 and L2 of \mathcal{D} to identify the stages directly relevant to the request. It then follows \mathcal{Z} to include stages coupled through shared state. This step captures mutually dependent stages even when they are structurally distant. Within these stages, BGPD selects the most relevant L3 entries and retrieves their source locators.

BGPD then expands the candidate set along call relations. In function-as-leaf mode, it uses the function-call graph; in file-as-leaf mode, it uses the induced file-call graph. External boundary nodes provide context but are never returned as edit sites.

Up to this point, BGPD operates on the handbook. It then opens the current repository \mathcal{R}, resolves the candidate locators, and retains only the sites that remain relevant to q. This yields the verified evidence \widehat{\mathcal{E}}_{q}. Each record contains a file path, an optional function or region anchor, and a current source excerpt. The handbook thus guides the search, while the repository remains the basis for the edit plan.

The planner converts \widehat{\mathcal{E}}_{q} into an edit plan \mathcal{P}. Each edit block specifies where the change should be made, which source evidence supports it, and what should change. The block records a target file, an optional function or region anchor, a current source excerpt, and the intended change.

For each edit, the planner also records an action declaration containing the target file, optional anchor, and one of three action types: modify, add, or remove. The resulting declarations are collected as Γ=(Γmodify,Γadd,Γremove). A rename is represented as one removal and one addition.

The executor applies \mathcal{P} to \mathcal{R} and produces the updated repository \mathcal{R}^{\prime}. The resulting diff is \Delta=\mathrm{Diff}(\mathcal{R},\mathcal{R}^{\prime}). Because Δ is the factual record of what changed, it drives handbook invalidation. By contrast, Γ is used only to check whether execution followed the plan.

Every non-empty diff Δ triggers Resyncg. Whenever possible, the procedure updates only the affected parts rather than rebuilding the entire handbook.

First, it reparses the changed source, refreshes the program graph, and aligns the old and new versions to identify added, removed, and modified units: in function-as-leaf mode, it matches functions using fingerprints that do not depend on line numbers, and in file-as-leaf mode, it matches files using file-set differences and content hashes.

Second, it determines the update scope. If the stage skeleton \mathcal{S} remains valid, only the affected entries and their enclosing structure are refreshed; otherwise, Algorithm 2 is rerun on \mathcal{R}^{\prime} with the same leaf mode g and stored configuration Θ.

Finally, content that cannot be parsed or classified is handled conservatively: it is frozen or recorded in the coverage record rather than guessed.

Once the update completes, the new pair (\mathcal{R}^{\prime},\mathcal{H}^{\prime}) becomes the starting state for the next request. Within resynchronization, model calls are limited to four semantic steps: classification, file assignment, within-stage organization, and description revision. All other operations are deterministic.

We evaluate Harness Handbook on two open-source agent harnesses around three research questions, describing the experiment setup in Section 4.1 and reporting results in Section 4.2.

Figure 3: Plan quality and planner token usage on Codex and Terminus-2. (a) Overall win rates aggregated across the three judges. (b) Win rates reported separately by GPT-5.5, Opus 4.8, and DeepSeek-V4-Pro. (c) Average number of planner tokens per request; lower values indicate greater efficiency.

Figure 4: Per-judge win rates for three evaluation dimensions. Rows show results for Codex and Terminus-2, while columns show Localization, Scope Control, and Reasoning.

This experiment evaluates localization and edit planning in the modification workflow. Given a natural-language request, a read-only planner built with NexAU [31] and powered by DeepSeek-V4-Pro produces an edit plan \mathcal{P}, and we score the quality of \mathcal{P} directly.

We compare two arms: the Baseline explores the repository directly, whereas the Handbook-Assisted arm locates relevant source code under handbook guidance using a BGPD-consistent navigation policy. Apart from handbook access and navigation, the two arms are identical in requests, model, repository, tool permissions, and decoding settings. The handbook used in the Handbook-Assisted arm is built from the same source.

Plan quality is judged independently by three models: GPT-5.5, Opus 4.8, and DeepSeek-V4-Pro.

Figure 5: Win rates by (a) modification request type and (b) localization difficulty. Q, CF, and SH denote Query, Cross-file, and Search-Hostile requests.

We evaluate Terminus-2 [32] and Codex [25], two open-source agent harnesses that adopt the two leaf modes from Section 3.2: Terminus-2 uses function-as-leaf because it has a reliable seed skeleton, and Codex uses file-as-leaf to infer the hierarchy at repository scale.

Each harness contributes 30 behavior-driven modification requests. They are grouped by type into Query (Q), which modifies existing behavior without revealing target locations; Cross-file (CF), which adds an end-to-end capability spanning files or modules; and Search-Hostile (SH), which places relevant implementations in locations that are hard to recover by keyword search. Requests are also labeled Easy, Medium, or Hard by localization difficulty.

We evaluate plan quality, localization accuracy, and planning cost.

Three independent judges score each plan on three dimensions: Localization (whether the edit sites are accurate), Scope Control (whether the plan stays focused, with less scope bloat), and Reasoning (whether the rationale and supporting evidence are adequate). The weighted score is

on a 0–100 scale, with Localization receiving the largest weight. Handbook-Assisted and Baseline are declared the winner when their scores differ by at least δ=3 points; otherwise the comparison is a tie. The win rate for any reported slice is the number of wins divided by the number of valid judge–request comparisons in that slice.

We compare each predicted edit plan with independent reference plans from Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5, reporting Recall, Precision, F1, and Wrong at file and symbol granularity. Wrong is the share of valid requests with zero overlap against the reference; lower is better.

We report the average number of planner tokens per request, including the handbook and source context consumed during localization and plan construction.

The results show three consistent patterns. Handbook guidance improves plan quality without increasing planner token use. It also helps a weaker planner produce file- and symbol-level predictions that more closely align with reference plans from stronger models. These gains persist across request types and localization difficulty levels. The following subsections examine each finding in turn.

Figure 3 summarizes plan-quality win rates and average planner token use. The Handbook-Assisted arm achieves a higher overall win rate on both harnesses: 38.3% versus 28.3% on Codex and 45.6% versus 26.7% on Terminus-2. The improvement is consistent across all three judges: the gap is 10.0 percentage points for every judge on Codex and ranges from 13.3 to 26.7 points on Terminus-2. Thus, the direction of the result does not depend on any single judge.

Figure 4 decomposes these judgments by dimension. Averaged across the three judges, the Handbook-Assisted arm has higher win rates for Localization, Scope Control, and Reasoning on both harnesses. The respective gains are 12.2, 6.7, and 4.5 points on Terminus-2, and 2.2, 1.1, and 3.3 points on Codex.

The quality gains are accompanied by lower planner token use. Average use falls from 0.102M to 0.089M tokens per Codex request (12.7%) and from 0.058M to 0.053M tokens per Terminus-2 request (8.6%). The simultaneous increase in win rate and decrease in token use shows that the improvement is not explained by a larger planning-token budget.

To assess whether handbook guidance helps a weaker planner approach stronger models in implementation-site localization, we compare its predicted edit sites with independent reference plans from Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 (Table 1).

Table 1: Reference-plan localization metrics (%). Predicted implementation sites are compared against independent reference plans generated by Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 at file and symbol granularity. Metrics are macro-averaged across valid requests; missing outputs and planner errors are excluded. Wrong indicates zero overlap with the reference plan at the reported granularity, so lower values are better.

Across both harnesses, both reference models, and both granularities, all 24 Recall, Precision, and F1 comparisons are higher for the Handbook-Assisted arm, with F1 gains ranging from 5.0 to 18.8 points. Recall and precision increase together, so the improvement is not explained by returning more candidate sites at the expense of focus.

The absolute agreement is highest on Terminus-2. With handbook guidance, the weaker planner reaches file-level F1 scores of 84.7% and 89.3%, and symbol-level scores of 77.1% and 89.3%, against the Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 references, respectively. Precision reaches 93.3% against GPT-5.5 at both granularities. The consistent direction across two independent references shows that the improvement is not specific to one reference model.

Handbook guidance also reduces complete localization failures. Wrong, the share of requests with zero overlap against the reference, never increases and falls by as much as 25.9 points. Thus, the gains include fewer complete misses, not only better overlap among already plausible plans.

Figure 5 stratifies the win-rate results by request type and localization difficulty.

All six harness-by-type comparisons favor the Handbook-Assisted arm, with gains ranging from 16.3 to 33.3 percentage points. Codex improves most on Query requests (26.7 points), whereas Terminus-2 improves most on Search-Hostile requests (33.3 points). Cross-file requests improve by 16.3 and 20.0 points, respectively. The gains therefore span existing-behavior changes, cross-file capabilities, and requests that are difficult to localize through keyword search.

All six harness-by-difficulty comparisons are also positive, ranging from 3.7 to 33.3 points. Codex improves most on Easy requests, whereas Terminus-2 improves most on Medium requests. Because the gains are not monotonic in labeled difficulty, the difficulty label alone does not explain their variation.

This work identifies behavior localization as a central challenge in evolving production-scale agent harnesses and introduces Harness Handbook, a behavior-centric representation that links behavioral descriptions to their distributed source implementations. Harness Handbook reorganizes repository knowledge around runtime behavior, constructs this representation directly from source, and supports modification through behavior-guided progressive disclosure and automatic resynchronization.

Our experiments demonstrate the value of this representation along three dimensions. First, handbook guidance improves plan quality while lowering planning cost: on Codex and Terminus-2, overall win rates rise by 10.0 and 18.9 percentage points, while planner token use falls by 12.7% and 8.6%, respectively. Second, with the handbook a weaker planner matches the implementation-site localization of substantially stronger models, improving all 24 file- and symbol-level Recall, Precision, and F1 comparisons against two independent reference plans. Third, these gains persist across request types and localization difficulty levels. Together, these results indicate that making the relationship between behavior and implementation explicit can improve both modification planning and localization efficiency without requiring a larger planning-token budget.

The utility of Harness Handbook extends beyond modification planning. As a behavior-centric repository representation that stays synchronized with the code, it can also support broader uses such as behavior auditing and regression-impact analysis. Our next step is to apply it to harness self-evolving: using the handbook as a shared behavioral memory, an agent can autonomously close the loop of localization, planning, execution, and resynchronization as the repository evolves, moving the harness toward self-improvement.
