This appendix expands the three construction phases in Section 3.2. The selected leaf mode g and construction configuration Θ stay fixed through construction and later resynchronization. Both modes work from the same static facts but organize them differently: function-as-leaf starts from a trusted seed skeleton \mathcal{S}_{0} and places functions within it, whereas file-as-leaf describes files first and infers the skeleton. Both ultimately produce the same reader-facing handbook—an L1–L3 document tree, a cross-stage state-register view, and source locators for L3 entries. Algorithm 2 summarizes the shared workflow and its mode-specific branches.

Algorithm 2 Harness Handbook Construction

Phase I is a single deterministic analysis shared by both modes. Language-specific adapters parse \mathcal{R} and build the program graph \mathcal{G}. An internal-function node records a function’s qualified name, source file, signature, line range, enclosing class, and observed state access; a boundary node represents a named external target, such as a library function.

The graph keeps a call edge only when the target resolves to an internal function or a named boundary; unresolved calls are written to an audit log rather than assigned a guessed target. Because this phase uses no LLM, every later organization step builds on the same source-grounded facts.

Phase II organizes the facts in \mathcal{G} around execution behavior. Its output is the current stage skeleton \mathcal{S} together with the mode-specific organization state \mathcal{U}_{g}. The two leaf modes differ in both their starting point and their unit of organization.

The function-as-leaf branch (g=function) starts from the seed skeleton \mathcal{S}_{0}, whose stage and state-register declarations initialize \mathcal{S}. On the first pass, it considers every analyzable internal function—that is, every non-synthetic function with usable source locations—and attempts to assign it to one or more stages. The decision uses the function’s source in \mathcal{R}, its callers and callees in \mathcal{G}, the current neighboring assignments, and the stage descriptions. A function is normally placed as a whole. If different parts serve different behavioral roles, it can instead be divided into contiguous source regions and each region placed separately.

A single pass may expose weaknesses in either the assignments or the seed structure, so later rounds review both. Each round first checks whether stages should be added, removed, merged, or split. A structural change is accepted only if the resulting hierarchy is valid and every state-register declaration still refers to an existing stage. Functions affected by an accepted change are then classified again against the revised structure.

After reclassification, a global audit checks whether whole-function placements remain consistent with the surrounding stages, and a separate pass repairs the boundaries of retained regions. Proposed changes must pass model-based review before they are applied. The rounds stop when the stage skeleton and all function or region assignments match the previous round and no function is waiting to be reconsidered. If this state is not reached, the process stops at the organization budget stored in Θ and keeps the remaining gaps explicit.

Every accepted assignment must name a valid stage, use a legal source range, and avoid conflicting actions. Region boundaries are aligned to parser-derived statement spans when possible, and the enclosed source is hashed for later comparison. A boundary that cannot be aligned is marked needs-review; Phase III then decides whether its locator can remain active or must be frozen.

Deterministic cleanup removes a redundant whole-function entry when retained regions already cover that function in the same stage, without disturbing its assignments to other stages. The pipeline then rebuilds cross-stage references, records all functions that remain unmapped, and orders entries within each stage using their purposes and stage-internal calls. If the proposed order is incomplete or contains duplicates, file and line order provides a stable fallback. Together, the finalized memberships, region anchors and hashes, boundary status, within-stage order, and record of unmapped functions constitute \mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{function}}.

The file-as-leaf branch (g=file) uses no seed skeleton (\mathcal{S}_{0}=\emptyset). It first describes each file, then infers \mathcal{S} from those descriptions, and finally organizes the files within each stage.

The pipeline attempts to create one file card for every scanned file, including files from which static analysis extracts no function. A successfully generated card describes the file’s purpose, repository role, and place in the execution lifecycle. When deep card generation is enabled, it also includes a static inventory of function identities, signatures, source ranges, and resolved calls. The model may explain this inventory but cannot change it.

Card generation uses a fixed fallback sequence. A file omitted from a batch is retried individually. If a deep card still fails, the source is retried in function-range chunks. If no prose can be produced, a fallback card is emitted; in deep mode, it retains the graph-derived inventory. The file stays available to later steps but is marked undescribed in the coverage record \mathcal{Y}, so no scanned file is silently dropped.

The pipeline groups cards by directory and combines their descriptions with graph-derived entry points and resolved calls. From this context, it drafts an ordered stage skeleton and attempts to assign each scanned file to exactly one primary stage, using its card description when available. That stage is the file’s home in the handbook. A genuinely cross-cutting file, such as a logging, protocol, type, or configuration utility, may also name one or two secondary stages. Missing assignments and assignments to unknown stages remain visible in \mathcal{Y} rather than being forced into the nearest stage.

The organization variant stored in Θ determines whether the initial result is refined. oneshot, the default, ends after one stage draft and one file-assignment pass. doctor starts from that draft and applies a reviewed refinement loop. agent uses an agent-generated draft followed by the same loop; if the agent cannot produce a valid draft, it falls back to the one-shot draft. A refinement round may add, remove, merge, or split stages, after which only affected or unassigned files are reconsidered. The loop stops when all files are assigned and the skeleton is stable, when neither coverage nor stage balance improves for two consecutive rounds, or when the organization budget is reached. Any files that remain unassigned stay visible in \mathcal{Y}.

For each non-empty stage, the file-call graph first provides a caller-before-callee order. The file cards are then used to refine that order into thematic groups and a readable sequence. A deterministic check removes unknown or duplicate paths and verifies that every assigned file appears exactly once. An omitted file is appended to a fallback group, and a failed organization call falls back to the deterministic flat order. This step can reorder files within a stage but cannot change the stage skeleton. Together, the file cards, stage assignments, within-stage grouping and order, and coverage record \mathcal{Y} constitute \mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{file}}.

Phase III turns (\mathcal{S},\mathcal{U}_{g}) into the document tree \mathcal{D} and state-register view \mathcal{Z}, records reusable generation outputs in the cache \mathcal{B}, and validates both against the repository before packaging.

In both modes, \mathcal{D} contains an L1 system overview, an L2 component overview for each included stage, and source-backed L3 entries. The modes differ in the direction of synthesis:

In function-as-leaf mode, each L1, L2, and L3 node uses a bounded generate–review–revise process. The best draft is retained, and generation stops when it passes the rubric, its score no longer improves, or the generation budget is reached. Independent stages can be processed in parallel, but L3 entries within one stage are generated in sequence so that a later entry can refer to earlier ones.

In file-as-leaf mode, file cards are rendered directly. Each stage and system summary is generated once, with a deterministic fallback if generation fails, and each parent summary waits for its child summaries.

The resulting descriptions and summaries are retained in \mathcal{B} so that unchanged content can be reused during later generation or resynchronization.

In function-as-leaf mode, the register identities and stage relationships in \mathcal{Z} come from the declarations in the current stage skeleton; generation turns these declarations into reader-facing descriptions without inventing new registers. In file-as-leaf mode, the pipeline instead proposes cross-stage registers from the top-level stage summaries and the purposes of data-model files. It repeats this search until two consecutive rounds add nothing or the register budget is reached. References to stages absent from the current structure are removed from the candidate mapping.

The static facts in \mathcal{R} and \mathcal{G} remain authoritative throughout synthesis. The model may add behavioral explanations, but it cannot alter file paths, function identities, signatures, source ranges, or resolved calls. Functions and files that cannot be placed remain explicitly recorded rather than being assigned by guesswork.

Before rendering, the pipeline resolves every L3 locator in \mathcal{D} against \mathcal{R} and compares the located source with the stored evidence. An entry that cannot be revalidated is marked frozen and excluded from localization until it is refreshed, keeping the repository authoritative even when prose is reused from the cache.

After validation, the pipeline renders \mathcal{D} and \mathcal{Z} as the reader-facing view \mathcal{V}. It then packages this view with \mathcal{D}, \mathcal{Z}, the fixed g, and the machine-readable resynchronization state \mathcal{K}_{g} as the handbook \mathcal{H}. Across both modes, \mathcal{K}_{g} retains the fixed leaf mode, program graph, current stage skeleton, mode-specific organization state, construction configuration, and generation cache. The stored configuration Θ records the selected organization or refinement variant, card-detail level, and the budgets for organization, generation, and register extraction where applicable. In function mode, \mathcal{K}_{g} also retains the original seed skeleton \mathcal{S}_{0}; no seed is stored in file mode. Saving \mathcal{H} in this form allows a later code change to refresh affected content without reconstructing unchanged parts of the handbook.

This appendix expands the four-step modification workflow in Section 3.3 using the package contract defined in Appendix A. It follows a request q through BGPD localization, edit planning, execution, and automatic resynchronization. Throughout the workflow, the handbook \mathcal{H} is paired with its matching repository \mathcal{R}, and the stored leaf mode g remains fixed.

BGPD guides a read-only agent through the handbook from coarse to fine. A locator enters the evidence set only after it has been resolved against the current repository.

Navigation begins at L1 and L2 of the document tree \mathcal{D} stored in \mathcal{H}. The agent reads the system overview and stage index to select the execution stages whose behavior matches q. It then follows the state-register view \mathcal{Z} to add stages coupled through shared state. This step recovers behavior that is structurally distant yet mutually dependent, such as a value written in one stage and consumed several stages later.

Within the selected stages, the agent opens the corresponding stage pages and chooses the most relevant L3 entries. Each entry exposes a summary and a source locator. Its body is disclosed only when needed, limiting unnecessary context.

The candidate set is expanded along call relations in the program graph \mathcal{G} retained by the synchronization state \mathcal{K}_{g}. In function-as-leaf mode, expansion follows the function-call graph; in file-as-leaf mode, it follows the induced file-call graph. Named external boundary nodes may supply context but are never returned as edit sites.

All preceding steps operate on \mathcal{H}. The agent then opens \mathcal{R}, resolves each candidate locator, and keeps only the sites that remain relevant to q. The result is the verified evidence \widehat{\mathcal{E}}_{q}. Each record carries a file path, an optional function or region anchor, and a current source excerpt. The handbook guides the search, while the repository remains the authority for the edit plan.

The planner converts \widehat{\mathcal{E}}_{q} into an edit plan \mathcal{P} whose blocks name a target file, an optional anchor, the supporting source excerpt, and the intended change. In our evaluation implementation, each change is expressed as a verbatim old/new pair. For every block, the planner also emits an action declaration. These declarations are collected as Γ=(Γmodify,Γadd,Γremove), with a rename encoded as one removal and one addition.

Execution is delegated to a separate agent that applies \mathcal{P} to \mathcal{R} and produces \mathcal{R}^{\prime}. The factual record of the change is \Delta=\mathrm{Diff}(\mathcal{R},\mathcal{R}^{\prime}).

In our implementation, the executor can read and write files, perform targeted replacements, and search within a file, but it cannot list directories or access a shell. It first applies each verbatim replacement directly and reads the target source only if the replacement fails. It then verifies the touched files and runs a target-specific syntax gate when one is configured. The diff Δ drives handbook invalidation, whereas Γ is used only to check whether execution followed the plan.

Every non-empty Δ automatically invokes Resyncg, which updates only the affected parts of the handbook whenever possible. If Δ=∅, resynchronization is skipped and \mathcal{H}^{\prime}=\mathcal{H}.

The procedure reparses \mathcal{R}^{\prime} and builds the updated program graph \mathcal{G}^{\prime}. It compares \mathcal{G}^{\prime} with the stored graph \mathcal{G}, using Δ to identify added, removed, and modified units.

In function-as-leaf mode, functions are matched using body fingerprints that ignore line numbers. A function that only moves is therefore treated as unchanged, and its locator is shifted by the corresponding line offset. A rename is detected by matching the body below the signature line. In file-as-leaf mode, file-set differences identify added and removed files, while content hashes identify changed files. A path rename therefore appears as one removal and one addition.

Before the observed actions are compared with Γ, a detected function rename is normalized to one removal and one addition. This audit does not alter the Δ-driven invalidation scope.

Resynchronization next checks whether the current stage skeleton \mathcal{S} can accommodate the change. If it remains valid, \mathcal{S}^{\prime}=\mathcal{S} and the affected part of \mathcal{U}_{g} is updated to \mathcal{U}^{\prime}_{g}. In function-as-leaf mode, this update removes deleted memberships, carries forward matched functions, and reclassifies new or changed functions. It also refreshes region anchors, source hashes, within-stage order, and unmapped status. In file-as-leaf mode, it removes obsolete cards and assignments, refreshes cards for new or changed files, assigns new files, reorganizes affected stages, and updates the coverage record \mathcal{Y} to \mathcal{Y}^{\prime}.

The pipeline then regenerates the affected L3 entries, their enclosing L2/L1 ancestors, and dependent state registers. This produces the updated document tree \mathcal{D}^{\prime} and state-register view \mathcal{Z}^{\prime}. Unaffected generation outputs are reused from \mathcal{B}. The updated cache \mathcal{B}^{\prime} retains these reusable entries and adds or replaces the refreshed outputs.

If \mathcal{S} can no longer accommodate the change, Algorithm 2 is rerun on \mathcal{R}^{\prime} with the same leaf mode g and stored configuration Θ. The function-as-leaf branch also reuses the stored seed skeleton \mathcal{S}_{0}. The file-as-leaf branch instead infers a new stage skeleton from the updated repository. During the full rebuild, Phase I produces \mathcal{G}^{\prime}, Phase II produces (\mathcal{S}^{\prime},\mathcal{U}^{\prime}_{g}), and Phase III synthesis produces (\mathcal{D}^{\prime},\mathcal{Z}^{\prime},\mathcal{B}^{\prime}). These components follow the shared validation and packaging contract described below.

Source that cannot be parsed or classified is not guessed. An existing L3 entry whose locator or source hash cannot be revalidated is marked frozen and excluded from localization. In function-as-leaf mode, new or changed functions that cannot be mapped remain explicitly recorded as unmapped in \mathcal{U}^{\prime}_{\mathrm{function}}. If a changed function previously had an active L3 entry, that entry is frozen until classification succeeds. In file-as-leaf mode, files without a valid card or assignment remain in the coverage record \mathcal{Y}^{\prime} within \mathcal{U}^{\prime}_{\mathrm{file}}.

Parsing, hashing, graph construction, locator roll-forward, and coverage checks are deterministic. Model calls are limited to classification, file assignment, within-stage organization, and description revision. These categories also cover a full rebuild. Stage and function decisions count as classification; file-to-stage decisions count as file assignment; and file grouping counts as within-stage organization. Regenerating cards, document nodes, or registers counts as description revision.

Both update paths then follow the packaging contract of Appendix A: the pipeline validates the locators in \mathcal{D}^{\prime} against \mathcal{R}^{\prime} and the stage references in \mathcal{Z}^{\prime} against the updated skeleton, archives \mathcal{G}^{\prime} and (\mathcal{S}^{\prime},\mathcal{U}^{\prime}_{g}) with \mathcal{B}^{\prime}, the fixed g, and Θ (plus \mathcal{S}_{0} in function mode) as \mathcal{K}^{\prime}_{g}, and renders and packages the validated (\mathcal{D}^{\prime},\mathcal{Z}^{\prime}) with \mathcal{K}^{\prime}_{g} as \mathcal{H}^{\prime}. The pair (\mathcal{R}^{\prime},\mathcal{H}^{\prime}) becomes the starting state for the next request.

This appendix details the setup summarized in Section 4.1, where every factor other than handbook access is held fixed across the two arms. It covers the two evaluated harnesses and their Phase I static facts, the modification requests (30 per harness, balanced across request type and localization difficulty), and the two evaluation arms with the SKILL.md manifest that exposes the handbook to the planner. The evaluation metrics are defined in Section 4.1.

We evaluate on two production-style agent harnesses that differ sharply in scale and language.

Following the selection rule in Section 3.2, Terminus-2 uses the function-as-leaf mode, since a reliable seed skeleton is available and function-level entries stay within budget, whereas Codex uses the file-as-leaf mode to infer the hierarchy at repository scale. Table 2 reports the Phase I static facts extracted from each repository together with the resulting handbook structure.

Table 2: Phase I static facts and resulting handbook structure for the two evaluated harnesses. The upper block reports the program graph \mathcal{G} produced by static analysis (Appendix A); the lower block reports the built handbook. For Terminus-2, an L3 entry covers a whole function or one or more contiguous regions of a function; for Codex, an L3 entry corresponds to one file.

The two repositories differ by roughly two orders of magnitude in files, functions, and call edges, which is precisely why they instantiate the two leaf modes.

Each harness contributes 30 behavior-driven modification requests, evenly split into three types. Each request states an intended behavioral change without revealing target locations. The two suites are built from the same behavioral intents but phrased against each harness’s own code, so the same goal lands on different implementation sites in Terminus-2 and Codex.

Table 3 gives a representative request of each type, chosen separately for each harness.

Require marking task_complete three times, with an “are you sure?” re-prompt, before grading.

Raise exec_command’s wait ceiling to 300 000 ms, keeping schema bound and docs in agreement.

An existing behavior must be found and altered; the difficulty is telling the target apart from similar triggers or rules.

Add a background flag that sends keystrokes without capturing output, across the terminal layer and both formats.

Add a per-command env override, threaded through the spawn path across both shell tools.

The capability spans coordinated sites (schema, pipeline, interface, docs) that must all be located together.

Mask secrets before any model snapshot and before writing the session recording.

Mask secrets in every capture path and before writing the on-disk rollout.

Relevant sites hide in mirrored, fallback, or cold paths, so keyword search alone misses some of them.

Table 3: Representative modification requests, chosen separately for each harness, with the localization challenge each type poses.

Requests are additionally labeled Easy, Medium, or Hard by localization difficulty, reflecting whether the change touches one primary behavior, requires coordination across stages and files, or requires discovering dependencies along indirect execution paths. Table 4 gives a representative request at each level for both harnesses.

Strip ANSI escape codes from all captured terminal output.

Add an informational comment field on both shell tools.

One well-defined site: the change maps to a single behavior that a keyword or one file read can pinpoint.

Add a per-command cwd, threaded through execution, the terminal layer, and both formats.

Add an expect output check on both shell tools, annotating the observation on failure.

Coordinated edits: one field or check must be threaded through parsing, execution, and documentation, so several related sites must be found together.

Keep run counters and step history consistent across a mid-run compaction.

Reconcile overlapping fields across exec_command, shell_command, and write_stdin.

Indirect coupling: the sites sit on cold or mirrored paths (post-compaction bookkeeping; parallel tool schemas) that keyword search rarely surfaces.

Table 4: Representative modification requests at each localization-difficulty level, chosen separately for each harness, with the localization challenge each level poses.

Figure 6: The SKILL.md manifest that exposes a handbook to the planner in the Handbook-Assisted arm. The same structure is used in both leaf modes; a leaf is a function in function-as-leaf mode and a file in file-as-leaf mode.

To isolate the effect of the handbook, both arms share the same configuration. The planner is an agent built on NexAU whose underlying LLM is DeepSeek-V4-Pro and whose repository tools are read-only, and both arms use the same requests, repository snapshot, planning contract, and decoding settings. They differ only in whether the handbook is available and in the corresponding localization instructions. The assisting handbook is built from the same repository snapshot used in the evaluation.

The handbook is exposed to the planner as a skill: a SKILL.md manifest tells the planner when and how to consult the handbook, and points to the reference files it navigates. Figure 6 shows this manifest. The same structure is used in both leaf modes; each stage’s leaf cards hold functions in function-as-leaf mode and files in file-as-leaf mode.

This appendix reproduces the main prompts used by the pipeline, organized by the stage in which they are used: those that build the handbook (Appendix D.1), those that localize and plan a change under BGPD (Appendix D.2), and those that score plans with an LLM judge (Appendix D.3). The listings are transcribed from the implementation; per-run fields substituted at runtime are shown as {{...}} or {...} placeholders, and a few non-ASCII characters are rendered in ASCII. Static fields such as qualified names, signatures, source ranges, and call edges are supplied by static analysis and cannot be overwritten by the model.

These prompts drive the construction pipeline of Appendix A: they organize source units into execution stages and synthesize the L1–L3 document tree. Throughout, the statically extracted identities stay fixed and the model only supplies behavioral descriptions.

Used in function-as-leaf Phase II to assign one function to one or more stages, as a whole or as contiguous regions. The rules block below is followed at runtime by the available stage list, the function’s metadata, its caller/callee context with their current stage assignments, and the line-numbered source.

Each proposed assignment is reviewed by a critic against the source, the stage definitions, and caller/callee evidence. The reviewer role block (the “engineer” role) is followed by the task context, the review evidence, and the proposal under review, then the output rules below. Reviewers lean toward APPROVE so the pipeline keeps making progress.

Used in file-as-leaf Phase II to summarize each scanned file. In deep mode—where the file is the handbook’s L3 leaf—the model reads the whole file and writes the card content, while the graph-derived function inventory, line numbers, and call relations are supplied as fixed facts. The deep-mode prompt is:

The two modes synthesize the document tree differently. In function-as-leaf mode, each L1, L2, and L3 node is produced by a bounded actor–critic–reflexion loop: an actor drafts the node from grounded inputs, a critic scores it against a tier-specific rubric and returns actionable findings, and the actor revises until the rubric passes, the score stops improving, or the generation budget is reached. L1 and L2 use long, tier-specific writing guides (a whiteboard-tour style for L1; a problem/main-flow/state-flow/hand-off structure for L2). In file-as-leaf mode, the validated file cards from Appendix D.1 already are the L3 content, and a single-pass rollup produces the L2 component overviews and the L1 system overview.

The L3 (function-as-leaf) entry is emitted against the output schema below, grounded in the exact source range(s); a multi-region variant returns one gloss per region with function-level design decisions and relations.

This is the planner prompt used under BGPD in the Handbook-Assisted arm: it localizes by routing through the handbook and then verifying candidate edit sites against the real source before emitting a self-contained edit plan. Per-harness fields substituted at runtime are shown as {{...}} placeholders.

Plan quality is scored in two steps. The judge first builds a leakage-safe answer key from the request and pristine source, before seeing any plan, and then scores each plan independently against that key.

The judge builds a leakage-safe answer key from the request and pristine source before seeing any plan (hint fields are stripped from the request). This is the Terminus-2 judge; the Codex judge mirrors it, using correct_approach in place of correct_localization.

Each plan is scored independently against the answer key on a 0.0–5.0 scale in 0.5 steps. The three dimensions are combined with weights 0.50 (localization), 0.25 (scope_bloat), and 0.25 (reasoning); scope_bloat is reported as Scope Control, where a higher value means a more focused plan.

This appendix walks through one real Handbook-Assisted run on Terminus-2 (case Q1, DeepSeek-V4-Pro planner), reconstructed from its recorded trace. The run makes concrete the two moves at the heart of BGPD: the planner first routes through the handbook to decide which code sites are in scope, and then verifies each candidate against the live source before writing a plan. Every tool call, source locator, and edit shown below is taken from the run; only whitespace is trimmed.

Change request (Q1: triple completion confirmation)

Right now the model only has to mark task_complete once to reach the “are you sure?” step, then once more to get graded. I want a higher bar: the model must mark completion three consecutive times before we actually grade. The first two times just re-show the terminal state and ask “are you sure you want to submit?”.

The request is Query-type: it revises an existing control-flow rule but names no file or function. The planner’s first task is therefore one of localization — finding every site that implements the completion handshake.

Guided by the SKILL.md policy, the planner reads the handbook top-down, narrowing the scope before opening any source:

SKILL.md → overview.md (L1) → index.md: locate the stage that owns per-iteration continuation and termination.

stages/stage-4.8.md (Completion Gate) and stages/stage-4.7.md (Command Execute): the handshake lives in the gate.

registers.md: the gate is backed by the state register reg-pending-completion, whose read and write sites span the loop, initialization, and per-run reset.

Two facts fall out of this. The change is confined to a single stage (Completion Gate) and a single register; and the register’s write sites reveal that initialization and per-run reset must change together with the loop, not just the obvious return branch.

Because the handbook is a pure location index and stores no source, the planner now opens the real terminus_2.py to confirm each locator. One search_file_content for _pending_completion returns seven occurrences, all in terminus_2.py, so the change stays within one file. Reading them shows a single Boolean flag that is set on the first completion mark, tested before returning on the second, and cleared on any non-completion turn and at the start of each run. This resolves the handshake to three concrete sites:

Terminus2.__init__ (∼L292) — initializes the flag.

Terminus2._reset_per_run_state (∼L1574) — clears it per run.

Terminus2._run_agent_loop (∼L1427–1440, L1552–1559) — the observation branch and the completion gate that read and write it.

With the sites confirmed, the plan replaces the Boolean _pending_completion with an integer counter _completion_confirmations: the loop increments it on each completion mark, resets it on a non-completion turn, and returns for grading only on the third consecutive mark. The change set is four modify actions, all in terminus_2.py — initialization, per-run reset, and the loop’s two branches. The completion gate itself is the representative edit:

#9817. N-able Takes N-central Platform Offline After Discovery of 33 Flaws

The RMM provider also released a hotfix as a recommended mitigation to address public exploits for the alleged zero-days, which allow for attacker takeover.

N-able is navigating a hectic crisis-management situation after the discovery of more than 30 alleged zero-day flaws in its N-central remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform, as well as the disclosure of exploits allowing attackers to execute commands, create administrator accounts, and escalate privileges to root.

Realizing the critical security nature of the situation, N-able took its hosted N-central environments offline earlier this week across the Americas, Europe, and Asia-Pacific after offensive security researcher Sean Bales on Sunday publicly revealed the flaws, collectively called Able2Shell, and subsequently published a series of exploits for them on the GitHub account "Oracle-Security." N-able also advised customers operating on-premises servers to shut them down until further notice.

"N-able sincerely appreciates the patience, flexibility, and partnership our customers have demonstrated throughout this critical security event," the company wrote in a security update Wednesday.

Related:Attackers Crash Claude's 'Office Party' Flaw to Run Malicious Code on Linux

The extraordinary scenario has major repercussions for the entire endpoint management industry, including managed service providers (MSPs) and IT managers who broadly use N-central to monitor, manage, and secure customer devices and networks remotely. The risk for users of vulnerable platforms is significant because of the "extraordinary privileges" these RMM platforms have "because they need them to do their jobs," observes Gene Moody, field chief technology officer (CTO) for autonomous endpoint management provider Action 1.

N-able and other RMM platforms can engage in critical tasks such as script execution, software deployment, and remote administration, often across many thousands of endpoints, Moody says. The downside? "That also makes them incredibly attractive targets," he says.

Indeed, with public exploit code available, attackers are already scanning for vulnerable systems, although no exploitation has yet been observed, N-able reported in a security update Wednesday. The company moved fast to remedy some of the most critical flaws, releasing N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 (build 2026.4.1.26) on Tuesday to address seven CVEs associated with them; the company says it also plans to release further security updates.

Flaws covered by the N-able hotfix are tracked as the following: CVE-2026-125883, which covers multiple XXE vulnerabilities; CVE-2026-125878, which covers multiple OGNL Injection vulnerabilities; CVE-2026-125879, a local privilege escalation flaw; CVE-2026-125880, described as stored XSS via MMS3 patch metadata; and CVE-2026-125881, a schema validation flaw.

Related:Google, Partners Disrupt 1.3 Million-Device-Strong XCPE Botnet

The patch also addresses CVE-2026-125882, which enables remote code execution (RCE) via file repository upload path traversal and was discovered by Nate Fair of Sprocket Security; and CVE-2026-91000, which leads to local privilege escalation via insecure IPC Channels.

Though Bales disclosed 33 separate flaws, some of them are steps in longer exploit chains built from other entries on the same list, according to a report from Tenable's Research Special Operations published today. All in all, Bales listed four exploit chains, with the XXE chain emerging as potentially the most significant of the issues, according to Tenable.

"The researcher describes the XXE chain as credential-free, and N-able's record for CVE-2026-125883 lists no privileges and no user interaction as required," the Tenable team wrote. That chain exploits an unauthenticated XXE flaw in N-central's service-import functionality and can ultimately turn an unauthenticated network request into a complete compromise of a central IT management system.

Indeed, the CyberSec Guru called the credential-free XXE exploit the "centerpiece of the release" and went into detail about how it can be exploited to create an attacker entry point into a system in a blog post updated Tuesday.

Related:'Aokigahara' Stealer Targets 'Developer Keyrings' & AI Assistants

Moreover, once an attacker has compromised a platform, the other vulnerabilities can help expand their access to take over privileged internal sessions and ultimately execute commands on the underlying server, paving the way for cross-customer compromise, according to the post. This scenario is especially concerning for MSPs managing infrastructure on behalf of many organizations.

The recently disclosed flaws are not N-central's first time dealing with a significant security incident. In August 2025, CISA added two N-central vulnerabilities, CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after they were exploited in the wild.

More recently, in August 2026, attackers exploited an authentication-bypass flaw (CVE-2026-18556), subsequently finding a way around N-able's initial fix through a related vulnerability, CVE-2026-18577. The second incident allowed attackers to gain administrative access to vulnerable N-central servers and use the platform's Take Control feature to access managed systems.

The recurrence of vulnerabilities in the same management platform raises broader questions about the security of RMM infrastructure, particularly given the extensive access these tools provide to MSPs and their customers, Moody says.

"I see this as yet another warning in a recent wave of attacks on these platforms; how much authority endpoint management platforms concentrate," he says. "They are essential, but MFA and role-based access cannot contain every platform compromise."

All in all, the situation has created a significant security quagmire for N-able and its customers, who — given that exploitation of the flaws could be imminent — are advised to apply the hotfix where necessary as well as take other immediate mitigation steps.

"The clock is ticking for anyone not taking this seriously," Moody observes, advising that any affected organization "keep on-premises N-central offline until N-able provides safe restoration instructions," while preserving logs before making any changes.

Moreover, they should "review authentication and administration since at least the beginning of November, just because this is exposed does not mean it was not leveraged prior to disclosure," he warns.

Researchers from Huntress also advised organizations affected to review login and authentication activity from Nov. 8 onward for unexpected or unauthorized access, according to a blog post published Monday. If they find it, they should involve incident response, as it could indicate that an attacker conducted RCE or privilege escalation on the server.

Huntress also advised organizations to examine audit logs for secondary indicators of compromise — such as anomalous remote access sessions or new scripts being deployed — since as during previous N-central exploitations, "threat actors were observed 'spraying' downstream environments with unauthorized scripts and tools."

Noting that CISA's March guidance called for least privilege, phishing-resistant MFA and second-administrator approval, Moody says he would go even further this time to protect N-able environments by keeping critical secrets and signing keys outside the platform, and making endpoints independently verify cryptographically signed approval for high-impact operations.

"Stealing a credential, or even controlling the console, should not automatically confer that authority," he says. "A login should no longer be considered enough to authorize protected operations."

#9816. CWE-bench v2: More coverage, quality, and transparency

CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

Our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:

Every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

Results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file (how). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space, where new models are added through a PR on the Space.

Open-weight models, from the dataset page:

All evaluated models, including API-only ones:

Of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

Every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:

-k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:

The tasks are also tagged rl-environment: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.

#9815. Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.

Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.

Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.

A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.

It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.

It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.

There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.

Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:

Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.

We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.

There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.

Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:

"Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance."

"The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart."

The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.

The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.

What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.

Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]]:

The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.

The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.

Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.

Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.

Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.

First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.

The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.

Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).

To measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.

We evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.

Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.

Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.

PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.

The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.

We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.

Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:

#9814. AI Raises the Stakes for Cyber Resilience

An organization's ability to quickly recover from a business disruption will be a competitive advantage in an era of AI-driven threats and business enablement.

Commvault SHIFT — Nashville, Tenn. — Enterprise data recovery practices must evolve from a last-resort response to a continuous operational discipline focused on minimizing business disruption and containing the blast radius of cyber incidents as quickly as possible.

That was the central message at Commvault's SHIFT 2026 conference this week, where security executives highlighted the growing importance of making operational resilience a business priority as AI-driven threats and increasingly autonomous business processes complicate the task of maintaining continuity.

"AI is changing the durable advantage you have built for your business, your brand, your supply chain, your data," said Sanjay Mirchandani, president and CEO of Commvault, in a keynote address at the event. "In the AI era, resilience will be your new competitive advantage."

Two developments are driving the trend. On the threat side, AI is giving attackers the ability to automate and accelerate reconnaissance, exploit development, social engineering, and lateral movement. The trend has compressed the time organizations have to detect and contain an intrusion, Mirchandani and other executives at the event noted.

Related:AI Coding Agents Leak Thousands of Secrets to GitHub

At the same time, enterprises are increasingly embedding AI into business processes, workflows and decision-making, creating new dependencies on data, applications and autonomous systems.

The result is a more complex operating environment in which a disruption can have wider and faster consequences, making the ability to contain incidents, preserve trusted operations and recover without derailing business activity more important than ever.

Attackers these days are able to move faster with a level of automation not available before, noted Rajeev Kottomtharayil, chief products officer at Commvault. Increasingly, recovery is becoming not just about speed but bringing back clean data. "If everything is under attack, how do we know what to trust? The real goal is to have a clean, safe space to recover even if everything around you has been compromised," Kottomtharayil said.

Business innovation and enablement are also driving the need for greater operational resilience. Resilient operations give organizations the confidence to experiment with AI and put it to work across the business, while ensuring they can recover quickly when something goes wrong, said Pragnesh Dave, head of generative AI and ML sales at AWS. "AI is collapsing the amount of time it takes to move from an idea to an outcome," he said during a keynote session. As a result, the competitive advantage will come not simply from how quickly organizations can turn intelligence into action, but from how quickly they can do so while managing the risks and consequences when those actions sometimes prove wrong.

Related:People Are Getting Weird About AI

Dave pointed to the operations model at Amazon that emphasizes the notion of the "door swinging both ways" when teams try to innovate. It is an approach that has enabled teams at Amazon to code more than four times faster than before, he said.

"The question for everyone is not if something is going to break," he said. Rather, it is about what the blast radius is and the time it takes from when something breaks to recovering to the prior trusted state. "If something goes wrong, you need to be able to recover quickly. You should be able to walk back a decision. Think of your recovery time as your innovation project."

Continuous detection and continuous recovery are going to become a baseline requirement for organizations, argued Peter Diamandis, futurist, entrepreneur, and founder and chairman of the XPRIZE Foundation. Over the next few years, he foresees all organizations harnessing AI to migrate a significant workload to the "digital edge" with humans providing judgement, taste, and oversight. "AI gives us all access to capabilities that were once scarce." The qualities that matter the most will be the speed at which an organization can innovate and that requires standing up capabilities to recover quickly when failures do occur, he said during a keynote address.

Related:AI Gave Your Incident Archive a Second Job

At the same time, recovery is not becoming a substitute for prevention, says Bill O'Connell, chief security officer at Commvault. Both are equally important. But "building the highest walls and the deepest moat" to keep threats out alone is no longer enough. Organizations have to equally focus on building an ability to recover quickly to a trusted state regardless of the reason for a disruption and to thoroughly test that ability before it becomes necessary.

The key to keep in mind is that while AI has dramatically accelerated the pace of change it hasn’t altered the need for traditional, and long-familiar, IT governance and controls around their assets, identities, access, authentication and authentication, O'Connell says. "The IT maintenance and housekeeping elements still matter." When organizations have supercharged tools which they are not entirely sure how to govern, they need to make sure those fundamentals remain in place.

In enabling better resilience, organizations should also evaluate what impact third parties could have on their ability to quickly restore operations, O'Connell says. For years, organizations have used questionnaires and external vendor risk-scoring services to try and assess third-party risk. In the AI era, security teams need to go a step further with their most critical suppliers, he adds. O'Connell suggested organizations have their technical architects work with their counterparts at third-party suppliers to understand how critical services are actually configured and what would happen if a provider experienced a breach or a disruption.

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#9813. Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

Say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:

The choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:

All three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

Cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

This is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

On a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

This isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

Parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

Try it on your own documents here. To learn more about Dharma-AI and the specialized models we build, visit dharma-ai.com.

#9812. XAUH: A Swiss Boutique Bets Gold's Next Buyers Will Carry It in a Chat App

Gold has traditionally been associated with physical ownership, secure vaults and long-term wealth preservation. However, blockchain technology is changing how investors access and transfer traditional assets. XAUH, a gold-backed digital token issued by Panama-based Herculis Tokens SA, is attempting to bring physical gold into the everyday digital economy.

Each XAUH token represents one gram of 999.9-fineness physical gold held in Switzerland. Built as an asset-backed payment token, it combines exposure to physical bullion with blockchain-based transferability. The project's broader ambition is to make gold accessible to smaller investors through familiar digital platforms, including Telegram.

XAUH is the first gold-backed token launched by the tokenization arm of Herculis Group, a Swiss investment boutique established in 2009. Its issuing entity, Herculis Tokens SA, focuses on structuring and tokenizing real-world assets (RWAs).

Introduced in 2025, XAUH was originally developed on the JAMTON.NETWORK protocol. The idea emerged from the founder's interest in gold tokenization, which initially began during the 2016 ICO boom. However, the project gained momentum in late 2024 after discussions with the team behind Jamton.

The collaboration offered access to TON and Polkadot ecosystems, along with an opportunity to reach Telegram's large global user base. With millions of users already familiar with cryptocurrency wallets, Telegram presented a potential distribution channel for making tokenized gold more accessible.

Unlike traditional bullion products that may require significant upfront investment, XAUH aims to reach smaller savers, particularly individuals in emerging markets looking for alternatives to local-currency savings.

The project's distribution strategy includes Telegram's AdsGram network and educational content designed for TON wallet users. Its long-term vision extends beyond simply purchasing gold, with plans to support a broader financial ecosystem where users can buy, earn, borrow and spend.

Those interested in the project's gold-backed digital asset model can learn more through the official XAUH website.

XAUH operates within a group structure that Herculis describes as deliberately conservative. Six entities cover different business functions, including asset management, fiduciary administration, gold trading, vaulting and tokenization.

According to the company, its experience in physical bullion operations provides an important foundation for its digital asset offering. Its gold trading and vaulting activities reportedly predate the token by more than a decade.

The company also identifies three custodians responsible for holding bullion: Herculis House, Brink's and Loomis. These arrangements are intended to provide additional separation between the token issuer and the physical assets backing the token.

Insurance and custody arrangements are also central to the company's operating model. Herculis argues that combining traditional bullion infrastructure with blockchain technology can help address some of the trust concerns associated with digital assets.

The central feature of XAUH is its one-to-one relationship with physical gold.

Each token represents one gram of Swiss LBMA 999.9 fine gold. It can also be divided into smaller units of 0.01 gram, allowing users to access fractional gold ownership without purchasing a traditional bullion bar.

Physical redemption is available starting from 500 XAUH, equivalent to 500 grams of gold.

The company identifies four important components of its reserve structure:

●      Gold Refining:  Bullion is refined by PX Precinox SA, an LBMA-listed Swiss refinery.

●      Custody Infrastructure:  Gold reserves are distributed across Herculis House, Brink's and Loomis.

●      Insurance:  Holdings are insured at fair-market value.

●      Proof of Reserves:  On-chain reserve information is made available through Chainlink and can be checked through the XAUH website.

This combination of physical custody and blockchain-based verification is intended to make the token's underlying gold easier to monitor.

For any gold-backed digital asset, the existence of physical reserves is one of the most important factors affecting investor confidence.

Herculis engaged KPMG SA in Switzerland to perform agreed-upon procedures under Swiss Auditing Standard 920. According to its report dated August 28, 2026, KPMG physically compared bullion with 18 PX Precinox certificates, matched selected bar and certificate serial numbers, and reported the presence of 15.5 kilograms of gold.

The reported reserve figure also corresponded with market data published by CoinGecko in September 2026. At that time, the platform reported a circulating and total supply of 15,500 XAUH, equivalent to 15.5 kilograms under the one-token-per-gram structure.

However, token supply and market information can change, making it important for users to consult current market data and reserve disclosures.

Regulatory classification is another important consideration. Herculis states that XAUH is an asset-backed payment token rather than a security under Swiss or Panamanian law. It also states that Herculis Tokens SA is reportable to Panama's Financial Analysis Unit (UAF). These represent the issuer's stated legal position and should not be interpreted as an independent regulatory determination.

Accessibility is not determined by the purchase price alone. Transaction costs, redemption requirements and custody arrangements also influence whether a tokenized asset is practical for everyday users.

Herculis has published the following fee structure for XAUH:

●      Tokenization of existing LBMA bullion:  0.3%.

●      Transfers on the Jamton protocol:  0.02% per transaction.

●      Redemption of one kilogram or more:  1%, plus transportation costs.

●      Redemption at the minimum 500-gram threshold:  3%, plus transportation costs.

●      Recurring custody and storage fees:  None once tokens are minted.

The redemption structure is particularly relevant for investors who want the option of converting digital holdings into physical bullion.

XAUH is also available across multiple blockchain networks and trading venues. CoinGecko identifies token contracts on Ethereum, TRON and TON.

The token trades on centralized exchanges BTSE and Biconomy.com, alongside decentralized platforms such as STON.fi on TON and Uniswap V2 on Ethereum. Fiat and stablecoin on-ramps are available through Wert.io.

Herculis has also outlined plans to collaborate with Frankencoin, a Swiss franc stablecoin, and Morpho, a decentralized lending platform. These partnerships could expand the token's potential role within decentralized finance.

For Herculis, XAUH is intended to be the beginning of a broader real-world asset tokenization strategy.

The company's roadmap includes potential tokenization of silver and fine art already held in Herculis vaults. The founder describes silver as "gold for the poor," highlighting its potential to appeal to buyers who want exposure to precious metals at a lower price point.

The strategy is to reuse the existing infrastructure for custody, insurance and verification rather than build separate systems for every asset category.

This approach reflects a wider shift in financial markets. Major institutions, including BlackRock and JPMorgan, have shown growing interest in tokenized real-world assets, bringing greater attention to blockchain-based representations of traditional financial and physical assets.

For Herculis, tokenized gold could provide an accessible entry point for people who are new to digital finance. Unlike more complex financial products, gold is already familiar to consumers across different markets.

The growth of tokenized assets will depend on more than blockchain technology. Investors will also consider the quality of underlying reserves, transparency of custody arrangements, redemption terms, regulatory clarity and the reliability of trading infrastructure.

XAUH represents one approach to combining established bullion operations with digital asset distribution. By connecting physical gold held in Switzerland with blockchain networks and Telegram's user ecosystem, Herculis is attempting to make gold ownership more flexible and accessible.

Whether this model achieves wider adoption will depend on its ability to maintain reserve transparency, deliver reliable redemption and build user confidence over time.

As the real-world asset sector continues to evolve, projects such as XAUH highlight how traditional assets may find new forms of ownership and distribution in an increasingly digital financial landscape.
